en: This is an interesting text. It appears that there are many original verses interspersed throughout the work, many of which are incomplete. Some of these verses do not conform to [the expected metrical pattern].
This text requires editing regarding its regular meter and certain portions. Some verses appear to be quotations, though I have not yet been able to trace their sources.
I have utilized Haridas Shastri’s edition.
and have not had access to another. It would be worthwhile to seek out other manuscripts in order to produce a truly critical edition.
In the first courtyard, within the interior of the Vṛndāvana palace, is a floor paved with wonderful golden and jeweled tiles that are not dull.
I take refuge in the Blessed Lord Govinda himself, who is seated together with his beloved, his equal. 1.
He who indeed appeared in the land of Gauḍa, desiring to uplift all the people of the Kali age who had fallen into the well of saṃsāra.
I take refuge in that Moon of Consciousness. //2//
Śrīmad-Rādhā-Gadādhara is the most beloved of Śrī Caitanya;
the service of Śrī Govinda, who is the form of His attendants, [is performed by him].
Of these two, Śrī Rūpa is the true vessel for pure love and an ocean of compassion;
may I always have devotion at his pair of lotus feet in Vraja. //3//
To that noble-minded lord of his service,
the sole temple of all auspicious qualities,
the ornament of the lineage of the Varendra Brahmins, his Guru;
I worship incessantly the one known as Śrī Haridāsa. //4//
By whose service the glorious Govinda, the son of Nanda and ocean of compassion, is brought under his influence, and who begs for cooked rice mixed with milk. //5//

Furthermore, it is a great renown that once, during a spring day while wandering in the rāsa-maṇḍala at night, he beheld the wondrous form of the daughter of Śrī Vṛṣabhānu as she moved about, and thereupon fainted at the foot of a tamāla tree.
He was indeed the attendant of that very beloved,
and it is said that he was a certain servant of those two by name;
[he remained] in the service of his own people.
He makes an effort for the sake of entering into wisdom. //6//
Indeed, this daily pastime of the Beloved of Śrīmat-Rādhā’s very life has been graciously revealed by the illustrious Śrī Kṛṣṇa Kavīndra. //7//
By the command of the illustrious Rūpa, and by that most excellent of his trusted disciples, this commentary was composed by me in accordance with their authoritative words. (8)
Now, therefore, apart from that [previous discussion], the worship of the Lord Hari himself in his form as mantra is briefly described here. (9)

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is also written here according to the sequence of each respective topic; however, it has not been included in the middle [of this section] for fear of excessive length of the work. This treatise will be completed with the tenth chapter (*kakṣā*). (10)
Therein, in the first section is the manifestation of the glorious service;
in the second is the discourse on the direct Lord, the illustrious Govinda. 11.
In the third [chapter], concerning middle adolescence, there is a description of the excellence of aesthetic flavor (rasa);
in the fourth, the meaning of the eighteen-syllable mantra is written out. //12//
In the fifth [chapter], the majesty of this land of Vraja is proclaimed;
in the sixth, the auspicious narrative of the manifestation of Śrī Bhānu’s daughter is told. 13.
Indeed, the discourse concerning the essential reality of that glorious Mahāprabhu and his circle of devotees has been proclaimed here, supported by the authority of various scriptures. (14)
In the seventh and eighth [chapters], however, the sublime and true discourse on Śrī Rūpa is proclaimed;
likewise, there is the description of devotion characterized by passion (rāgātmikā) and the path of loving attachment (rāgānugā). //15//
In the ninth section it is to be written, and again in the tenth is written the description of the reality of the glorious Blessed One, such as his various forms of devotion and so forth. //16//
Then, by Śrīmad Rūpa and Sanātana, as well as by Śrīla Paṇḍita Gosvāmī’s disciple Śrī Paramānanda Gosvāmī,
all service was performed at the Śrīmad Vṛndāvana Yoga-pīṭha and other sites for the self-manifested Supreme Lord Śrīmad Govinda-deva, and for Śrīman Madana-gopāla and Gopīnātha.
"By the glorious will of the Lord, their respective services have been manifested in their respective places;
yet manifestation is not counted among the divisions, for it is not separate [from them]. (Laghubhāgavatāmṛta 1.18)
The service of the Blessed Lord Śrīmad-Govinda himself, which yields supreme bliss upon the Yoga-pīṭha in Vṛndāvana, has been made manifest through the compassionate form of Śrī Caitanya’s grace. 17.
The auspicious service of the Lord of Gopāla, which bestows supreme bliss, was manifested right there in the form of Śrī Sanātana. //18//
On the ground beneath a glorious nīpa tree, a place of supreme bliss, cooled by the contact with the waters of the Kālindī and fashioned as if by fire. //19//
The disciple of Rādhā-Gadādhara, named Paramānanda,
has quickly revealed Gopīnātha, that ocean of mercy,
on the auspicious bank of the glorious Yamunā at the foot of the Vaṃśī-banyan tree. (20)

Then, by Śrīla Rūpa and Śrī Sanātana, who understood the true nature of everything, their respective services were offered in their own respective positions within the retinue of Śrī Rādhā and Gadādhara— the primary forms of the original potency— in accordance with the command of Śrīman Mahāprabhu.
Therein also, it was offered by Śrī Rūpa to the venerable Paṇḍita Gosvāmī’s disciple, Premī Kṛṣṇadāsa Gosvāmī. For instance,
the true nature of this Śrīmad Gadādhara is his primary characteristic.
Knowing this, Śrīla Rūpa offered his service unto him. //21//
Śrīla Sanātana Gosvāmī offered this service of Śrī Madana Gopāla Deva to his most intimate disciple, Śrī Kṛṣṇadāsa Brahmacārī;
likewise, it was offered by Śrīmad Rūpa and Advaita.
The illustrious Raghunātha offered the service of the two glorious Kuṇḍas and their surrounding grounds to Śrī Govinda;
likewise, the service of Śrī Gopīnātha was performed by Śrī Paramānanda Gosvāmī.
This is dedicated to Śrī Madhu Paṇḍita Gosvāmī;
moreover, he is indeed the beloved of the three divine forms (vigrahas) of Śrī Hari Dāsa Gosvāmī, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Dāsa Brahmacārī Gosvāmī, and Śrī Madhu.
And it has been elucidated by the learned Gosvāmīs.
Now, [one should meditate upon] the royal lion-throne at the pericarp of the eight-petaled lotus of the Yoga-pīṭha, which is the most excellent limb of Śrī Vṛndāvana.

The sovereign of all forms, the root of all illumination, the Lord Himself— the son of the illustrious King of Vraja, Śrī Govinda-deva, established in the prime of His youth— is indeed the supreme monarch of Śrī Vṛndāvana.

Just as among many princes, although they are equal in their status as princes, yet only one becomes the king worthy of the royal throne because of his preeminence in the Śrutis, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, and so forth; likewise, in the Great Rāsa-dance in Vraja, although there is no difference in their abode (dhāman), [the distinction arises] through the difference in their retinues (parikara) among all the groups (yūtha).
Remaining in the state of the most perfect light (*pūrṇatama-prakāśa*), He Himself shines resplendent by the side of Śrī Rādhikā; likewise,

having manifested the seal of silence (*mauna-mudrā*) and so forth during the pastimes of His embodied form, while remaining there and elsewhere among all the manifestations of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, [He is] that very Śrī Kṛṣṇa Caitanya Mahāprabhu.
Having accepted the service of Śrī Rūpa, who is the manifestation of the form of unsurpassed compassion for the associates, Śrī Govindadeva himself shines forth;
likewise, he is the essence of the mahābhāva that is the core of the hlādinī-śakti.
For it is well known that he alone shines forth together with Śrī Rādhā— who is celebrated in the Śrutis, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, and other texts as the sovereign of Vṛndāvana—
just as it is stated in the Brahma-saṃhitā (5.37):
He who, being the self of all, dwells in Goloka itself by means of those very potencies which are manifested from the essence of bliss and consciousness as His own inherent nature.
I worship that Govinda, the primordial Person.
As it is said in the *Harivaṃśa*:
"I am indeed Indra among the gods, while you have attained the lordship of cows;
therefore, people on earth shall eternally praise you as 'Govinda'."
And in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (10.21.23): Urged by the celestial sages and the mothers of the gods, Indra anointed the descendant of Daśārha and addressed him as "Govinda."

And the commentary says: "By the divine mothers"—having considered that he finds (vindati) the cows, meaning cattle, or the earth, or heaven, by virtue of his state as Indra, they bestowed upon him the name Govinda; that is, they gave him that name.
Furthermore, in that very same tenth book (10.27.28),
it is said: "Having thus consecrated Govinda, the lord of the cows and Gokula,
Śakra, being permitted by him, departed for heaven surrounded by the gods and other celestial beings."
In the *Padyāvalī*—
[He whose] lotus-feet shine at the foot of a wish-fulfilling tree on the banks of the Yamunā, who rejoices in soft songs accompanied by the flute made resonant by his gently swaying fingers;
May the illustrious Lord of Vṛndāvana, the Moon-Kṛṣṇa— who is dense with the abundant nectar-taste of the gentle smiles from the moon-like face of Rādhā— be for your prosperity.
In the Mathurā-khaṇḍa of the Skanda Purāṇa, as spoken by Nārada:
"In that Vṛndāvana is the meritorious abode of Govinda, crowded with His servants; it is there indeed that I dwell."
O King, on this earth, that Vṛndāvana is Govinda-Vaikuṇṭha,
where servants such as Vṛndā and others dwell, ever longing for Govinda.
O protector of the earth, those supreme persons by whom the great abode in Vṛndāvana has been seen have achieved their life's purpose upon this earth.

For it is said thus in the *Śrī-kṛṣṇa-sandarbha*, quoting from the sixth canto of the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam* (6.8.20): "May Keśava protect me with his mace at dawn; may Govinda, holding his flute, protect me during the forenoon."

And as for the commentary: those two are indeed well-known by their respective names as the great seats of yoga (*mahā-yogapīṭha*) at Śrī Mathurā and Vṛndāvana; and they appear there, from the perspective of the worldly people, in the form of glorious images.
And they are manifested through the vision of one's own kin;
therein, the supreme form is well known from the *Brahma-saṃhitā*, the *Govinda-stava*, and other such works.

Therefore, the meaning of the phrase "the commentary on the relevant textual passage" is that these two [verses] are recited here specifically within the section concerning the direct manifestation of the multitude of forms (*sākṣād-rūpa-vṛnda*).
For instance, [this refers to] the excellence of the bliss of the Blessed Lord, Śrīmad Govinda, in his direct manifestation.
For it is said in the Śrī-Caitanya-caritāmṛta (1.8.50–51):
"In Vṛndāvana, there is a desire-tree and a golden mansion..."
Seated upon that great yoga-throne and that jewel-encrusted lion-seat is the very personification of Śrī Govinda, the delighter of the Lord of Vraja,
manifest as the subduer of Manmatha himself.

In every region, various forms of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s manifestations— both ancient and new, made of metal or stone— are seen; some, by virtue of their affection for their devotees, manifest His dynamic power as worshipable deities,
while others appear as ordinary forms of the manifestation of Śrī Nanda-nandana.
If it is argued that "even the Blessed Lord Śrī Govinda-deva himself is like that," [we reply]:
no; for although he appears in such a manner, he is nonetheless being worshipped as an arcā.
The Supreme Distinction (Viśeṣa), who is self-effulgent, is directly the son of the Lord of Vraja himself.

Regarding this, he relates an ancient Puranic story supported by sound reasoning and excellent examples: In the city of Pratiṣṭhāna, which is another name for the City of Love, there was once a certain king.
He had five sons,
and in his old age,
he reflected thus in his mind: "Among my sons, who is capable of protecting the kingdom and other affairs, and who possesses love for me?"
And thinking, "I shall entrust the kingdom and so forth to him," he acted outwardly as if he were dull-witted.
Upon seeing him, all the people were grieved in their hearts;
however, those among his sons who were of wicked conduct rejoiced in their hearts, intending to seize the kingdom and enjoy the pleasures of the senses.
They began their service;
among them, a certain wise and learned man, having even before this won the affection of his parents, engaged himself in their service.
The king, having observed his devotion, entrusted the burden of the kingdom and other responsibilities to him;
however, when the other sons heard of this, they inflicted punishments and the like upon him. [The king] punished them.
Having seen this, all the ministers reported the matter to the king.
Upon hearing it, the king abandoned his feigned nature of dull-wittedness and the like, cast out those other sons, and performed the consecration of that son according to his own will.

Likewise, this Śrī Govindadeva, though He is the manifest prince of Vraja, remains resplendent together with Rādhikā, having assumed a state of silence and other such gestures in order to demonstrate the varying degrees of love among contemporary devotees.
In this regard as well, there are many authorities such as the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas.
Among them, in the Śrī-Gopāla-tāpanī (1.9–10):
The Lord has eyes like beautiful white lotuses, the luster of a cloud, and garments of lightning;
he is two-armed, enriched with the gesture of knowledge (jñāna-mudrā), and adorned with a forest garland. 9.
"Surrounded by cowherds, cowherdesses, and cows, and seated beneath divine trees," and so forth;
"To that one Govinda, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss," and so forth;
"Obeisance, obeisance to Gopāla, to Govardhana, to the beloved of the cowherd folk."
For it is said in the Ūrdhvāmnāya:
"Gopāla alone is Govinda, eternally manifest and unmanifest;
he himself is constantly situated in Vṛndāvana, the seat of Yoga."
Throughout all four ages, this Lord of Śrī Vṛndāvana has been worshipped by Nanda, Gopa, and others, and is also most highly honored by Kṛṣṇa himself.
The stealer of the garments of the women of Vraja, the fulfiller of their vows,
He whose form is the very stone of consciousness and bliss, the all-pervading Lord within the circle of Vraja.
In that regard—
[it is] Candrāvalī’s Durādharṣa, the temple of Rādhā’s good fortune.

For it is stated thus in the Atharvaveda: "In the Gokula forest within the district of Mathurā, in the midst of Vṛndāvana, upon a thousand-petaled lotus, in the center of its sixteen petals, amidst the filaments of its eight petals, Govinda is dark-complexioned, clad in yellow garments, two-armed, with a peacock-feather crown and a flute and staff in his hands; He is both devoid of attributes (nirguṇa) and possessed of attributes (saguṇa), both formless (nirākāra) and possessing form (sākāra)."
"He shines forth, motionless yet active"—
referring to the two sides, Candrāvalī and Rādhā, and so forth. And likewise, it is stated in the Saṃmohana-tantra:
I perpetually bow down to Rādhā, who is accompanied by Govinda, who is devoted to manifold gestures and emotions, and who is the sovereign lady of the seat of yoga.
For it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"There dwells Acyuta in the form of an image, named Govindasvāmin;
sporting with Gandharvas and Apsarases, he rejoices."
For it is said in the Brahma-saṃhitā (5.1):
"Kṛṣṇa is the Supreme Lord, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss;
He is Govinda, without beginning, the beginning of all, and the cause of all causes."
In this verse, Kṛṣṇa is the subject;
elsewhere too, Govinda is the subject, as for example:
"He who in Vraja bore the name Govinda and attained the sovereignty over the cattle."
That very [self] becomes Kṛṣṇa (the Black One) because of drawing (karṣaṇa) the mind, the eyes, and so forth.
And in the Brahma-saṃhitā (5.39):
"Abiding by the regulation of His portions within the forms of Rāma and others, He manifested various incarnations in the worlds; however—"
Kṛṣṇa himself became that Supreme Person; I worship Him, Govinda, the primordial Puruṣa.

And the commentary (*ṭīkā*) says: "I worship that Lord Kṛṣṇa himself, who, while abiding in the forms of Rāma and others by means of the regulation of his *kalās*, performed various incarnations, and who has now become manifest. Thus it is stated in the *Śrī-Gopāla-tāpanī* (1.35, 39–42, 45).
Salutations again and again to Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the Gopīs, Govinda.
For it is thus:
to him who is habituated to playing the flute, who subdues the serpents,
who wanders along the banks of the Yamunā, and who wears swinging earrings;
Salutations again and again to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who wears a garland of lotus-faces— the gopīs— who performs a dance, and who protects those who bow before him.
Salutations to the destroyer of sins, to the upholder of Govardhana,
to the ender of Pūtanā’s life, and to the one who took away the breath of Tṛṇāvarta.
Salutations again and again to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is partless, free from delusion, pure, the enemy of impurity, non-dual, and the Great One.
"O Keśava, remover of afflictions! O Nārāyaṇa, Janārdana!
O Govinda, supreme bliss! O Mādhava, lift me up! and so forth.
In that regard, in the Ūrdhvāmnāya:
"The illustrious Madanagopāla is also well-established right here. Thus it is said.
And in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (10.19.16): "The gopīs experienced supreme bliss upon seeing Govinda."
For thus it is said:
"O friend, Vṛndāvana spreads the fame of the earth because it has obtained the splendor of the lotus feet of the son of Devakī."
"Following Govinda’s flute, the intoxicated peacocks dance, while all other creatures on the mountain ridges cease their activities.
Thus it is said; and likewise in the *Śrī-Govinda-līlāmṛta* (21.28):

This stainless bank known as Śrī-Govindasthala is the seat of union with Kṛṣṇa, the crown jewel of the Vṛndāvana forest; it bows down on all sides toward the Kūrma-pīṭha, resembling its surface in appearance; it is rich with the petals of rows of forest groves, possesses the excellent pericarp of jeweled mansions, and is adorned with golden plantain trees.
She beheld the whorl of its filaments, which resembled a lotus with a thousand petals.
In the Śrī Padma Purāṇa (5.69.79–85), Pārvatī said:
"O Govinda, whose body is fashioned from beauty, what is so wonderful about you?"
Therefore, I wish to hear it; please speak, O treasure-house of compassion.
Īśvara said: In the midst of beautiful Vṛndāvana,
which is adorned with the splendor of charming anklets and decorated with the branches and sprouts of excellent trees extending for many yojanas;
In the center of that, within the abode of Mañjuśrī, is a brilliantly shining yoga-seat,
fashioned as an octagon, enchanting with its manifold radiance.
And above that is an auspicious lion-throne made of ruby-jewels;
upon it is a lotus with its petals vanished, providing a comfortable resting place within its pericarp.
What can be said of the supreme abode of Govinda?
It is his glory, frequented by the throngs of cowherd girls who abide in the mantra of the illustrious Govinda.
I worship Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Vṛndāvana, who possesses divine age and form as a cowherd boy, the sovereign of Vraja with eternal sovereignty, the sole beloved of the children of Vraja.
With youth emerging from childhood and a form wondrous by virtue of His age—
[as stated] in the Varāha-saṃhitā: "O Vasundharā, those who behold Govinda in Vṛndāvana..."
They do not go to the city of Yama; they go to the destination of those who have performed meritorious deeds.

And its commentary says: Now, while describing the greatness of seeing all [other] forms (arcā), he speaks of the greatness of seeing Śrī Govindadeva— the manifest Lord who appears as a particular form of the glorious arcā— manifesting ever more intensely, beginning with the words "In Vṛndāvana."
For it is said thus in the fifth chapter of the Varāha-tantra:
Śrī Varāha said— "That pericarp is the great abode, the imperishable station of Govinda."
There, upon a golden pedestal above, it was adorned with a pavilion of jewels.
For instance:
in the pericarp is Mahālīlā, the essence of whose pastimes is that mountain,
where Kṛṣṇa eternally resides as the Lord of the Vṛndā forest.
Kṛṣṇa has attained the state of Govinda; what is the use of further elaborate speech? This third leaf is beautiful, the most excellent and supreme of all.
For instance: What can be said of the greatness of this place, the beloved abode of Govinda?
There resides Govinda himself, the darling of the multitude of cowherd girls.
He possesses divine age and form in Vraja, increasing the joy of the cowherd women; he is the lord of Vraja with absolute sovereignty, the sole beloved of the children of Vraja.
For instance, the Earth said:
"Kṛṣṇa, known as Govinda, is the supreme cause, higher than the highest."
The eternal Lord of Vṛndāvana, the sole cause of the attributeless [Brahman].
Varāha said:
[He saw] Govinda seated upon a golden throne together with Rādhā,
possessing the previously described form and beauty, exquisitely beautiful and adorned with divine ornaments.

There, upon that very seat of yoga (yoga-pīṭha) covered by a golden lion-throne, is the one who is gracefully bent in three places, beautiful and very tender, the pupil of the eyes of the cowherd girls.
The primary consorts of Kṛṣṇa, such as Lalitā and others, are intensely absorbed in the passionate embrace of his every limb; Rādhikā, however, is the primordial nature (mūla-prakṛti).
Goddess Lalitā is in the center, and Śyāmalā is in the northwest;
the others—Śrī, Madhumatī, Dhanyā, and Hari-priyā—are in the northeast.
Viśākhā is likewise in the east, Śaivyā in the southeast, and thereafter Padmā in the south and Bhadrā in the southwest, situated in their respective order.
At the corner of the Yoga-pīṭha, her dear consort is the beautiful Candrāvalī;
by nature there are eight others who are the primary beloveds of Kṛṣṇa.
The primordial nature is Pradhānā, and Rādhikā is in every way supreme;
there are also Citrarekhā, Vṛndā, Candrā, and Madanasundarī.
Supriyā, Madhumatī, Śaśirekhā, and Haripriyā are likewise situated in the cardinal and intermediate directions in the sequence beginning with Saṃmukhā.
The sixteenth nature is the most excellent, the primary one, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa;
she is Rādhā, the Mistress of Vṛndāvana, while Lalitā is her dear companion.
In the Gautamīya Tantra:
situated upon a jewel-throne resting on a mountain of jewels,
he is located within a golden pavilion standing in the midst of a wish-fulfilling tree.
By this [statement], it should be discerned that this is indeed a qualification of Govinda;
for the *Tāpanī* says: "That one Govinda, whose form is existence-consciousness-bliss (*sac-cid-ānanda*)."
And by the feet of Śrī Jayadeva (Gg 2.19):
"I behold Govinda surrounded by the circle of the beauties of Vraja, and I rejoice."
In the *Śrī Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu* (2.1.43):
"The excellence of His beloveds through His playful love, and the sweetness of His flute and form— these four are declared to be the extraordinary attributes of Govinda."
In that very place (1.2.239):
[I behold her] smiling, with a sidelong glance wide and familiar with three-fold expressions,
the sprout of her lower lip resting upon the flute, radiant with a crescent-shaped ornament.
O friend, if you have a desire for the company of your kinsmen, do not look upon the body of Hari known as Govinda here on the banks of Keśitīrtha.
In the *Śrī-Dānakeli-kaumudī*, Arjuna says: "O Viśākhā!
This is indeed very little."
Listen to this:
it is said that he, who is like a thunderbolt to the ears,
who is capable of overwhelming with the weight of his delusion, and who stands above all, is destroying the entire herd of my dear friend’s cows.
"Whose pride would not be humbled by the great festival of the coronation of Govinda?

Thus, when the manifest pastimes of Śrī Govindadeva—who had previously remained as if embodied in silence through such signs as the seal of silence—were revealed, that seal of silence and so forth was withdrawn. And so it is said:

At the time of manifest pastimes, [the Lord] indeed manifests for the sake of demonstrating His devotion to the devotees. In that regard, as well-known from the *Śrī Gopāla-tāpanī* and other texts, having at times manifested with two arms in silence— (1.10) [He remains] silent.
And it is said, "abounding in mudrās.
Furthermore, in the *Śrī-kṛṣṇa-sandarbha* (153):
"Thus, in that regard, the pastimes (*līlā*) of Śrī Kṛṣṇa are of two kinds: unmanifest (*aprakaṭa-rūpā*) and manifest (*prakaṭa-rūpā*)."
Because it is not manifest to the worldly people of common experience, yet it is manifest to them [who have realized it].
Among these, that which is unmanifest is where Kṛṣṇa resides, concentrated with his three powers.
"The Lord, together with Rukmiṇī, Rāmā, Aniruddha, and Pradyumna" (GTU 2.36). Thus it is stated;

and in the *Śrīgopālatāpanī* and other texts that establish the reality of Mathurā, such as "in palaces with heaps of wish-fulfilling gems and desire-trees" (BhP 5.40); and in the *Brahmasaṃhitā* and other texts that establish the reality of Vṛndāvana.
She is perceived as being slightly distinct from her manifest pastimes;
she is unmixed with worldly beings or worldly objects; and her own continuous flow is devoid of limitations such as beginning, middle, or end, just like time itself.

The manifest form of the Blessed One, characterized by daily activities such as sitting upon the great throne appropriate for the Lord of the Yadavas and the Crown Prince of Vraja, and by pastimes such as tending the cows, is indeed possessed of a glorious physical body that remains indefinable by time and other limiting factors.

Having attained its commencement and completion through the very power of her own will-nature (*icchātmaka-svarūpa-śakti*), she is characterized by birth and other states, permeated by the objects of both the phenomenal (*prāpañcika*) and non-phenomenal (*aprāpañcika*) worlds.
In that regard, she is unmanifest (*aprakaṭā*) in two ways.
It consists of both that which arises from the practice of mantras and that which is spontaneous.
The first is, for example, that which has a fixed location in one or another specific place and consists of meditation on a particular mantra.
As in the introduction to the *Bṛhaddhyānaratnābhiṣeka* and other works in the *Kramadīpikā*:
"Now I shall explain meditation (*dhyāna*), which destroys all sins."

and his mind eager for the pleasure of wandering through the forest where he plays in the lake, that wearer of yellow garments shone resplendent.

Then, the vision of the pair beginning with Pūrṇimāsī: their bodies are like lightning and clouds, they possess clouds and lightning as garments, and their faces are beautiful with naturally gentle smiles.
I joyfully bow down to Rādhā and Mukunda, whose inner hearts are pinned together by the arrows of their mutual sidelong glances.

In this manner, the glorious Sovereign Lady (Īśvarī) should be depicted with her twelve ornaments, sixteen amorous graces (śṛṅgāra), and so forth. Specifically, she is bathed, wearing a garment shimmering with a jewel fastened at the tip of her nose, holding a shuttle, with her hair tied in a braid,
adorned with ear-ornaments, her limbs anointed, her locks blossoming with flowers, wearing a garland, and holding a lotus in her hand.

With her chin blossoming with clusters of drops from her betel-filled mouth, her eyes darkened with collyrium, beautifully adorned, her feet radiant with the red lac of Rādhā, and marked with shimmering forehead-tilakas— she is this one who possesses the sixteen digits of perfection.

The twelve ornaments are as follows: a divine crest-jewel, a pair of earrings fashioned from gold, a girdle, a breast-plate necklace, a discus, a pair of rods, bracelets, a collection of armlets, and finger-rings for the neck-decorations.
With necklaces that imitate stars, armlets and anklets fashioned from jewels,
and the luster of her high toe-rings— Rādhā shines with these ornaments that are like so many suns.
Just as she concealed the collection of ornaments on her limbs with a variegated red undergarment, and upon that, a fine blue cloth called a *daṇḍikā* around her hips;
O Goddess, what need have you to veil all your limbs?
For upon seeing you, the Lord’s heart rejoices within and he attains a state of blossoming joy.
(From the *Vilāpa-kusumāñjali*, 28)—
O beautiful one, let it be known that the bodice which I placed upon your breasts here, indeed with the desire to conceal your dark [complexion], shall not remain forever.
But when her lord Kṛṣṇa suddenly obtained it, he himself immediately concealed that pair of his own treasures, which were dearer to him than even his life.
Her glance steals the beauty of the startled cakorī bird; her face has eclipsed the fame of the moon, the beloved of Rohiṇī, on the full-moon night.
Behold Rādhā, who possesses the glorious beauty of a horse that has shaken off all impurities with its every limb, and who is a vessel of honey for the sweetness [of love].
In this manner, one should provide garments and other items appropriate to the occasion,
as well as various ornaments such as those inlaid with gold, silver, pearls, and gems.
Now, regarding the looking into a mirror for the purpose of seeing [her] tilaka and so forth,
as described in the *Śrī-Govinda-līlāmṛta* (2.104–105) by the venerable Īśvarī:
At that very moment, Sugandhā, the daughter of a barber and an expert in the conventions [of the time], displayed a mirror before him with a jewel fastened upon it.
Beholding her own form and attire, worthy of curiosity regarding Kṛṣṇa’s eyes, reflected in the mirror,
that excellent woman became tremulous with the desire to approach Kṛṣṇa.
For a special costume has as its fruit the sight of one's beloved.
Then, in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (10.35.10), concerning the glorious Lord:
"He whose tilaka is beautiful, who is intoxicated by the honey of the divine-scented tulasī from the forest garland..."
When he, having joined his flute, honored the beloved song sung loudly by the swarms of bees.
Now, the ritual offering of *tulasī* according to the procedure for worship accompanied by songs of devotion (*rāgānugīya*), as follows (10.30.1):
"O auspicious *tulasī*, beloved of Govinda's feet...
and so forth.
"O Mother Tulasī, you who cause joy to the heart of Govinda," and so forth.
Then follows the offering of incense, lamps, and other articles:
"That beautiful incense and lamp [is offered] to the lotus-face of Śrī Govinda."
But those who perceive [the Self] within the erotic sentiment go to the supreme state;
they sport together with him in that world for eternal years.

Then follows the offering of cooked food; then the presentation of betel leaf prepared with camphor and other ingredients; and then the offering of various kinds of grains, side dishes, flour-based cakes, milk pudding, savory juices, sweet syrups, and so forth.
In this very place, Śrī Govinda himself requested *dadhi-kaḍamānna* from Gosvāmī Priya-pūjāri, as follows:
"The *dadhi-kaḍamānna* is sweet; it belongs to me, the worshiper of Govinda’s beloved."
I pay homage to the Blessed One himself, by whom [the Dharma] was brought after being requested.
Then the *ārātrika* [ceremony];
all having gathered together, they behold it.
Now, the fruit of beholding the *ārātrika*:
The work named Śṛṅgārātrika brings happiness to Govinda;
it bestows loving devotion and destroys sins upon being seen.
Now, the procedure for the royal offerings is written:
having offered garments, ornaments, and so forth, the temple attendant likewise returns from there, performs the washing of the temple and other rites, and then presents incense and lamps.
That, however, was the concealment.

Then the cooks— supremely aesthetic, supremely attentive, with restrained senses— prepared various kinds of vegetables, side dishes, flatbreads, cakes, milk puddings, flour preparations, and so forth.
They serve *śikhariṇī*, *rasālā*, and other delicacies— prepared with the six flavors of what is to be licked, sucked, drunk, and chewed— in golden vessels and the like,
as well as fruits and other items appropriate to each respective season.
Thus, on the days of vows such as Ekādaśī,
one should perform the daily preparation of cooked food and other duties for the venerable Lord and the venerable Goddess according to the rules of good conduct;
the priest, with his senses restrained and being attentive, should prepare the materials for the meal according to the prescribed ritual.
According to the view of Rāgānugā, one should perform the rites within ten ghaṭikās and then return home; however, for the *pūjaka*,
there is a formal request (*vijñapti*) regarding the offering of the food oblation (*naivedya*),
as stated by the venerable Śrī Rūpa Gosvāmī Pāda in the *Śrī Padyāvalī* (verse 118):

The satisfaction you derive from milk offered by Śyāmalā, from molasses bestowed by Kamalā, from sweetmeats given by Bhadrā, or from the essence of sweets presented by Sobhābhayā— may I, by the command of Rādhā, experience a hundredfold more of that same satisfaction.
O Hari, since he has perished, direct your delight toward beautiful offerings before you.

In the *Āhnika-kaumudī* (3.9–10): "Just as a cook may eat all kinds of excellent side dishes, arranged in order starting with vegetables, according to her satisfaction, for the sake of pleasing her mother, yet still doing so to delight the mind of the cook herself."
Making them all laugh with pleasant words while eating together, he gladdened them exclusively by saying, "Eat; do not leave anything behind."
He ate some rice with condiments and some condiments with rice;
yet even though it was sufficient, there was no lack of longing for the various side dishes.
And each of those desired families of flour-cakes and varieties of dairy products [was enjoyed].
And always, having offered my greetings to each one individually, I took my meal with them in mutual delight.

The worshipper, having offered cool water and other offerings, should exit the temple and perform his ritual observances (niyama), recitation (japa), and so forth. At the conclusion of the recitation and observances, he should play the bell and other musical instruments according to the rules, enter the sacred temple, and then,
having offered the *ācamana* (sipping water) with Yamunā water scented with *pāṭalā* flowers and other ingredients provided by the water-servant, [he should wipe the deity] with a fine cloth.
One should perform the cleansing of the face and so forth;
then, the bringing of the great prasāda; then, the cleaning of the temple by the temple attendant.
Then follows the offering of betel and other items, as follows: with powdered areca nuts filled with cardamom and cloves,
and with masses of powder perfumed by an abundance of camphor.
With leaves whose sides were finely sliced by a sharp knife, he enjoyed that betel-roll of the excellent *nāgavallī* vine.
Then, during the heat of summer, there is the sprinkling [of water] with various kinds of fragrant water by means of various water-machines and the like;
likewise, there is the recitation of various seed-mantras and so forth consisting of mantra;
and similarly, there is the holding of fragrant substances and other items before [the deity].
In this way, one should arrange garlands, groves, and small huts with fragrant flowers and other such items;
likewise, it should be understood that these are to be prepared as appropriate during the rainy season and other times.
Then, all having gathered together, there is the viewing of the *ārātrika* lamp;
thereafter, the fruit of that viewing, as follows:
This unsurpassed *ārātrika* ceremony, known as the "Royal Service," was performed by the Blessed Lord Śrīmad Govinda himself, who is an ocean of compassion.
O Goddess, the mantra-practitioner who possesses great devotion and beholds this with faith shall obtain all desires and supreme devotion to her two feet.

In this manner, the illustrious Queen offered food, water for rinsing the mouth, betel, and so forth; for it is said: "Rūpamañjarī, the enchanting one, served food to them with affection, just as the goddess Mohinī sequentially offered nectar to the gods."
Then, having prepared a bed and other furnishings upon a jeweled couch, one should cause [the deity] to recline there with a mind endowed with devotion.

Thereafter, the primary officiant of the service, having brought all the Vaiṣṇavas— including those who perform worship, those who cook, and others who possess nothing— should join with them and, with great devotion, [partake of] the *mahā-prasāda*.
"O Lotus-born One, that which was placed before me from time immemorial is now perceived by my eye; I taste the flavor upon the tongue of the servant."
That which, when consumed, pacifies the entire multitude of sins, delights all the senses, turns one away from saṃsāra, and leads once again to the pair of feet of Hari—
that is the grace of Śrī Govinda, and it is indeed the nectar of his feet.
Clothing, sandalwood, garlands, and so forth, as well as a single tulasī leaf, [are offered].

Furthermore, relying upon the qualities of one who is a candidate for the Middle Path (*madhyamādhikārī*), and out of compassion and concern for the preservation of the path of proper discipline (*maryādā-mārga*) among those Vaiṣṇava groups, he gave annual gifts such as clothing to the Lord’s devotees there and, with affection, made them attentive in the service of Śrī Śrī.
Then all the worshippers and others, having performed their respective bodily activities and so forth, should listen to the narrations of the Śrī Bhagavān.
Thereafter, having all performed bathing and other rites, they should remain attentive to their respective services.
[These things] occur.
Then, in the afternoon, having performed the ritual opening of the doors according to rule, there follows the awakening of the venerable Blessed One;
thereafter, the washing of the venerable face and so forth; from that, the consumption of cooked food; and from that, [the offering of] cardamom, cloves, camphor, and other [fragrances].
The offering of refined betel leaves and so forth;
then the offering of incense, lamps, and so forth, as well as the fruit of beholding that [deity].
Those people on earth who behold the incense and the lamp during the rite of awakening go to the supreme, eternal, and imperishable abode of Viṣṇu.
"Having the splendor of a mass of gold," and so forth;
likewise for the illustrious Īśvarī.
Now, the procedure for the three twilight rites (*sandhyā-trika*) is written.
At twilight, one should offer cooked food,
followed by cool water, well-prepared betel leaf, and so forth.
Then follows the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*) and the great auspicious rite (*mahā-maṅgala*).
Then, while the gods, lords of sages, humans, and others look on, there arises the cry of "Victory! Victory! accompanied by songs and instrumental music.
For it is said thus in the *Ānanda-Vṛndāvana-Campū* (13.141):
With his dark, curly locks shimmering like smoke from burning cow-dung, his turban bound askew, wearing a fresh cluster of *kaṅkara* flowers swaying, bearing a peacock feather,
and possessing the beauty of earrings whose lotus-like tips are touched by the rays of the sun; ||| 10 ||
The beauty of his exceedingly soft, perspiring temples was streaked with lines of emerging filaments.
In the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (10.35.15): Having heard that repeatedly, the lords of the gods,
led by Śakra, Śarva, and Parameṣṭhin, [were filled with wonder].
The poets, their minds with necks bowed in contemplation, fell into a state of dejection, as they could not ascertain the truth.
Next, regarding the greatness of the vision [of the Lord]:
those men who behold the face of the god Kṛṣṇa at twilight during the rite of the lamps (sārātrika) go to that supreme, imperishable abode.
Likewise for the illustrious Īśvarī.
Next, the ritual for the night vigil at the bedchamber is described.
Then, the worshipper [prepares] the ornaments such as jewelry and gems.
Having led her out as appropriate for privacy, she should be dressed in a pair of garments and so forth;
likewise with the garlands, ointments, and other items.
Then, there should be a pause for a short moment for the purpose of looking at one another.
Wearing beautiful garments on his hips that put to shame a string of camphor, bearing a lovely red turban upon his excellent head, with eyes half-closed in sleep,
he accepts the auspicious *ārātrika*— which bestows happiness and fulfills all desires.
Govinda always brings you well-being at the end of the night.

Then follows the preparation of the food: the offering of various kinds of cooked grains, side dishes, prepared foods, milk-rice, flour cakes, and so forth—exquisitely sweet, delicious, beautiful to behold, praised by the world, pleasing to oneself, and pleasing to the Blessed One; and therein, the incense and lamps that are to be kept secret.
Then, for the sake of food, there was a waiting for the appointed time;
by whose service the glorious Govinda, the delighter of Nanda, was brought under control.
The ocean of compassion requested rice accompanied by milk.

Thus he previously demonstrated. Therefore, there is sipping of water (ācamana) for the purpose of cleansing the mouth and the offering of a cloth; after that, the bringing of the great grace (mahā-prasāda).
Then, the temple attendant performs the cleaning of the dining area; thereafter, he offers betel leaf and other items prepared with cardamom, cloves, nutmeg, camphor, and so forth;
and then, during the winter, he provides a protective covering.
It is made of silk cloth known as *phalgula*, fashioned like a snowy elephant, obtainable at a great price,
and adorned everywhere with various golden patterns.
Shining from the crown of the head down to the pair of feet.
I praise Govinda, the primordial person, the son of the King of Vraja, who beholds the stainless Lord Agni;
he is of incomparable, ruddy complexion.
When shall I behold Govinda, whose garment is variegated and adorned with many jewels, and whose face is smiling?
Now, regarding the wearing of the *tānīya* in summer:
it is made of fine cloth, divided into three parts,
and adorned with gold thread and pearls at all its borders.
I take refuge in that most cool garment, which shines with the dark deity in its center, is resplendent, and dries up the heat of summer.
Wearing a reddish uṣṇīṣa with its casing folded like a bud, and bearing a variegated dhotī over it;
May Śrī Govinda, with the knot of his bodice slightly loosened, manifest within my heart.
Likewise, there is the cool water of the Yamunā scented with camphor, various fragrant substances, and fans and so forth; then,
at intervals of ten ghaṭikās, the night offering (ārātrika) and the fruit of beholding that [deity].
Those people who behold the most excellent night-vigil of Hari’s reclining are undoubtedly filled with the compassion of Lord Govinda.
Therein, one prepares a bed and so forth upon a jeweled couch.
Beneath that couch, for the purpose of enjoying them at night, one places well-perfumed, cool water, cooked food, betel leaves, and other such items.
Then, having led her out from the temple with a mind full of devotion, he awaits the time for the bed;
and likewise for the illustrious Queen.
For fear of excessive length, it is not written out in detail;
such is the fruit of the vision of the fivefold Ārātrika.
Beginning with the auspicious night-rite and ending at the time of retiring to bed—
those people on earth who thus behold the fivefold ārātrika ceremony [attain prosperity].
Having obtained all their desires— sons, grandsons, and wealth—
they finally go to that supreme abode by the grace of Lord Govinda.
Śrī Vijaya Govinda is like the dark tamāla tree of Śrī Rādhikā-Mādhavikā,
amidst the vines of her circle of friends and the spring breeze.
I praise Govinda, the friend of the lotus, who is the beloved of the lotus-like Rādhā, and whose complexion is like that of a victorious lotus.
Through the victory over Kaṃsa and others who were subject to conception and birth, his victory is proclaimed;
through the conquest of Kāma, who is born of the mind, he is celebrated as Vijaya (the Victorious One).
Because of the verse beginning with "O Indra, you [are the finder] of the cows," he is called Govinda;
therefore, the wise indeed speak of Vijaya-Govinda in this way.
Alternatively, because by worshipping him one conquers enemies such as desire,
the wise declare him to be Vijayagovinda.
I bow to Vijaya-Govinda, whose form is the non-duality of Govinda;
by the mere sight of whom the mind certainly becomes fixed upon Govinda.
Now begins the ancient account of the arrival of Śrī Mahāprabhu in Śrī Vṛndāvana:
I bow down to the venerable Lord of Kāśī, by whose power of affection the divine Caitanya-deva himself came out of grace to the western land.

Now, having heard a certain account from the mouth of a personal associate of Śrī Mahāprabhu, Śrī Mahāprabhu once said to Śrī Kāśīśvara: "You should go to Śrī Vṛndāvana and reside in the presence of Śrīla Rūpa and Sanātana."
Upon hearing that, he was filled with joy and wonder;
then the crest-jewel of the omniscient ones, knowing his heart, spoke again: "The venerable Kṛṣṇa who dwells by the side of the illustrious Jagannātha..."
Bringing forth Vigraha, he himself said, "Know that you are non-different from me, the Blessed One; therefore, serve him. Having heard that, he became silent.
Then, by Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who possessed a fair body, [he was addressed] regarding Vigraha.
The Great Lord also took his meal in one place;
thereafter, Śrī Kāśīśvara prostrated himself like a staff before the fair-complexioned form of Govinda and brought him to Śrī Vṛndāvana.
This very Śrī Mahāprabhu was by the side of Śrī Govinda;
therefore, just as there is a prescribed method of service for Śrī Govinda, so too is there one for Śrī Mahāprabhu.
Likewise, for fear of excessive prolixity, it is not written out in full detail.
[He] has conquered Madana with the splendor of his words,
and with the splendor of his face, he has stripped the lotus and the moon of their pride.
May Gaura-Govinda, whose feet are sheltered by Śrī Rūpa, show mercy toward me.
In this manner, the birth-anniversary festival (janmāṣṭamī) and other rites for Śrī Mahāprabhu should be performed;
likewise, service to the associates (pārṣadas) of Śrī Mahāprabhu should be rendered.
The primary authorities must also observe the lunar days (tithis) in secret.
Now, the majesty of Śrī Vṛndādevī:
Vṛndā, whose feet are worshiped by the eyes and other senses, [resides] in the forest of Vṛndāvana and so forth.
Or by speech, trees and creepers may be made to flower at the wrong time as well as the right time.

I bow to the Goddess who bears upon her crest a crown of beautiful gems and jewels; whose head is adorned with two radiant earrings fashioned of gold and set with enchanting diamonds; and who wears a golden breast-plate, a girdle, exquisite necklaces, armlets, and anklets.
Vṛndā, wearing most beautiful garments, stands beside the glorious Govinda within Vṛndāvana.
The lotus feet of Śrī Vṛndā, uniquely worshiped by all the worlds,
when served with devotion, remove the impurities of the Kali age and grant all desires;
what more need be said here, since even the celestial realms are difficult to attain without worshipping them?
A person who dwells in the place known as Śrīmad-Vṛndāvana is liberated from all sufferings.

Her own vision is recorded here: once at night, while the illustrious Lord Śrī Haridāsa Gosvāmī was asleep, Vṛndā instructed him, saying, "O authorized servant of the worship of Śrī Rādhā-Govinda! You ought to give the food of the great prasāda of my Lord."
Thus [are described] the service, garments, ornaments, and so forth for the illustrious Īśvarī.
Now, the procedure for the annual festival (vārṣikā-yātrā) is written.
He caused a great festival for his devotees, accepting millions of eyes as the supreme offering, and first performed the most auspicious ablution with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*).
As the Lord bore upon his head curd, honey, sugar-candy, clarified butter, and other substances, [the people rejoiced].
Does the Ganges flow with a hundred streams over the mountain of sapphire?
On the fifth day, during the first season of spring, is there the god Govinda Hari,
seeing whom those such as Śiva, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu have immediately attained their goal?
Out of greed for drinking the nectar from his feet, Brahmā and the other gods followed him as he walked;
assuming human forms and attire, they entreated their devotees.
They offered the incomparable tunic to the Lord, and presented the turban and the variegated waist-cloth that he wore.
O friend, behold Śrī Govinda sporting with his own beloved.
Although the spring festival (vasantotsava) proceeds from the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha until the full moon of Phālguna; nevertheless,
[it specifically continues] from the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna until the first day of the dark fortnight of Caitra.
This is the primary rite.
During those five days, the Lord always shines resplendent together with His beloved;
all the deities, beginning with Brahmā, are filled with supreme bliss and tranquility.
Indra and the other gods dwell here together in the circle of Vraja.
Śrī Govindasthala is to be known as the foremost among all the circles of cowherd settlements (vraja-maṇḍala);
there He wears garments and other attire appropriate for the spring season.
His crown is interlaced with divine jewels; he wears earrings, a beautiful necklace, a breast-jewel, a girdle, excellent anklets and bracelets, armlets, and bangles;
he wears a yellow garment consisting of four pieces, and his fingers are adorned with rings set with clusters of gems.
I praise the God who is attended on his left side by his own most beloved consort.
Likewise—
[he gave] a most divine crest-jewel, a crown made of gems, earrings, pearl necklaces, a golden medallion, a girdle, pairs of pins, bracelets, anklets, and rings.
I take refuge in Rādhikā, who dwells on the left side of the moon that is the youth of Vraja, wearing a red silk garment upon her hips and a beautiful blue one equal to its cessation.
Now, the Spring Festival:
they cast about heaps of various kinds of cloth garments, clusters of flowers and balls, and soft water-jars.
With love, the Śrīpūjaka and others sprinkled their own deity with fragrant waters released from the water-machines.
At first, the earth, the heavens, the cardinal directions, and the intermediate points were pervaded by fragrant powders of various colors;
their roots were severed by the downpour of fragrant waters.
Afterwards, he obtained the state of being a Chitracandrapatva.

Then, on the ninth lunar day (Navamī) of Śrī Rāmanavamī, when the five planets were in their exaltations along with Jupiter and the Moon, while the Ascendant was Cancer, and the Sun had entered Aries conjoined with the Vasu (the eighth sign, Scorpio);
All the palāśa fuel-sticks departed from the sacred grove of Ayodhyā, and there appeared a certain singular, unprecedented splendor of immense power.
We pay homage to the Great Lord, the shatterer of Hara’s bow,
the delight of Jānakī’s heart, the sandalwood tree to the Raghu dynasty.
Now, the Swing Festival (Dolotsava): At the foot of the wish-fulfilling tree in the glorious Vṛndāvana forest,
amidst various flowers, within a divine swing;
I remember the glorious Śrī Rādhā and Śrīla Govinda-deva, served by the circles of their devotees.
He was placing flowers upon his incomparable crest and crown, and beautiful diamond earrings upon his ears;
he was wearing a forest garland made of various exquisite blossoms upon his chest,
and another beloved woman was placing upon his knees a garland of bees that she was gently pulling away.
Behold Govindadeva, together with his own most beloved wife named Vaijayantī.
With flowers, there is the arrangement of a series of bowers, the moonlight of flowers,
swings fashioned from various blossoms, and flutes made of clusters of flowers; a flower-forest, both artificial and as if created by the gods, shines forth on all sides.
And thus, on this swing, the God of gods is served by his beloved attendants.
In front, behind, and on the sides, Govinda, joined by his beloved,
was joyfully swung upon a swing by his attendant folk.
On the exceedingly swaying swing, that beloved lady, trembling with fear, embraced her lover;
and with those radiant devotees full of love, she joyfully cried:
"Victory to the Lord of Vṛndāvana! Victory to the Queen of Vṛndāvana!"
Victory to you, O root of joy and bliss, the bestower of all happiness!
Thus Brahmā and the other gods, singing and rejoicing in heaven,
showered down a rain of flowers, each intent upon his own service.
The hosts of lords of sages and lords of gods, including Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, and Cāraṇas, remained concentrated in meditation,
eager to swing that palanquin.
Having attained their own unfitness for that state, they then remained [there].
Those fortunate men on earth and likewise the gods in heaven beheld Govinda joined with his beloved during the festival of the swing.
Now, the Sandalwood Festival (in the Āryā meter):
The third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, which bestows auspiciousness, brings me incomparable joy,
for on that day Śrī Govinda is served with sandalwood paste by His devotees.
I bow to the divine Śrī Gaura-Govinda, whose every limb is anointed with celestial sandalwood paste mixed with the essence of saffron.
Upon his head and turban, and over all his limbs beneath his tunic, he was anointed with a thick paste of camphor, saffron, and liquid sandalwood;
while on all sides a multitude of devotees celebrated with auspicious songs and instrumental music.
May this Gaura-Kṛṣṇa, who has been served, grant you auspiciousness.
Just as,
beginning from the month of Vaiśākha until the end of Āśvina,
devotees should diligently perform the fanning of Lord Hari with fans, mechanical devices, and so forth.
An aspersion with extremely cool water mixed with fragrant sandalwood,
issuing forth from a water-machine, was performed before the Lord.
Now the auspicious fourteenth day of the month of Jyeṣṭha, dedicated to Śrī Nṛsiṃha— the Śrī Nṛsiṃha-Caturdaśī— arrives;
may it gladden my heart through the performance of its great festival rites.
Because the Lord Hari himself— the glorious God Govinda, Nṛsiṃha, and so forth— is non-different from the seed of all incarnations.
On each of those very days of birth, devotees perform a festival according to the prescribed rites, accompanied by the sounds of songs and musical instruments.
Starting from the fourteenth day, with great care, one should offer divine food that has not been stale by name, combined with curd and other such items.
Now follows the ritual for mounting the chariot in the month of Āṣāḍha:

The lunar day of the full moon in Āṣāḍha, specifically the second day of the bright fortnight, bestows auspiciousness; on this day, the preparation for the Lord’s mounting of the chariot brings about divine exhilaration.
In this case, the provisions for the meal must be doubled;
all matters concerning ornaments, dress, and so forth must be conducted with the status of a great king’s son.
"O friend Rādhā, this Tṛtīyā of Śrāvaṇa, which bestows happiness upon you, has arrived;
having commenced the festival of the swing, prepare an incomparable ornament of many jewels."

The twelfth day and the Saubhāgya-Pūrṇimā;

To him who created Brahmā in the beginning, and who protects the Vedas for him— that Kṛṣṇa,
the divine, the light of self-knowledge— [I seek refuge].
One who desires liberation should indeed go for refuge. //166//

Regarding the number of recitations, as stated in the *Gautamīya-tantra* (15.4): "By this hundred-thousand-fold recitation, one beholds Kṛṣṇa with the eye. The phrase "by this" means that the direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of Kṛṣṇa occurs either through his actual form, or in a dream.
This is the meaning.
As for the procedure for the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*) and so forth, it should be consulted in the commentary on the *Śrī-Brahma-saṃhitā*, the *Gopāla-tāpanī*, and the *Hari-bhakti-vilāsa*.
That, however, should be specifically observed at a yoga seat.
Those who recite the five-word mantra of Govinda interspersed with the syllable *oṃ*—
He reveals his own form to them; therefore, one who desires liberation should practice for the sake of perpetual peace. //167//
From him, other five Manavas of Govinda were born among men;
they, beginning with Daśārṇa, were also [born] from those beginning with Saṅkrandana.
They are practiced correctly by those desiring prosperity. //168//
Furthermore, in that very same place it is said:
"That Brahmin, having meditated upon me incessantly and praised me, at the end of a *parārdha* became enlightened;
a person dressed as a cowherd appeared before me."
Then, having been bowed to by me with a devoted heart, He granted me His eighteen-syllable form for the purpose of creation and vanished;
yet my desire to create arose once more.
It appeared,
manifesting within those syllables the form of the future world;
therein, from *ka*, water (*āpaḥ*) [arose].
From *lā* comes the earth;
from *ī* comes fire; from the bindu comes the moon.
From that sound, "arka," I created the syllable *klīm*;
from "kṛṣṇa" came space, and from the subsequent "yat vāyuḥ," I brought forth the fragrant *vidyā*.
From that which followed it—
From that [consciousness], this entire world of women, men, and so forth arises as "this" and "that. //169//
And so it is said in the Gautamiya:
"The head of the Śruti declares that he created the universe from the syllable *klīm*;
from the letter *la* the earth was born, and from the letter *ka* the origin of water. (170)
From the vowel *ī* fire is produced; from the nasal sound (*nāda*) life-force (*āyuḥ*) was born;
from the bindu arises space (*ākāśa*). Thus is the mantra consisting of the elements.
By the word "own" (sva) is meant the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), and by "weapon" (heti) is meant the supreme nature of consciousness (cit-prakṛti).
The arising of their unity is the coloring that covers the face.
For this very reason, the dissolution of the universe occurs within its own source. //171//
Furthermore, that sacred revelation (Śruti) states:

"By the sacrifice of this very [fire], Candra-dhvaja, having realized himself to be free from delusion, repeated the mantra situated within the Oṃkāra; being devoid of attachment, he attained [liberation]."
"The wise always behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu, like an eye stretched across the sky; therefore, one should practice this constantly. (172) and so forth.
In that very same [text], it is stated further on: "From his first foot, the earth arose; from the second, the water-born [lotus];
from the third, fire was produced; and from the fourth, the wind. (173)
From the fifth [stage], there is the arising of the ether; one should practice that very same [state] alone.
Viṣṇu, whose banner is the moon, went to that supreme, imperishable state. //174//
Then there is that very state consisting of five steps, which is pure, stainless, free from sorrow, and in which all attachment to greed and the like has been utterly cast out.
He is Vāsudeva, than whom nothing else exists. //175//

"I, together with the hosts of Maruts, constantly satisfy that one Govinda—the embodiment of existence, consciousness, and bliss—who sits beneath the celestial trees of Vṛndāvana, by means of this five-line supreme hymn. Thus [it is said].
Furthermore, following the hymn:

Whoever should repeat this five-word mantra goes effortlessly to that very state, which is alone, unmoving, swifter than the mind; even the gods did not reach it, for it was ahead of them. Therefore, Kṛṣṇa alone is the supreme deity; one should meditate upon him, taste him, and sacrifice to him—*oṃ tat sat*.
And in the Trailokyasaṃmohana Tantra,
in the very context of the eighteen-syllable mantra spoken by Śrī Mahādeva to the Goddess:
The Lord of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa is the Lord of the World;
his illustrious incarnations exist by the thousands.
Among those incarnations, his childhood was exceedingly rare;
and various superhuman deeds were performed by him.
I shall proclaim the unsurpassed mantra of him by whom everything is established in the power to bestow curses and favors, together with its limbs and subsidiary limbs.
By the mere knowledge of which a person attains omniscience;
one desiring a son obtains a son, and one desiring dharma acquires wealth.
One will undoubtedly become a master of the meaning of all treatises;
one shall bring the three worlds under one's control and agitate the universe.
He shall delude all and he shall slay all enemies; what need is there for much speaking here? One who desires liberation shall attain liberation.
Just as the wish-fulfilling gem is supreme, just as the cow, just as the virtuous wife,
just as the twice-born, and just as the Gaṅgā, so too is this mantra the most excellent.
Just as the Vaiṣṇava scripture is entirely excellent according to its own tradition,
and just as well-refined speech is supreme, so too is this mantra the most excellent.
Moreover,
O Queen of the Gods, for this reason I recite this mantra every day;
there is nothing equal to it in this world of the moving and the unmoving.
Also in the Sanatkumāra-kalpa:
"There are thirty-three types of mantras concerning Gopāla;
among all those mantras, hear this king of mantras."
"O bull among sages, you must preserve with great effort this most serene mantra within the tantra called Sammohana; it is to be kept secret by you."
By means of this king of mantras, Purandara attained the status of Mahendra,
the lord of the gods, which was swiftly bestowed by Viṣṇu.
Formerly, afflicted by misfortune due to the curse of Durvāsas,
he indeed regained the state of being fortunate through that very same [means].
What is the use of saying more here? Even without the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*) and means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), one obtains everything desired through mere recitation (*japa*).
I bow down to that Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇacaitanya, the supreme among gurus,
by taking shelter of whom even an ordinary person may somehow become the highest.

Thus ends the narration of the majesty of the Gopāla-mantra within the exposition on the majesty of mantras in the *Śrī Hari-bhakti-vilāsa*. Regarding the extraction of that mantra, as stated in the *Brahma-saṃhitā* (5.24):
"Kāmaḥ kṛṣṇāya govinda ṅe gopī-jana" (the desire for Kṛṣṇa, O Govinda, [in the dative case] for the sake of the Gopīs).
Your beloved wife will give you the mantra dear to Agni.
The letter *ka* is the power of play (*līlā-śakti*); the letter *la* is the power of the earth (*bhū-śakti*);
the letter *ī* is the power of Śrī; the letter *ma* is the principle (*tattva*).

"Viśiṣṭaḥ" means "to Kṛṣṇa," that is, to the attractor of all minds. Alternatively: "The word *kṛṣi* has the meaning of 'existence' (*sattā*), and *ṇa* has the nature of bliss (*ānanda*). Thus, the Self would be of the nature of happiness because it consists of the bliss of being. So it is said.
"Govindāya," as before.
He is Govinda because he finds (*vindati*) the earth (*gām*), the host of senses (*indriya-kulam*),
and the mountain Govardhana (*gām*).

He is Govinda because he lifts up and protects—that is, preserves—by bestowing supreme sovereignty; to him, "the beloved of the gopīs. Here, "gopī" should be understood as *prakṛti* (primordial nature), and "jana" as the collection of principles (*tattva*).
The substratum of these two is Īśvara by way of pervasion and causality.
Regarding the first meaning, with the word *svāhā*, I thus surrender my self to Him who has become such.
In that regard, the sequence—
In the *Dīpikā* (1.1):
"He whose form is assumed from a fraction of Māyā which itself has been taken from a fraction [of Śiva], and who is delightful with the sound of his flute resonating with musical notes."
May the Beloved of the Gopīs— who, dwelling in the heart, agitates the three worlds— be for your prosperity.
Now, the extraction from the *Saṃmohana-tantra*:
[The seed-syllable] Vāgbhava, conjoined with the power of Madana and united with Indirā, is adorned by the entire vidyā.
This mantra, consisting of the letters of the world (bhuvanārṇa), has been declared;
when recited in reverse order, it accomplishes all desired aims.

Now, regarding the characteristics of mantra-accomplishment: first there should be the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and so forth; after that, the purification of the hands; then the pervasive placement on the fingers and the placement on the heart and other limbs.
Three rhythmic claps (tāla) and the binding of the directions (digbandha), followed by breath control (prāṇāyāma),
meditation (dhyāna), worship (pūjā), and recitation (japa)— this is the procedure in all tantras.
The ritual of placement (nyāsa-vidhi) according to the service of the venerable Vraja-ācārya Śrīmad Rūpa Gosvāmī:
"Obeisances to Saṅkarṣaṇa, the presiding deity of the purification of the elements (bhūta-śuddhi), because He is the presiding controller of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra).
O Lord Saṅkarṣaṇa, be gracious; show Your mercy."

Show mercy so that the five elements, which have transformed into the bodily form of this person, may be immediately purified and become fit for the practice of worship. Now follows the meditation on the Mātṛkās:
She whose hair is adorned with peacock feathers, who bears in her right lotus-hand the Knowledge (Vidyā) in the form of a lotus upon full and lofty breasts,
and who holds a pot of curd in her left hand— she is Tuṅgavidyā.
I praise the form of Mātṛkā, possessing the splendor of the rays of the nectar-moon.

The meditation on Keśava’s fame and so forth: with one arm, broad and radiant at its corners, which steals away their hearts from one another, they lick their eyes while being closely embraced by the other arm, which is covered in profuse horripilation.
I remember Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, fair and dark, wearing a pair of garments that are dark and fair respectively, their intense thirst for love manifesting in amorous play.
Vāsudeva is the presiding deity of that respective month;
he should be known here as slightly dark in complexion.
His meditation is as follows:
It is said:
[He is] dark as a rain cloud, with silken garments like flashing lightning,
smiling, and his hands radiant with a playful lotus.
I bow to the one who has peacock feathers as his crest-ornament, whose nature is that of Vāsudeva, the most beloved of Kṛṣṇa, the little Kṛṣṇa.
The wise one should meditate on the mass of bliss; there,
upon that excellent floor, he should visualize the radiant seat of yoga.
Therefore, those who enjoy the bliss of abiding in that resplendent lotus with its broad pericarp,
possessing a luster that mocks both fresh clouds and gold—
And I meditate upon Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā.
He who does not know the meaning of the mantra, the consciousness of the mantra, and the *yonimudrā*,
will achieve no success even through a hundred million recitations.
Furthermore, regarding the extraction of mantras, as stated in the *Sāradā-tilaka*, there are ten purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*):
birth, life, striking, and likewise confinement;
then consecration, purification, and replenishment once more.
Satiating, inflaming, and concealment—these ten are the purificatory rites of mantras.
Furthermore:
"In that regard, the seven expedients spoken by Śaṅkara should be employed:
causing to wander, obstructing, subjugating, afflicting, nourishing, drying up,"
One should perform [the rite] ending with cremation in due order; then the mantra will become perfected.
Success comes from recitation, success comes from recitation, success comes from recitation—of this there is no doubt.
The mantra practitioner who, with a disciplined mind, recites [the mantra] day and night,
will undoubtedly behold Hari wearing the guise of a cowherd.
Now, the procedure for the abbreviated preliminary practice (khaṇḍa-puraścaraṇa):
beginning from sunrise until the next sunrise,
by reciting the mantra during that interval, one shall become a master of all accomplishments.
In the first [moment], there is arising after arising;
in the second, arising and ceasing;
in the third, for those free from desire, there is the arising of cessation.
In the fourth [chapter], there are eight times eight. Therein, for those who are free from desire, direct realization will occur by this very means;
for those with desire, all goals shall indeed be accomplished—let everyone take hold of devotion.
The wise person who performs this five-limbed preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa) indeed triumphs in the world through knowledge, sovereignty, sons, and other blessings.

Thus, he describes the ritual applications beginning with the "liberation from the morsel" (*grāsād vimukti*) up to the lunar eclipse on the new moon day of the month of Vaiśākha, as well as the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), in the *Bṛhadgautamīya*.
By performing one hundred thousand recitations with this [mantra], one beholds Kṛṣṇa with one's own eyes,
beginning from the first day of the dark fortnight of Vaiśākha until the full moon.
Now he describes the five-day practice:
beginning on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight in either Caitra or Vaiśākha, up until the full moon.
"Two tens of thousands for the *mantra* [of five syllables],
and likewise forty thousand for that of ten syllables"— thus [it is said].
The procedure for the *puraścaraṇa* known as *pūrva-sevā* is stated in the *Kramadīpikā* (5.49–69):
The man who always worships Vāsudeva in the evening attains all desires and, at the end, goes to the supreme goal.
If at night one should worship the son of Devakī, whose mind is overcome by the god of love,
who is weary from the rāsa dance and situated in the midst of the circle of gopīs;
Having fixed a peg into the ground that is broad, well-rounded, smooth, and one span high,
and having stepped upon it with both feet while grasping each other—
This is indeed the Rāsa assembly, with hands [clasped together]. //51//
Inhabited by a breeze that removes all distress, which carries the pollen of withered land-lotuses and is filled with a multitude of spray droplets from the waves;
Upon the vast and stainless banks of the Yamunā. //52//
In [the sky] crowded with hundreds of millions of women whose bodies were shattered by the arrows of Love, the moon—
the lord of stars— made the quarters of the horizon bright, acting like an elephant.
In the expanse where swarms of female bees wander about. //53//
By Vidyādharas, Kinnaras, Siddhas, and gods; by Gandharvas, Bhujaṅgamas, and Cāraṇas—
each accompanied by their consorts and seated upon magnificent celestial palaces.
[They were] standing firm, showering down heaps of beautiful flowers. //54//
In the performance of the rāsa-dance pastimes fashioned by throngs of women with hands joined together,
even a jeweled stake was perceived by Him in this very form.
Having manifested his own divine body in many ways. //55//
For those of clear vision, the two [arms] of each [couple], held between the two beloveds with their arms entwined around them,
were like the fire of the god of love expanding through union with its own source.
Of those whose limbs were ablaze and who were joined with rows of shimmering horripilation. //56//
Whirling with these [ladies] amidst groups of rhythms (*tāla*) and scales (*mūrcchanā*) consisting of the seven most charming notes, distinguished by various melodies (*śruti*). With noble jewels...
Exceedingly beautiful with the tinkling of clearly visible ornaments. //57//
Thus, with its body divided by jewels as if it were a single mass of gold joined together,
it shone with a central pin fashioned of gems.
Seated in the center of a vast, crimson lotus. //58//
A youth with a body having the luster of an *atasī* flower,
with eyes like the petals of a young, crimson lotus,
and shining with beautiful clusters variegated by fresh sprouts;
With her mass of hair bound by a crest of peacock feathers. //59//
Her eyebrows were playful, her face equal to the moon,
the pair of her cheeks adorned with jeweled earrings,
and her lips resembling the blood of a rabbit.
Adorned with various kinds of ornaments made of the king of jewels. //60//
Clad in radiant garments that conceal her hips, she is the dwelling place of exquisite grace,
with the soles of her auspicious feet like fresh coral.
His body shines with a garland swarming with bees. //61//
His chest reddened by the saffron mingled from the embrace of a young woman's breasts, moving with the gait of a bull,
and intent on singing songs inspired by Śiva’s flute.
The sole preceptor of the world, overwhelmed by passion. //62//

One should worship, according to the rule, that which is both with form and formless, unborn, in the most excellent seat first arisen; having first worshipped that, one should perform the ritual service of its limbs.
Then one should worship the couples residing in the [six] flavors. //63//
Upon the sixteen petals [of the lotus], he is accompanied by the group of vowels,
together with the Śaktis, engaged in the supreme rāsa dance,
the delighter of Saramā, joined with his own digits.
Then [he should offer] to those called Mithuna, and to Indra-pāvaka, headed by the sages (vipra). //64//
Thus, having properly worshipped Hari— who is encompassed by fourfold offerings— with a moistened mind,
[he offered] the [milk-rice] with sugar in a cup fashioned of silver.
Let him present well-boiled, excellent milk to him. //65//
When wealth permits, having offered milk mixed with sugar into sixteen separate cups made of bell-metal, one by one to the couples;
Then, one should perform everything just as before. //66//
He who, with a noble heart, constantly worships this ordinance that deludes all the worlds night after night,
is indeed worthy of worship by the entire world.
Having attained incomparable glory, he goes to the infinite. //67//
One should always worship Acyuta with devotion either at night or at the end of the day;
for both of these times yield equal fruit.
He who desires to cross over the ocean of saṃsāra. //68//
Thus, whoever worships the enemy of Madhu in his human form at the three times of day—
for him alone, who is beloved by all classes of beings and whose abode is the daughter of the ocean,
the trees of Dharma, Artha, Kāma, and Mokṣa, which are sought after by the virtuous, reside in the palm of his hand.
The rows of their fruits distill the liquid of the great essence of intense bliss. //69//
He states the application for the daily duties: *Oṃ namaḥ śrī-kṛṣṇāya*.
*Oṃ*, of this *Śrī-Bhagavad-gītā-mālā-mantra*, the Blessed Lord Vedavyāsa is the seer (*ṛṣi*), and the meter is *anuṣṭubh*.
Chanda is Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self; the deity is [Śrī Kṛṣṇa]; the application is in the recitation (*japa*).
"You have grieved for those who should not be grieved for, yet you speak words of wisdom" (2.11)—this is the seed-syllable (*bīja*).
"Renouncing all duties, take refuge in Me alone" (18.66)—this is the power (*śakti*).
"I shall liberate you from all evils; do not grieve"—this is the *kīlaka*.
"They speak of the imperishable *aśvattha* tree as having its roots above and its branches below" (15.1).
Thus ends the armor [mantra].
Its application is in such-and-such a rite.
Weapons do not pierce him; fire does not burn him (2.27).
"Thus, homage to the two thumbs.
"Neither do the waters moisten him, nor does the wind dry him up" (2.27); thus, homage to the two index fingers.
"Indestructible is this, unburnable is this, undissoluble is this, and truly un-dryable" (2.24)—
homage to the two middle [fingers].
"Eternal, omnipresent, stable, immovable, and ancient is this" (2.24).
"Thus, salutation to the two ring fingers.
"Behold my forms, O Pārtha, by the hundreds and by the thousands" (11.5); thus, salutation to the two little fingers.
"Various divine [weapons], of various colors and forms"—
thus, *namaḥ* to the palms and backs of the hands.
"Weapons do not cut him"— thus, *namaḥ* to the heart.
"The waters do not moisten this"—to the head, *svāhā*.
"This is uncuttable, this is unburnable"—to the crest-lock (*śikhā*), *vaṣaṭ*.
"Eternal, omnipresent, immovable"—to the armor (*kavaca*), *hūṃ*.
"Behold my forms, O Pārtha"—*vauṣaṭ* to the three eyes.
"Of various kinds and divine"—*phaṭ* to the weapon (*astra*).
The application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of chanting for the pleasure of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
(The Greatness of the Śrī-Gītā)—
which was personally taught to Pārtha by the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa himself,
and subsequently composed within the Mahābhārata by Vyāsa, the sage of the Purāṇas.
O Mother Bhagavad-gītā, you who shower the nectar of non-duality, consisting of eighteen chapters and hating worldly existence, I meditate upon you.
Homage be to you, O Vyāsa of vast intellect,
whose eyes are like a parasol over a full-blown lotus;
by you, [this work] filled with the oil of the Bhārata was composed.
The lamp consisting of wisdom is ablaze.
Salutations to Kṛṣṇa, who is embraced by his devotees, who holds a whip and a single cane in his hand, who possesses the mudrā of knowledge, and who yields the nectar of the Gītā.
All the Upaniṣads are the cows; the Son of the Cowherd is the milker;
Pārtha is the calf; the wise man is the enjoyer; and the great nectar of the Gītā is the milk.
I bow to Kṛṣṇa, the son of Vasudeva, the divine one who crushes Kaṃsa and Cāṇūra, the supreme bliss of Devakī, and the teacher of the world.
The river has Bhīṣma and Droṇa for its banks, Jayadratha for its waters, Gāndhārī for its blue lotuses, Śalya for its crocodiles, Kṛpa for its current, and Karṇa for its turbulent shores;
it has Aśvatthāman and Vikarṇa for its fearsome sea-monsters, and Duryodhana for its whirlpools.
The ocean-river of the Pāṇḍavas has indeed been crossed; Keśava is the fisherman.

The stainless lotus of the words of Pārāśarya (Vyāsa), intensely fragrant with the scent of the meaning of the Gītā, possessing the filaments of various narratives, awakened by the opening of the story of Hari,
is daily drunk with joy by the bees that are the virtuous in this world.
May this lotus of the Bhārata, which utterly destroys the impurities of the Kali age, lead to our ultimate welfare.
I bow to that Mādhava of supreme bliss, by whose grace he makes the mute eloquent, enables the lame to leap over mountains, and grants success to all.
He whom Brahmā, Varuṇa, Indra, Rudra, and the Maruts praise with divine hymns;
whom the chanters of the Sāmaveda sing with the Vedas, including their limbs, word-for-word recitations, and Upaniṣads;
and whom the yogis behold with minds absorbed in meditation upon Him—[to Him, I bow].
"Salutation to that God, whose limit the hosts of gods and asuras do not know.
(12.13.1) Thus ends the procedure for the ritual placement (*nyāsa*).
[He who is] one whose own nature is afflicted by the defect of wretchedness...
With my mind bewildered regarding dharma, I ask you:
tell me decisively what is best for me; I am your disciple, instruct me who have taken refuge in you. (2.7)
