The number of recitations for the ritual observance is one hundred and eight,
or else one thousand.
He states the practical application:
(The Śrī-Gopāla-Kavaca) Pulastya said:
O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, regarding the armor (*kavaca*) which has been revealed—
Out of compassion, he formerly bestowed upon Brahmā that which is named the Trailokyamaṅgala.
This supreme reality, the most profound secret, which is the embodiment of the Vedic mantra-stream, was told to me by Brahmā; out of great affection, I shall now declare it to you.
By wearing and reciting which, Brahmā perpetually expands the creation;
by wearing and reciting which, Mahālakṣmī protects the three worlds.
Through recitation and retention, Śambhu, the destroyer and knower of all principles,
and Durgā, the mother of the three worlds, [subdue] the great asuras such as Mahiṣa.
Since he slew those arrogant of their boons merely by reciting and retaining [this mantra],
so too may Indra and all others attain complete sovereignty.
One should reveal it to a disciple who is endowed with devotion and to a practitioner;
but likewise, one should not reveal it to a rogue, to the disciple of another, or to a slanderer.
By giving [this] to one devoid of devotion to Hari, to one who delights in the wives of others, to one who is miserly, or to one of evil conduct, one shall meet with death.
For the armor-mantra (kavaca) known as Trailokyamaṅgala, Prajāpati is the seer (ṛṣi),
the meter (chandas) is Gāyatrī, and the deity is Nārāyaṇa himself.
The application [of this mantra] is proclaimed for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
May Oṃ, the Praṇava, protect my head; and may "Namaḥ Nārāyaṇāya" protect my forehead. May the eight-syllable mantra, which bestows devotion and liberation, protect the pair of my eyes.
May *klīṃ*, the single-syllable mantra that deludes all, protect my pair of ears;
*klīṃ kṛṣṇāya* always protects my nose; *govindāya* protects my tongue;
and *gopī-jana-vallabhāya svāhā* protects my face.
May the eighteen-syllable mantra protect the throat; may the ten-syllable mantra protect [the heart];
and may "gopī-jana-vallabhāya svāhā" protect the two arms.
May *klīṃ glauṃ klīṃ* protect my hands; may *klīṃ kṛṣṇāya* protect my limbs;
may the venerable Bhuvaneśa protect my heart; and may *klīṃ kṛṣṇāya klīṃ* protect my breasts.
May *gopālāya agnijāyām* always protect that pair of bellies;
may the supreme mantra *klīṃ kṛṣṇāya* always protect the pair of sides. May the two mantras *kṛṣṇa* and *govinda*, preceded by *smara* and joined with the dative suffix *ṅe*, be the protectors.
May the eighteen-syllable mantra protect the navel; the two-syllable mantra "Kṛṣṇa" protects the back;
"klīṃ kṛṣṇakaṅkālaṃ klīṃ kṛṣṇāya svāhā" protects the thighs;
and "śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ" may it constantly protect the two legs.
May the seven-syllabled protect the thighs; may the thirteen-syllabled guard [them].
Śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ, followed by the words *padataḥ* and *gopī-jana*, then *vallabhāya svāhā*; may this ten-syllable mantra—klīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ—protect [me].
May the ten-syllable mantra *hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ* always protect the knees;
may the thirteen-syllable mantra, bearing the discus and other weapons, protect the shanks;
and may the eighteen-syllable and twenty-syllable mantras, preceded by *hrīṃ* and *śrīṃ*, protect [the rest].
May the powerful Lord of Dvārakā always protect all my limbs;
salutations to the Blessed One, Vāsudeva, who is the Supreme Goal.
May this twelve-syllable mantra beginning with *tārā* protect me always in the east;
likewise, the ten-syllable mantra *śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ*, and the sixteen-syllable mantra *klīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ*.
May Viṣṇu, armed with the mace and other weapons, protect me in the direction of Agni;
may the ten-syllable mantra "hrīṃ śrīṃ" always protect me in the south.
"Tāraṃ namo bhagavate rukmiṇī-vallabhāya ca svāhā"— may this sixteen-syllable mantra protect [me] in the southwestern direction.
The mantra *klīṃ* followed by the word *hṛṣīkeśāya namaḥ*—
this eighteen-syllable mantra ending with *kāma* (klīṃ)— may it always protect me in the northwest.
*Śrīṃ*, *māyā* (hrīṃ), *kṛṣṇāya*, *hrīṃ*, and *govindāya*— this mantra of twenty-two syllables [ending with *namaḥ*] [protects me in the north].
May Viṣṇu, whose self consists of twelve syllables, always protect me in the north.
Vāgbhava, Kāmabīja, Kṛṣṇāya, Hrīṃ, Govindāya, and after that.
"Śrīṃ gopī-jana-vallabhāya svāhā"—
may this thirty-two-syllable mantra protect me eternally in the northeast;
[the mantra] that [describes Him] performing divine dance in the midst of the hoods of Kālīya.
I bow to the son of Devakī, the eternal King, the infallible Acyuta.
May this thirty-two-syllable mantra also protect me from all sides; may it protect me from below.
"Oṃ klīṃ, let us know Kāmadeva; let us meditate upon him whose arrows are flowers;
may that Anaṅga inspire us"—may this [mantra] protect me from above.
"O Brahmin, I have thus related to you the armor named *Trailokyamaṅgala*, which is of the nature of Brahman and embodies all mantras and medicinal herbs;
it was heard from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa by the sovereign lords headed by Brahmā and Īśvara."
Out of affection for you, I have told this; it must not be spoken to anyone.
If one should recite the armor-armor (*kavaca*) after duly prostrating to the Guru, [the goal will be attained].
Whether once, twice, thrice, or according to his knowledge, he too consists of all austerity;
he is undoubtedly a teacher in all mantras whatsoever.

One hundred and eight recitations are prescribed as the procedure for its preliminary service (*puraścaryā*). Having performed the fire-oblations and other rites with a tenth part of that number, one will certainly achieve success,
provided that the powerful one himself becomes the armor of accomplishment.
For one whose mind is purified by faith, the accomplishment of mantras shall occur through the performance of the preliminary rites (puraścaryā); Lakṣmī and Vāṇī shall dwell in his mouth.
Having offered eight handfuls of flowers, one should recite [the mantra] once with the root mantra;
one shall obtain the fruit of ten thousand years of worship.
If one writes [this] on birch bark, places it in a pill within gold, and wears it on the neck or the right arm, he too is Viṣṇu; of this there is no doubt.
Thousands of horse sacrifices, hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices,
and whatever great gifts there may be— O Bhava, all these are equal to a single circumambulation.
Those [other means] do not equal even a fraction of this, since it grants liberation by being recited but once;
by the grace of this armor-mantra, a man becomes liberated while living.
It truly agitates the three worlds, and one becomes a conqueror of the three worlds.
If a person should worship Puruṣottama without knowing this armor (*kavaca*),
the mantra will not grant success even if recited ten million times.
Thus ends the Śrī-Gopāla-Kavaca, named Trailokyamaṅgala, in the ninth chapter of the Śrī-Nārada-Pañcarātra within the Sanatkumāra-Tantra.
Now follows the procedure for the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*), and so forth.

Śrī-Viṣṇu, Viṣṇu, obeisances unto Him! On such-and-such a month, in such-and-such a fortnight, on such-and-such a lunar day of the sun, I, the servant named so-and-so of such-and-such a lineage, desiring the perfection of the Trailokyasaṃmohana-kavaca for the deity Śrī-Kṛṣṇa as described in the Trailokyasaṃmohana-tantra— tat.

I shall perform the *puraścaraṇa* consisting of one hundred and eight recitations of the *kavaca*, followed by a fire-oblation (*homa*) of one-tenth that number, an offering of libations (*tarpaṇa*) of one-tenth that number, a consecration (*abhiṣeka*) of one-tenth that number, and the feeding of Brahmins of one-tenth that number;
the accomplishment of the rite shall be achieved in a single day.
The ritual application (*prayoga*) is according to the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavata*, beginning with the first auspicious invocation (*maṅgalācaraṇa*) of the *Śrī-Bhāgavata* for the *Daśārṇa-mantra*.
[The following section is perhaps not in all manuscripts.]
Now, he states the result of seeing the shadow-person:
"In the forenoon, a pure man, placing the solar disc behind his back,
should gaze without blinking at his own shadow above the throat."
In that case, if one sees a person arisen from the shadow,
complete with all limbs and auspicious, it is recorded as the limit for the duration of the rains.
When the unseen reaches the heart, the man [is liberated] from the hand and the ear.
The [number of days] for the soul [to depart] are respectively seven, twelve, ten, one, three, two, and one;
if it is not seen in the head, it remains for six months; if in the heart with the aperture, for seven [days].
One should not speak of this great and divine knowledge to a wicked disciple.
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Daivajña-cintāmaṇi* composed by the venerable Kaṃsāri Miśra Yaśodhara.
[The following are] the Gāyatrī mantra, the mantra of Rādhā, and that which is supreme for Kṛṣṇa.
The excellent mantra of the Great Lord, likewise the name of Hari,
and mental service— these are known as the five purificatory rites (saṃskāras).
Salutation to Saṅkarṣaṇa, the presiding deity of the purification of the elements (*bhūta-śuddhi*), because he is the presiding lord over the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*).
O Saṅkarṣaṇa, may [this body] be purified immediately; please act so that it may be fit for spiritual practice (*upāsana*). Now follows the meditation on the Mātṛkās:
She whose hair is adorned with peacock feathers, who holds in her right lotus-hand the Knowledge (Vidyā) in the form of a lotus,
and who bears a pot of curd in her left hand— she is the goddess of lofty learning, possessing full and elevated breasts.
I praise the form of Mātṛkā, whose splendor is like the rays of the nectar-rayed moon.
The meditation on Keśava’s fame and so forth:
with their eyes’ broad radiance meeting at the corners, they lick each other while being embraced by arms that are covered with abundant horripilation.
I meditate upon Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa— the fair and the dark— who wear a pair of garments, one dark and one fair, and who possess an unrestrained thirst for the playful dalliance of Love.
In that regard, Vāsudeva is the presiding deity of the Nyāsa; he should be known here as the slightly dark-complexioned one, and his meditation is described as follows:
[He is] dark like a rain-cloud, with silken garments shimmering like lightning, smiling, and with hands resplendent with a playful lotus.
I bow to the one who has a peacock-feather crest, whose form is that of Vāsudeva, the most beloved of Kṛṣṇa, the Little Kṛṣṇa.
During breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should meditate upon those two deities who are one’s own chosen ones:
their arms, bristling with joy, are locked in a mutual embrace; they possess the hue of vermilion and gold, wear a set of four silken garments of radiant beauty, and have lotus-faces in full bloom.

I bow to Rādhā and Mukunda, who together gather the materials for their pastimes, who adorn the forest with the assistance of their attendants, whose fair and dark limbs radiate splendor, and whose faces are sweet with smiles.
Having formed the *kara-kacchapikā* mudrā, one should then meditate upon one's own deity,
being praised with fervor by the Siddhas, the gods, and the sages— who, though empowered, are not yet bold enough to question— while remaining at a distance, composed and offering salutations.
Her splendor was gazed upon with longing even by the attendants of Vaikuṇṭha and other realms;
her sweetness was a consecration for the expansion of wonder throughout the three worlds.
With mountain ridges crowded with clusters of fresh sprouts of grass, their slopes shimmering, adorned with the beauty of streaks of every mineral,
and featuring caves embellished by flowing waterfalls; he ascended the mountains.
In some places, the ground was adorned yet indistinct, as if it were being prepared for a ritual performance.
Of those lakes whose waters are exceedingly charming, bearing curds and milk in measureless abundance, where *kāraṇḍava* ducks warble amidst clusters of full-blown lotuses,
and where the trees on their banks are rubbed by the tips of the arms of light waves;
The dense mass of clouds was shattered by the torrents of rivers.
By the charming cranes intoxicated with passion,
by the waters of the lakes flowing swiftly and repeatedly,
and by the splendor of the lotuses blooming upon those lakes—
It was made radiant by a multitude of lotus ponds.
In an instant, she was beheld by the throngs of her companions, who were delighted by the fragrance of the Sindhu-born [lotus];
they were filled with the splendor of young sprouts resembling the rising sun, and possessed the sweetness of nectar.
The heat of the sun was blocked by the trees, which were lush and leafy, bearing fruits that shatter pride.
With the humming swarms of female bees intoxicated by the honey-pollen, which produced a languid grace like that of a forest in the height of passion for the enemy of Smara,
and with the weight of fully blossomed clusters causing them to bow down on all sides;
Its banks are marked on all sides by broad clusters of creeping vines.
With *kapiñjala* birds, *valākikā*, sparrows, *cātaka* birds, and *upayaṣṭika*;
with cuckoos, mynas, parrots, *kaliṅga* birds, and pigeons;
with *śatacchada* and *śitacchada* birds, as well as *karaṭa*, *khañjarīṭa*, and others.
It was made resonant within by the unceasing calls of birds.
O Ānanda, the throngs of cowherds, like the cakora birds, were unable to abandon their longing for the moon-like [complexion] of those women;
thus, they attained a resemblance to their tresses through the clusters of peacock feathers.
Where there were high dances by flocks of intoxicated peacocks,
and where there were *kiṭi*, *kirīṭin*, *śalya*, *bhalla*, monkeys, deer, *sṛmara*, *camara*, *golāṅgula*, *mūru*, and *camūru* antelopes.
The interior was filled with vast, broad-necked lions, free from the fear of predatory beasts,
as if they were animals liberated from inauspiciousness; it was also crowded with camels whose humps were formidable with dullness, and even with milch goats.
It was also obstructed by herds of wild buffaloes, which were as dark as boulders fallen from mountain crags and as formidable as a gathering of demons.
Resplendent in some places with level grounds shining like crystal pavements and in others with emerald-green meadows as if made of emeralds,
it surpasses the beauty of its own mansions with its own intense sweetness.
And it was made beautiful by clusters of excellent groves, lovely with their abundance of blossoms.
It is said that she was propitiated by the wind, who delights in following the flow of the lotus-like daughter of Kalinda,
and who makes the multitudes of living beings throughout the moving and unmoving world bloated with bliss.

First, having searched through the Vṛndā forest which is exceedingly beautiful, may I repeatedly remember it as being intermingled with the various, complete, and melodious humming sounds of swarms of bees. (A Kulaka)
Here is a flower garden whose roots are drenched with thick nectar and which perfumes the quarters of the sky with its fragrance.

In this world, the wise man should meditate upon the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa), whose shoots are coral, whose leaves are emeralds, whose buds are excellent diamonds, whose fruit is rubies, and from which flows a stream of nectar.

One should here meditate upon that most excellent lotus, which is eternally manifested in the midst of the golden shore by the seasons, which is thought of as the greatest thing on earth, and which possesses eight petals with the splendor of the rising sun.
There, the wise one should remember the shimmering jeweled floor, which is a mass of supreme bliss.

There, upon that excellent mosaic floor of radiant splendor, having visualized the seat of yoga (yogapīṭha), one should contemplate those two who enjoy abiding bliss, seated upon its brilliant and vast central pericarp (karṇikā).
I meditate upon Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā, whose splendors rival the luster of a fresh rain-cloud and gold.
Adorned with the beauty of peacock feathers bound upon their crests and clusters of curling locks of hair,
and marked by shimmering, radiant saffron tilakas;
Their beautiful forehead marks were adorned with musk.

Her cheeks are blooming with the radiance of shimmering flower-clusters that form her ear-ornaments, where bees rejoice in the affection for her most delightful fragrance; and her moving shark-shaped earrings flash against those blossoming cheeks.
Whose ear-lobes are licked by the luster of various jeweled earrings.
Marked by the luster of an autumnal moon and a wide red border like a *damanaka* flower, with the play of her heavy,
tremulous, and long glances—
[She is] one who has surpassed the young *khañjarīṭa* bird in sweetness,
whose lord is the crescent moon placed upon the forehead of Śiva, and whose forehead is adorned with two streaks of musk.
Her eyebrows, which were preeminent in shaking off the arrogance of the amorous play of the flower-bowed god,
throbbed like the moving pegs on a painted cloth.
Her head was encircled by an excellent noose,
and her face was graced by the luster of a large, round pearl hanging from the tip of her nose.

Possessing the beauty of a face that triumphs over the splendor of the full-moon lord of autumnal nights, with the radiance of their noses like the beauty of freshly blossomed *tila* flowers and *damana* blossoms,
and with the luster of their cheeks surpassing the excellence of a shining bimba fruit;
Possessing the great splendor of blossoming jewel-mirrors and the wealth of a radiant smile.
With the deep resonance of celestial drums, the soft warbling of sweet-voiced cuckoos,
and trunks encircled by blossoming, fresh creepers, it was adorned with garlands of flowers and pomegranate trees that had reached full maturity.
To her whose radiance is like that of the twice-born [brāhmaṇas] who have conquered the king of seeds;
whose neck is adorned with a jeweled necklace and precious gems rolling upon her conch-like throat.
With shoulders beautifully arched by their height and breadth, he seemed to mock the serpents with his pair of radiant arms— arms that were smooth, appropriately beautiful, and slightly bent.
She captivated the splendor with her arms adorned by shimmering armlets; her hands, possessing beautiful fingers made radiant by jeweled rings, were further graced by the glow of flashing bracelets.
His firm chest, resplendent with door-panels of emerald,
is adorned with a forest garland mingled with necklaces and clusters of guñjā berries; his breasts mock the shimmering, dense fruits of the pomegranate tree.
[She is] adorned with a profuse garland of pearls forming the crest upon her two peaks.
To her whose slender waist is beautiful, adorned with three folds that surpass a row of bees and a line of hair, and who,
O sister of Yama, conquers the noble whirlpools of the celestial river as it flows toward her.
With a deeply indented navel region and possessing the beauty of broad hips and a belly.
Possessing the lovely beauty of a yellow silk garment encircled by a jeweled girdle that rivals the dense curves of her hips,
and enriched by a jeweled belt upon a crimson silk cloth—
...delightful with her hips embraced by her upper garment.
With thighs as beautiful as the trunk of an elephant slow with the weight of fresh rut;

with shanks fashioned into a radiant beauty by two perfectly rounded calves; with a pair of incomparable ankles that are hidden from view; and with feet glowing with reddish nails and adorned with jeweled anklets.
Her back was being rubbed on both sides by her beloved’s right arm, which was bristling with joy as he stood there,
while she rested her head upon the root of his left arm.
Her pair of side-glances darting from the banks of her lotus-face.
With his neck turned away, his long side-glances flickering toward the lotus-face of his beloved, his flute humming against his quivering lips,
and his right foot resting upon his left thigh as he stands poised in the midst of fear;
With a moving garland of *cilli* flowers upon his forehead and blossoms serving as an ornament upon the slope of his arm.
Upon seeing His form, her eyes became entranced; upon touching Him, her skin thrilled with joy;
at His voice, her ears were uplifted; by His fragrance, her nostrils were touched;
her tongue was captivated by the touch of His lips; and as she leaned toward Him, her lotus-face bent down.
Possessing great fortitude that was merely disgorged through hypocrisy, she was externally agitated by surging emotional transformations.
The flute, caressed by the playful breath slightly exhaled from his mouth,
emits a melody that shatters the steadfastness of the entire world;
though its power is fragmented by his inner state of being overcome by the touch of his beloved.
He was immediately making his own doctrine understood through a clever play upon musical notes.

Even when the knot of her lower garment had become exceedingly loosened, she— whose waistline was held fast by the friendship of a mass of perspiration, whose girdle was like a riverbank on a high stage, and whose heart was overwhelmed by the first onset of melting passion— had forgotten all other emotions.
To her who understands the intense agitation produced by a mass of deep longing.
Their bodies were thrilled with horripilation, their lotus-faces bathed by streams of tears they had heard,
and they trembled for a moment, their voices rich with an intensely suppressed stammer.
I remember those two whose minds were intoxicated by the passion of love.
Adorned with nine apertures,
her stature equal to that of the seed-syllable *Guru*,
and her lower lip embellished by a ruddy hue.
With a straight bamboo flute held in his hand.
With her most praiseworthy form, which could be measured by her own fist within, was charming at the measure of three cubits,
and was preponderantly endowed with a dark luster;
The right elbow is supported by a staff or similar object.
With his dark, unchanging body, which has broad roots and is positioned at the front,
his form is bound by a waist-cloth of fine cloth.
It was frequented by Pūru with his excellent horns.
By her soft, playful lotus, she warded off the bees that were restless with the abundance of fragrance from the mouths of her friends;
while her moon-like faces were being gazed upon, the flood of nectar—
With a wide and graceful sidelong glance.
With Viśākhā, whose hands shone with fresh and delicate *cāmara* flowers,
and Citrā, [she was seated] on the right and left [sides].
Their bodies were being fanned with graceful playfulness.
With her lotus-like hands trembling as she held a betel-roll fashioned from *nāgavallī* leaves within a casket,
she was like a *campaka* creeper swaying with the wind.
The two banks, whose wealth of forms has been seen and beheld.

Accompanied by the spreading resonance of the lute played before her by one who knows all virtues, and blended with the sweet songs of Ramyendulekhā that harmonize with the playful melodies of the flute.
Indeed, they were made actors on the stage of worldly existence by means of their lofty learning.
While the goddess Raṅgā,
with her undulating limbs, gently stroked his right side, and the noble goddess Sudevī likewise stroked his left side with a soft touch—
The streams of sweat and tears [were wiped] with the hem of her garment.
The Auspicious Hymn of Remembrance:

That service of love, which is inaccessible even to Keśava and others, which is to be accomplished through the lotus feet of the Lord who is the life-breath of Śrī Rādhā, and which is attainable only through intense longing by those devoted to the pastimes of Vraja; [may that service be attained].

I bow to that daily service of his, performed by the travelers on the path of passion, which has now become manifest so that they may extend their mental service to him who has reached [the state of perfection]. //1//

At the end of the night, he enters the cow-pen from the forest bower; in the morning and evening, he performs the play of milking and feeding the cows; at the time of the first light (saṅgava), he grazes the cattle with his friends;
then at midday and at night, he sports in the forest; and oh, in the afternoon, he delights with Rādhā!
May that Kṛṣṇa, who goes to the cow-pen at twilight and delights his friends, protect us. // 2 //
At the end of the night, awakened by the many cries of terrified flocks and by the charming and uncharming songs of parrots and mynas, the two rose from their pleasant sleep;
seen by their friends, they were thrilled, their amorous play having arisen at that moment, yet filled with apprehension at the harsh words [of the birds].
I remember Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, though full of longing, having reached their respective couches in their own abodes. //3//
At dawn, Rādhā had bathed and adorned herself; summoned by the waters of Vraja, she had prepared the cooking of food in her house with her friends and was eating what remained from Kṛṣṇa’s meal.
Kṛṣṇa, having finished his bath, had reached the cowshed, completed the milking of the cows, and was awakened.
Then, having bathed well and taken their meal, she and he sat down together with their companions upon a seat.
In the forenoon, Kṛṣṇa— accompanied by His cowherd friends, following the herd from the cow-pen, and longing for the attainment of Rādhā— reached the bank of that lake to pursue Her;
meanwhile, having seen Kṛṣṇa, Rādhā, out of respect for Him, had already returned home to perform the worship of the sun.
I remember her, whose eyes followed the path of her own friend sent by Kṛṣṇa to obtain news of him. // 5 //

At midday, they are enchanted by various ornaments arising from their mutual union; they are intensely restless with longing for each other, having attained joy through the playful jests of their friends such as Smaramakhālalatā;
their pastimes include swinging, wandering in the forest, seizing the flute, amorous dalliance, drinking honey-wine, and the worship of the Sun.
I remember Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, full of longing, being served by a multitude of attendants. // 6 //
Śrī Rādhā had returned home for the sake of her lover, having prepared various offerings;
she was well-bathed and beautifully attired, filled with joy at the sight of her beloved’s lotus-like face.
And Kṛṣṇa, too, in the afternoon, had set out from Vraja accompanied by the herds of cows and his companions.
I remember [Him] who is satisfied by the sight of Śrī Rādhā, joined with His father's face, and caressed by His mother. // 7 //
In the evening, Rādhā— her heart delighted by her friend bringing many kinds of food sent for her own beloved, and by that friend having eaten the remnants of the Lord— approached the moon of Vraja,
who had returned to his home after bathing, dressed in beautiful attire, cherished by his mother, and arrived at the cow-pen.
I remember you returning to your own home after milking the cows, having finished your meal. // 8 //
At twilight, Rādhā— clad in attire suited to the dark and light of night,
having set out for the bower on the bank of the Yamunā at the instruction of her circle of female messengers—
beheld Kṛṣṇa in the assembly hall, who was attentively observing the qualities and artistic skills of the cowherds. Her eyes were moist with affection.
I remember how, having been brought with effort and placed upon my lap, she would then quietly enter the bower.
Those two, having ascended [the mountain] and obtained their assembly, were served by Vṛndā with many attentions;

they shone with their beloved companions amidst songs, jokes, riddles, sweet speech, and dances— the performances of the rāsa and lāsya— and their minds were absorbed in amorous delight as they drank the finest honey-wine.
The two teachers of play, having raised their outstretched arms, engage in various amorous battles within the bower.

Attended with affection by their circle of devoted female companions with betel-leaves, perfumes, garlands, fans, cool water, and the massaging of their feet— having attained their desires through endearing words and secret amorous sentiments— the two of them slept in the grove amidst throngs of bees.
I remember Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, having attained sleep upon a bed of exquisite flowers during the night. // 11 //
Thus ends the *Smaraṇa-paddhati* composed by Śrī Rūpa Gosvāmī.
May Śrī Rūpa be victorious!
Thus concludes the auspicious hymn of remembrance (*smaraṇa-maṅgala*).
Thus ends the fourth stage.
*** FIFTH STAGE:
Now, [one asks] which [aspect] belongs to the Blessed Lord himself, who is an ocean of the nectar-ambrosia of supreme sovereignty and sweetness?
"In response to the inquiry, 'What is that abode where this Blessed One dwells?', he says:
'His residence is renowned in four places, beginning with Purāṇa.'"
In Vraja, Madhupura, Dvāravatī, and indeed in Goloka itself.
For it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"Whatever cities exist on earth that are dear to the Lord, they exist likewise in Vaikuṇṭha, being honored there for the sake of His various pastimes," and so forth.
Regarding the classification of that [residence], it is stated in the *Ākāra* (LBhāg 1.4.497–8, 502):
"His abode is said to be twofold, namely Māthura and likewise Dvāravatī.
And they say that Māthura is also twofold: Gokula and Puram."
That which is named Goloka is indeed the glory of Gokula; its nature as that very glory is due to the exaltation of His majesty.

The meaning of this is as follows: the glory (*vaibhava*) of Gokula is the sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) of the cowherd community, which is of the nature of light. That Gokula possesses that very glory as its own self; that Goloka is that whose glory is its own self.
For the sake of the exaltation of its majesty—
that is, for the purpose of the exaltation of the majesty of that Goloka—
otherwise, [there would be] the non-manifestation of Goloka in Gokula.
If [the Lord] were manifest, the establishment of four abodes would follow; if, however, He were an abode by virtue of being unmanifest,
then Madhupurī and Dvārakā— being both unmanifest and manifest— would result in six abodes.
To the question, "Where then is the location of Goloka? he says:
it is precisely at the very top, above the supreme ether (para-vyoma). Śrī Brahma—
In the Saṃhitā:
"O Goddess, in His own abode named Goloka, and below it, in those various abodes of Maheśa and Hari..."
"I worship that Govinda, the primordial Person, by whom all those various accumulations of power were ordained. Thus [it is said].
"The beloveds of Śrī are His beloved; the Supreme Person is the wish-fulfilling tree," and so forth.
I worship that Śvetadvīpa, which they here call Goloka, where the great ocean of milk flows from the Surabhi cows and where even the time known as half a *nimeṣa* does not pass.
"Only a few of them, being wise and moving about sparsely across the earth," and so forth.
For this very reason, in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (10.2.7), [Kṛṣṇa says]: "Go, O auspicious goddess, to Vraja."

In the *Śrī-caitanya-caritāmṛta* (Ādi 4.29), the words of Śrī Goloka-nātha follow the manifest pastimes, beginning with: "In my own realm, [I am] in the mood of a paramour toward the multitude of gopīs," and so forth.
In this context, within Goloka, Śrī and the others are of the nature of restatement (anuvāda),
while Kāntā and the others are of the nature of what is to be enjoined (vidheya);
thus, "even beyond."
Goloka, Śvetadvīpa, Vaikuṇṭha, and so forth, are merely descriptive (anuvāda-rūpa);
Vṛndāvana, Gokula, and so forth,
are the primary objects of injunction (vidheya-rūpa).

Furthermore, if people were to perceive that this Kṛṣṇa is a mere manifestation of Nārāyaṇa existing above Goloka and the supreme ether (paravyoman), their immediate engagement [with Him] would become difficult to achieve;
therefore, [the Lord manifests] His attendants [in this world].
There is a constant realization: "This Lord of All is our Master.

Furthermore, because the pastimes of His youth (*kaiśora*) in Goloka are permeated by divine sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), the Lord of Goloka, when engaged in those pastimes, lacks the characteristics of childhood (*bālya*) and boyhood (*paugaṇḍa*); thus, the pastimes are of a single uniform nature due to being situated in youth.
And when that [state] exists,

because there is no manifestation of the thought "this Supreme Person is the possessor of power and we are His powers," and because there is no grasping of the hand [in marriage], pastimes such as giving away [the bride] or bridal processions do not exist.
In that place, not even a moment known as half a blink of an eye passes;
for since there is no day or night, there is an absence of those pastimes which are characterized by nocturnal dalliance.
Because it is unsuitable for the women who have gone there— women who possess love that is both secondary and harmonious—
it follows that Goloka is superior even to Dvārakā.
[This may seem] deficient; nevertheless, in the *Śrī-stavāvalī* (Vraja-vilāsa 5) by Śrī Dāsa Gosvāmī:
"Dvāravatī, though surrounded by brothers and sons, is dearer even than Vaikuṇṭha, where the Lord sports with hosts of principal queens who surpass hundreds of Lakṣmīs."
Mathurā is a field of love even more so than that; yet Śrī-Vraja, where Hari was born, shines most brilliantly there. Therefore, I eternally worship that very place.
Thus, by virtue of their mutual relationship, even Dvārakā is inferior to Mathurā. However, the region of Mathurā is the most excellent, as is agreed upon by both Śruti and Smṛti.
As it is said in the Padma Purāṇa:
"Aho! Madhupurī is blessed and even more venerable than Vaikuṇṭha.
Thus, among the seven cities, the one at Mathurā is the most excellent.
O Goddess, hear now its majesty, which is superior even to the realm of Vaikuṇṭha. Thus it is said.

Therefore, in the *Śrī-Bṛhad-bhāgavatāmṛta*, one’s own mind would not find satisfaction merely by observing the respect and honor shown to that very Lord—the crest-jewel of all-knowing ones—by the cowherd boys of Goloka and His attendants. As it is said (2.4.110–113):
"To that very Lord, the crest-jewel of all-knowing ones..."

I meditate upon the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha, the son of Nanda, the beloved of Lakṣmī and the others, as well as Rādhikā, the faces [of the gopīs], and the hosts beginning with the servants— the children of Vraja.
Nevertheless, because I do not see the Lord dwelling here in this land of Vraja along with His entourage, my mind is pierced by the god of love.
Sometimes I see him sporting playfully there in the groves, and at other times I see him standing amidst herds of cattle.
And on his own seat, just like his own lord, in every respect.
Nevertheless, because of the reverence and honor arising toward that son of Nanda, who is indeed the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha and the Supreme Lord;
Without that love, one’s own mind would find no satisfaction.
And in the *Śrī-stava-mālā* (Nandāpaharaṇa, verse 19):
"There is no place more beautiful than the forest of Vṛndāvana..."
May that Mukunda protect you— he who, having clearly shown the realm of Vaikuṇṭha to his circle of kinsmen by saying "it is nowhere else," led them back once more to the cowherd settlement.
As it is said in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (10.28.10):
"But Nanda, having seen that super-sensory and great glory of the world-protectors,
and having observed their deference toward Kṛṣṇa, spoke in amazement to his kinsmen."

Then, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is supremely compassionate, seeing that [the cowherds] were bewildered by the commentary— due to being so overwhelmed by supreme sweetness that they lacked any perception of His divine sovereignty— showed Goloka to His circle of kinsmen, headed by Nanda,
and led them back again to Gokula.

Goloka, Bhū-vṛndāvana, and so forth are clearly described in the tenth book of the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam; furthermore, after the residents of Vraja, headed by Nanda, beheld Vaikuṇṭha, their return to Vraja is explicitly stated.
Therefore, [the realm] is self-effulgent—

Since this earthly Vṛndāvana is manifest yet simultaneously unmanifest and shines eternally, its distinctness from and inferiority to Goloka—which is called Gokula—is clear, due to the absence there of sweetness (*mādhurya*) and opulence (*aiśvarya*). And as for sweetness, it is described by such passages as: "Those demons who were difficult to slay... and so forth.

In some places, those such as Indra, who are unskilled in [discerning] sweetnesses, have shown an identity between the two abodes, Goloka and Gokula, based on the equality of their sovereignty; however, the identity of Goloka [with Gokula] exists because its nature is the manifestation of the glory of Gokula.
"But manifestation is not counted among the divisions, for it is not separate from us;
and therein it performs those [functions] which [occur] within manifestations."
"Even though there are millions of unmanifest [forms]" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.5.451).
Although a distinction is counted among those things that are self-luminous and luminous, nevertheless, in the *Caitanyacaritāmṛta* (Madhya 8.83):
If one investigates from an impartial standpoint, there exists a gradation [of excellence].
And therein, within the context of the Great Rāsa-līlā, it was previously considered that among those [excellent forms], one particular form remains as the "noose of Rādhā" (rādhā-pāśa). Or rather:
This has been explained specifically in the twentieth chapter of the *Śrī-Caritāmṛta*, within the section on the instructions of Śrī Sanātana Gosvāmī concerning the middle pastimes (*madhya-līlā*);
or else, it may be resolved through the power of inconceivable potency (*acintya-śakti*).
Furthermore: "Just as one does not abandon the nature of Kṛṣṇa even when possessing four arms, so too this [nature] must be manifest in Him, even in His two-armed form. (LBhāg 1.1.23)

By such logic, because He lacks agency in acts such as deluding Brahmā, there is manifestation even though the sweetness of the form of the Supreme Perfection (Pūrṇatama) residing in Gokula is absent in the manifestations of Śrī Kṛṣṇa who went to Mathurā and Dvārakā; likewise,
in Goloka, there is manifestation even though the sweetness of the sweet sovereignty found in Śrī Vṛndāvana is absent.

The state of being the domain of both the non-conceptual and the conceptual is like the form of Śrī-Gokula, which is both extraordinary and ordinary; it is described as the nature of the Cintāmaṇi jewel and so forth by way of restatement (*anuvāda*), yet it is specifically the form of the land of Mathurā by way of what is to be enjoined (*vidheya*).
Regarding the phrase "even though limited, yet wonderful," and so forth;
and regarding the phrase "The Māthura and Śrī-Gokula—the wise say that Māthura is twofold: Gokula and the city itself," and so forth.
Furthermore, its eternal nature is heard in the *Pādma-purāṇa*:
"Know Mathurā to be eternally mine, as well as the forest of Vṛndāvana.
In this very place, even the entire series of cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa-mālā*) finds its fulfillment.
Even in a mere symbol of Vṛndāvana, that which has been experienced by the Creator himself.
Thus, what wonder is there that even hundreds of millions of young women gathered there on the banks of the Yamunā during the rāsa-līlā?
These are visible to the people who are their respective attendants of the divine pastimes, and not to others;
for they manifest at the appropriate time for those specific pastimes and so forth.
It is a marvel that even when existing together in one place at one time,
they certainly remain in every respect with natures entirely unmingled with one another.
Adorned on all sides by the pastimes of Kṛṣṇa’s childhood and other stages,
there exist numerous forms of mountains, cow-pens, forests, and so forth.
Even though this region of his is rich in divine play, it is said that at times it appears entirely empty to others who are otherwise capable of perceiving it.
Therefore, because the Lord, his beloveds, the abode,
and the pledge possess inconceivable power, there is nothing here that cannot be accomplished.
His fourfold sweetness shines forth preeminently in Vraja alone:
that of His sovereignty, His pastimes, His flute, and likewise His glorious form. (LBhāg 1.5.526)
Therefore, according to the principle that "whatever exists on earth [is but a manifestation]," the names Dhāvakā, Mathurā, and Gokula are indeed the independent abodes of the Blessed One;
[Gokula] is renowned as the manifestation of the glory of that [Mathurā].
The name "Goloka" is well-known in the scriptures as being above the supreme ether (paravyoman), as in the words of Śakra in the Harivaṃśa:
Above heaven is the world of Brahmā, frequented by hosts of Brahman-sages;
there also is the course of Soma and of the great-souled luminaries.
Above that is the world of the cows; indeed, the Sādhyas protect it.
For that, O Kṛṣṇa, is all-pervading, great, and situated within the great ether.
Even there, your path consists of asceticism;
it is one that none of us can discern, even by questioning the Grandfather (Brahmā).
The goal for those rich in tranquility and self-restraint is heaven, the destination of those who have performed meritorious deeds.
For those engaged in Brahmanic austerity, the world of Brahmā is the supreme goal;
but as for the world of cows, that goal is indeed difficult to ascend.
"But that world, O Kṛṣṇa, was being oppressed; it has been sustained by you, the self-realized one, who are steadfast, O hero, as you strike down the calamities of the cows. Thus [it is said].
But Indra, despite having learned of the supreme sovereignty over Gokula during the delusion of Brahmā and other events, [remained unaware of his] supreme sweetness—

Having been deluded again as if by the vision of Brahman, he describes Goloka, which is the manifestation of that very wonder, and then, by indicating its non-difference from Gokula, he says: "But that world, O Kṛṣṇa, was created by you.
Therefore, the word of Śrī Kṛṣṇa in the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam (10.25.18):
"Therefore, I protect this cow-pen—which has Me as its refuge, Me as its lord, and Me as its protector—by means of My own yoga; this is the vow I have undertaken.
For this reason, it is entirely appropriate that His residence is said to be in the four places beginning with Purāṇa. Furthermore:
Because of the qualifying attributes "having Me as his sole refuge," "having Me as his lord," and "being My possession," even those beginning with Brahmā have no qualification here;
what then to say of others?

Furthermore, it is observed elsewhere that within the sacred field of Śrī Puruṣottama, which extends for ten yojanas and five krośas in the shape of a conch, the local ruler does not possess independent authority.

What need is there for more? Therefore, the supreme attainability, the supreme secret nature, and the supreme loveliness of the self-luminous land of Vṛndāvana are described in the Śrī Bhāgavata (10.21.10):
"O friend, Vṛndāvana spreads the fame of the earth because it has obtained the fortune of the lotus feet of the son of Devakī.
Furthermore, in that very same place, in the *Brahma-stava* (10.14.34):
That birth here in the forest of Gokula is some kind of abundant good fortune, for it involves bathing in the dust of the feet of whichever [cowherd] boy; indeed,
that life is entirely blessed when the Lord Mukunda [is found there].
Yet even now, the dust of Your feet remains something to be sought after by the Vedas alone.

Furthermore, in that very same passage from the words of the illustrious Uddhava (10.47.61): "O, may I become even a mere shrub, creeper, or herb in Vṛndāvana for those who enjoy the dust of their feet."
In the Ādi-purāṇa it is said:
"In the three worlds, the earth is blessed where the city of Vṛndāvana is;
and even there, O Pārtha, the Gopikā named Rādhā is mine."
For instance:
"O Gopikā, do not think that those in Vraja are different from Me; behold, the cowherds and the cows there are indeed My own forms of bliss."
But those few who perceive me as distinct from the inhabitants of Vraja—
those of deluded intellect have no destination in the hereafter either.

In the *Brahma-saṃhitā* (5.56): "The trees are composed of clusters of wish-fulfilling gems, the ground is made of cintāmaṇi jewels, the water is nectar, the speech is song, the dance is the movement, and even the flute is a dear friend."
That supreme light is both consciousness-bliss and that which is to be tasted.
And in the Śrī-Gopāla-tāpanī (2.36):
"In their midst is Gopāla-purī, which is Brahman manifest. [Also] in the Bṛhad-gautamīya:
This beautiful Vṛndāvana is indeed my own exclusive abode. Whatever animals, birds, trees, insects, humans, or gods dwell here in my sanctuary, upon their death they go to my own abode.
The cowherd girls who dwell here in my abode are yoginīs; they are constantly devoted to my service.
My forest, which is the form of my body, extends for five yojanas;
here flows the Kālindī, known as the Suṣumṇā, which carries the supreme nectar.
Here the gods and all living beings exist in subtle form;
since I am composed of all the gods, I shall never abandon this forest.
"In this age after age, may there be for me manifestation and concealment;
this beautiful, radiant [form] is invisible to the eye of flesh."
Vṛndāvana is the twelfth [place], protected by Vṛndā;
it is presided over by Hari and served by Brahmā, Rudra, and others.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "Then there is the meritorious Vṛndāvana, which is inhabited by the goddess Vṛndā,
presided over by Hari, and served by Brahmā, Rudra, and others."
Just as Lakṣmī is most beloved, and just as men devoted to bhakti are most beloved,
so too is Vṛndāvana on earth the most beloved of Govinda.
There, in Śrī Vṛndāvana, is the place known as Śrī Govindasthala;
as it is said in the *Śrī Govinda-līlāmṛta* (21.28):
"This pure bank known as Śrī Govindasthala is the throne for union with Kṛṣṇa."
She beheld the Vṛndā forest, which resembled a lotus with a thousand petals: its head was the excellent Vṛndāvana forest; it was bowed down on all sides by the feet [of the Lord];

it had the appearance of a tortoise-shell pedestal [the earth]; it was rich with the petals of rows of groves; it possessed fine pericarp-cups in the form of jewel-like mansions; and it had filaments in the form of rows of golden plantain trees.
Thus, she saw it as equal to a lotus of a thousand petals.

Therefore, in the auspicious verse of remembrance (*smaraṇa-maṅgala*), regarding the phrase "from the grove" (*kuñjāt*), because the grove is the primary element, it should be understood as the grove situated at the place of Śrī Govinda.
This is stated in the Mathurā-khaṇḍa of the Skanda Purāṇa (Mathurā-māhātmya, verses 399–401):
In that Vṛndāvana is the meritorious abode of Govinda, crowded with his servants; it is right there that I reside. O King, on this earth, that Vṛndāvana is the Vaikuṇṭha of Govinda.
Wherein there are servants such as Vṛnda and others, who are devotedly longing for Govinda.
O protector of the earth, those supreme persons by whom the great abode in Vṛndāvana has been seen have achieved their life's purpose upon this earth.
There, the meditation on the venerable Lord Govinda at the Yoga-pīṭha is as follows,
according to the *Kramadīpikā* (3.1–36): Now, [He is] like a blossoming, fragrant *mallikā* flower from which the honey has overflowed with manifest fragrance...

A person of pure intellect should meditate upon the auspicious Vṛndāvana, which is cooled by trees whose branches are bent low under the weight of clusters of flowers and fresh sprouts, and which are entwined by graceful creepers adorned with blossoming new clusters of blossoms. 1.

Its interior was made resonant by the humming of birds such as pigeons, parrots, mynas, and cuckoos, which, emerging from the openings of their moving beaks, were sweet with the tasting of the nectar of blossoming flowers.
It was filled with the cries of peacocks— the enemies of serpents— dancing here and there,
and was greyed by the pollen from the bellies of blossoming lotuses carried along by the droplets of the moving waves of the daughter of Kalinda.
It was constantly attended by breezes that stirred the garments of the playful women of the cowherd settlement, whose passion had been kindled,
and which possessed sprouts of coral, emerald leaves, and diamond buds.

One should meditate upon that [central] wish-granting tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*), which has buds in the form of clusters of stars, various fruits with the luster of lotuses, is most massive, is constantly served by all the seasons, and is raised up even beyond that [central lotus]. //4//
Beneath that mountain, whose range of golden peaks shines like the rising sun, there is a golden ground sprinkled with droplets of nectar,
featuring a floor of blazing jewels and radiant with heaps of flower pollen.
Furthermore, the wise one, remaining unwearied and free from the sixfold army of passion, should again recollect [the deity].
Having visualized a reddish lotus with eight petals situated upon a magnificent yoga-throne set within a pavement of jewels; //5//
Then, one should contemplate Mukunda seated comfortably in the midst of that [mandala], possessing the splendor of the rising sun,
resembling a mass of clouds of crushed collyrium and sapphire gems. 6.
Possessing a luster equal to that of freshly bloomed blue lotuses,
with a mass of hair that is very glossy, deep blue, thick, and curled,
and crowned with a crest like the beautiful dark plumage of a royal peacock; //7//
His lovely face possesses the splendor of the full autumnal moon, his eyes are as wide as lotus petals,
and he is radiant with the light from the shimmering jeweled *makara*-shaped earrings.
With cheeks like mirrors and a high, beautiful nose;
with lips more lovely than vermilion, and limbs illuminated by the splendor of smiles as white as the moon, jasmine, and *mandārava* flowers.
His conch-like neck was beautiful and radiant with a necklace fashioned from a cluster of forest sprouts and flowers;
it was graced by long, hanging locks frequented by intoxicated bees. //9//

His shoulders were adorned with a garland of celestial flowers; his broad chest was resplendent with a series of necklaces and a cluster of stars; and he shone with the Kaustubha gem gleaming upon the surface of the sky-like expanse of his breast. //10//
He was well-marked with the auspicious Śrīvatsa sign, possessed broad shoulders, and had well-formed arms that were thick and rounded down to his knees;
he had a deep-seated belly and a noble, profound navel.
[He beholds] the beautiful line of hair like a swarm of female bees;
[and] the arrangement of armlets, bracelets, waves of necklaces, girdles, anklets, and breast-bands, all fashioned from various jewels.
Her slender body was encased in a cage of reddish-yellow pigment,
her rounded hips were draped in yellow garments,
and her thighs, knees, and shanks were smooth, beautiful, and well-proportioned. //12//

His lotus-feet are beautiful, with foreparts raised in a lovely manner that puts to shame the splendor of the tortoise, and they shine with rows of nails like gleaming mirrors of rubies, while the covering of his jewel-like toes is exquisite. //13//
Delightful with the palms of his reddish hands and feet marked by the fish, goad, lotus stalk, banner, barley, lotus, and thunderbolt;
his limbs fashioned from the very essence of all beauty.
[He] whose bodily splendor surpassed that of the God of Love through his beauty;
[he who was filled with] divine melodies produced by the fingers of his trembling hand as they moved the holes of the flute, which was brought to life by his lotus-like mouth. //14//
The continuous stream of the lineage of all sentient beings, eternally melted and drawn forth, is an infinite ocean of the waters of bliss. //15//
Then, [he beheld] the beautiful cowherd girls, Sulalitās,
whose gait was slow due to the weight of their broad hips and buttocks,
and whose waists were bent by the heavy burden of their full breasts.
Of those possessing a line of body hair manifested by three folds. //23//
For those whose limbs and feet have been made to sprout with the nectar-essence of that exceedingly sweet and beautiful flute-playing,
there arises a delightful blossoming of horripilation.
Of those whose vine-like bodies were adorned with village ornaments. //24//
By the water of passion expanded by the moonlight of her exceedingly beautiful, gentle smile,
[the ocean was filled] with droplets from the breaking of its most restless waves.
Of those whose continuous streams of sweat-drops are equal to the [flow from] a water-jar. //25//
With the rain of the sharp arrows of Māra discharged from the bow of his exceedingly lovely and slow-moving pupils,
her entire vital points were shattered and her limbs became overwhelmed.
Of those whose pain from unbearable trembling has spread throughout their bodies. //26//
By those two who were longing for the ritual of drinking the nectar of the beauty of his exceedingly charming deeds and form,
[the rivers] carrying floods of the water of affection...
With her lotus-eyes languid and tremulous. //27//
Frequented repeatedly by swarms of bees greedy for the honey-drops trickling from the full blossoms of their loosening tresses,
and with soft voices faltering from the intoxication of passion, [the women] have their girdles trembling and rising...
The splendor of their hips was revealed as the ends of their Chinese silk garments slipped loose from their waist-knots. //28//
Of those whose quarters were filled with the tinkling of jeweled anklets from the gentle impact of their stumbling, graceful lotus-feet,
and whose petal-like lips quivered as their long-lashed eyes blossomed like buds.
Of those with blossoming lotuses in their two lakes and shimmering earrings. //29//
Of those whose sprout-like reddened lips withered from the heat of the wind of their longest sighs,
and whose lotus-hands shone with various offerings.
Constantly attended on all sides by the female bees. //30//
His entire body was worshipped by them with garlands of full-blown blue lotuses resembling their long, tremulous, dark eyes; he was the locus of manifold amorous graces,
and he tasted the honeyed nectar trickling from those charming lotus-faces of theirs.
Wearing a captivating garland of bees that are his eyes, intoxicated with love. //31//
One should visualize outside and in front of him the host of gods, including the gopīs, gopas, and cattle,
who are seeking wealth from Brahmā and Śiva.
Preceded by a hundredfold wrath, it is devoted to praise. //32//
To its right, [he saw] a multitude of sages who firmly desired the Dharma and were devoted to the traditional teachings; then,
behind them, the lords of yogis who sought liberation.
Through meditative concentration, [he perceives] Sanaka and the others who possess pride. //33//
Then, on the left side, [he saw] the Yakṣas, Siddhas, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, and Cāraṇas together with their consorts,
as well as the Kinnaras and the principal Apsarases.
Those who desire sensual pleasures [should worship] with dance, song, and instrumental music. //34//
[He who is] white as a conch, the moon, or a jasmine flower; who knows all the Āgamas; whose mass of matted hair is tawny like a multitude of lightning flashes;
and [he who possesses] unwavering devotion directed toward his lotus feet.
Desiring [him], having utterly abandoned all other attachments. //35//

He was delighting that great assembly with the rising, heart-stealing modulations (*mūrchanās*) belonging to the three scales (*grāmas*), which were endowed with various collections of Vedic hymns and the seven musical notes (*rāgas*).
One should contemplate the Lord of Sages, the son of Dhātṛ, in the sky. //36//
Here, the chapter from the Padma Purāṇa (5.69.4–118) is written down in sequence:
Pārvatī said:
The supreme abode of Viṣṇu, situated both within and outside the infinite millions of cosmic eggs, is the primary, most excellent, and highest among them. //4//
O Great Lord, I wish to hear all about that most delightful place dear to Kṛṣṇa, beyond which there is nothing else; please tell me. (5)
Īśvara said: This secret, more secret than the secret, which produces supreme bliss, is a most wonderful place of solitude—the highest, ultimate bliss. (6)
O Goddess, it is the most difficult among the difficult to obtain, the supreme deluder, composed of all powers, and hidden in all places. //7//
The eternal place named Vṛndāvana, situated above the cosmic egg, is the preeminent abode of the Sātvatas and is extremely difficult even for Viṣṇu to attain. //8//
The complete Brahman is eternal bliss, sovereignty, and imperishable joy;
Vaikuṇṭha and other realms are but portions of its portions, while Vṛndāvana itself is that very essence upon the earth. //9//
Whatever sovereignty belongs to Goloka is established in Gokula;
indeed, whatever majesty belongs to Vaikuṇṭha is established in Dvārakā. //10//
That Brahman which is supreme sovereignty, eternal, and centered in Vṛndāvana—the supreme abode of Kṛṣṇa—is especially present within the midst of those forests. //11//
Therefore, within the three worlds, the earth is renowned as blessed, because it contains that which is called Mathuraka, the sole beloved of Viṣṇu. (12)
The region of Mathurā is its own preeminent name;
it is a manifold, secret place situated within the city. //13//
The Mathurā-maṇḍala has the form of a thousand-petaled lotus;
through the revolution of Viṣṇu’s discus, it is indeed the wondrous abode of Viṣṇu. 14.
The extent of the petals of the pericarp is said to be the Secret Tree;
the greatness of the primary Twelve Forests has been described in sequence. //15//
Bhadra, Śrī, Lohabhāṇḍīra, Mahātāla, and Khadīraka; Bakula, Kumuda, Kāmya, Madhu, and likewise Vṛndāvana. //16//
The number of these [forests] is twelve; five are said to be on the western side of the Kālindī, and on the east is Pāñcavana, where there is a supreme secret. (17)
The great forest known as Gokula, as well as Madhuvana and Vṛndāvana, and other groves are declared to be the places for the nectar of Kṛṣṇa’s pastimes. //18//
The Kadamba-khaṇḍana, Nanda-vana, Nandīśvara, as well as the Nanda-nandana-khaṇḍa, and the Palāśa, Aśoka, and Ketakī groves. //19//
Sugandhamānasa, Kaila, Amṛta, Bhojanasthala, Sukhaprasādhana, Vatsaharaṇa, and Śeṣaśāyika. //20//
Śyāmapūrvadadhigrāma, likewise Cakrabhānupura, Saṃketadvipada, and Bālakrīḍanadhūsara. (21)
There was a beautiful grove of wish-fulfilling trees, full of longing, where there were various kinds of flavorful sports and grounds for manifold playful delights. //22//
The great abode called Gokula is described as a secret tree, a support for the expansion of the Nāgas, and a thousand-petaled lotus. //23//
That is the pericarp, the great abode, the supreme station of Govinda;
there, upon a golden pedestal, it is adorned with a pavilion of jewels. //24//
In the pericarp, the petals are said to be located in sequence in the cardinal and intermediate directions;
that petal which is declared to be in the south is the supreme among the most secret and excellent. (25)
Upon that petal is the great sacred seat (mahā-pīṭha), difficult to access even through the Vedas and Agamas, hard for even the lords of yogis to attain—that Gokula which is the soul of all. 26.
The second petal is in the southeast; likewise, that is the petal of the secret.
Therein are the two-footed convention and the hut; these two reside in that family. (27)
The eastern petal and the third, the preeminent and supreme station, are remembered as being a hundred times more meritorious than the touch of all sacred fords (tīrthas), such as the Gaṅgā. //28//
In the fourth petal, in the northeast, at the Siddha-pīṭha, that very word [is found];
there, by practicing this, a young cowherd girl shall obtain Kṛṣṇa as her husband. (29)
The seizing of garments and ornaments is declared for that petal;
the fifth petal is said to be the northern one, the most excellent of all petals. (30)
In this very place is the twelve-sun lotus, equal in size to the pericarp;
the sixth petal is in the northwest, where the Kālī-lake is said to be. //31//
The supreme among the supreme is indeed called the primary station; the leaf that is the best of all is remembered as the seventh in the west. //32//
It grants the desired boons to the hosts of sacrificial wives;
even an asura attained liberation here, a state difficult for the gods to achieve.
Right here is the petal that deludes Brahmā, which brings about the lake of Brahmā;
in the southwest is declared the eighth petal, which destroys the void.
The slaying of Śaṅkhacūḍa, which is a place for the essence of various pastimes, is declared to be the eighth petal, situated within the Vṛndā forest. (35)
The beautiful and glorious Vṛndāvana, situated to the south of the Yamunā, was seen;
there stands the Śiva-liṅga known by the name Gopīśvara. 36.
Outside of that is a sixteen-petaled [lotus] filled with Śrī; one should worship that Lord in all directions, as prescribed, proceeding clockwise in due order. //37//
The great station, the great abode, known as the support of its own light, is the first and foremost single petal; its majesty is equal to the pericarp. //38//
There, on the delightful Govardhana mountain, which is the eternal abode of rasa,
in the pericarp lies the Great Pastime (mahā-līlā), a deep cavern of the essence of that pastime.
Where Kṛṣṇa, the eternal Lord of the Vṛndā forest, resides—Kṛṣṇa who has attained the state of Govinda—what is the use of further words? (40)
The third petal is declared to be the most excellent and supreme of all;
the fourth petal is declared to be the ground of the most wonderful aesthetic flavor (rasa). //41//
The delightful Nandīśvara forest is there, where the abode of Nanda is remembered;
the greatness of the pericarp and petals is described as the fifth petal. //42//
The presiding deity here is Gopāla, who is devoted to the protection of the cows;
that which is called the sixth petal is known as Nandavana. //43//
The seventh petal is proclaimed to be the delightful Bakulāraṇya;
there is the eighth, Tālavana, where the slaughter of the cow is recorded to have occurred. //44//
The ninth petal is proclaimed as the delightful Kumudāraṇya;
the tenth is Kāmāraṇya, the supreme cause of all. //45//
The adornment of Brahmā, the manifestation of Viṣṇu’s disguise, and the locus of the aesthetic flavor of Kṛṣṇa’s play—this is called the primary petal (pradhāna-dala). //46//
In the eleventh [chapter], the construction of the Setubandha—a site consisting of various groves—is declared to be the cause for bestowing grace upon devotees. //47//
The delightful and enchanting Bhāṇḍīra forest has twelve groves;
there Kṛṣṇa, intent on play, is surrounded by Śrīdāmā and his companions. //48//
The thirteenth petal is excellent, and therein it is known as Bhadravara;
the fourteenth petal is declared to be the place that bestows all spiritual accomplishments (siddhis). //49//
There lies the beautiful Śrī-vana, the cause of all sovereignty, composed of the petals for Kṛṣṇa’s pastimes, which increases the splendor, beauty, and fame [of the Lord]. (50)
The fifteenth petal is the most excellent; therein lies what is known as the Iron Forest (Lohavana).
The sixteenth petal is said to be equal in majesty to the pericarp. //51//
There the Great Forest is sung of; there exists the supreme secret.
There he is, surrounded by cowherd boys, delighting in their play. //52//
Therein are the slaying of Pūtanā and others, and the breaking of the twin Arjuna trees;
there the presiding deity is Bālagopāla at the age of five years. //53//
He is called by the name Dāmodara, an ocean of the nectar of the bliss of divine love;
this celebrated petal is declared to be the most excellent among all petals. (54)
The play of Kṛṣṇa is called the filament (kiñjalkī), and the petal (dala) is said to be the vihāra; the petal and filament are also declared to be the preeminent Siddhas. //55//
Pārvatī said: "O Great Lord, what is the greatness or the wonderful secret of Vṛndāvana? I wish to hear that; please tell me. (56)

The Lord said: O most beloved, I have told you that which is the secret of secrets, the highest of the high, the secret among secrets, and the most difficult to attain among all things difficult to attain. (57)
O Goddess, this place is protected by the three worlds, highly honored by the Lord of Gods, desired by Brahmā and others, and frequented by the gods, Siddhas, and the rest. //58//
For the lords of yogis are always solely intent on meditating upon him with devotion, while [the place] is filled with constant dancing and singing by Apsarases and Gandharvas. //59//
The glorious Vṛndāvana is enchanting, the abode of the nectar of perfect bliss;
its waters are like abundant cintāmaṇi jewels, filled with the nectar of immortality. //60//
There, one should visualize a tree as a venerable great tree, frequented by swarms of fragrant bees;
the woman as Lakṣmī and the man as Viṣṇu, arising from a tenth part of that [tree]. //61//
Therein [he beholds Him] eternally in the bloom of youth, whose very form is bliss, whose movement is dance, and whose face is constantly adorned with sweet speech and smiles. //62//
That forest was inhabited by pure-hearted Vaiṣṇavas full of love;
it was immersed in the bliss of the perfect Brahman, vibrating with His form and consisting of Him alone. //63//
It was enchanting with the sweet warbling of intoxicated cuckoos, bees, and other birds; it resounded with the song of parrots on its walls and the humming of thousands of frenzied bees. 64.
Abounding in the dance of peacocks—the enemies of serpents—and possessing the playful fragrance of all [flowers], it was filled with pollen from various colored blossoms. //65//
It is like the full moon, ever-rising; it is served by the gentle rays of the sun;
it is free from suffering, the cessation of suffering, and devoid of old age and death. //66//
Free from anger, devoid of envy, undivided, and without egoism;
it is the essence of the nectar of perfect bliss, an ocean of the happiness of full love. //67//
The great abode transcends all qualities; its very nature is perfect love, where even trees and other plants manifest horripilation and shed tears of the bliss of divine love. //68//
Furthermore, what more can be said of those devotees of Viṣṇu who are endowed with conscious intent?
By the touch of the dust of Govinda’s feet, Vṛndāvana is eternally present upon the earth. (69)
Vṛndāvana is the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus;
by the mere touch of which, the earth becomes blessed throughout the three worlds. (70)
More secret than the secret, delightful, situated in the center of Vṛndāvana on earth, it is the imperishable, supreme bliss, the eternal abode of Govinda. //71//

The liberated state is the complete Brahman, the abode of bliss, which is non-different from the body of Govinda; what more need be said of its majesty, since even the touch of its dust brings liberation? //72//
Therefore, O Goddess, with your whole being, make that forest abide within your heart—Kṛṣṇa, whose form is youthful, amidst the pastimes of Vṛndāvana. (73)
And the Kālindī river performed a circumambulation around its pericarp, which possessed water that was profound with playful stillness and enchanting with fragrance. //74//
It is a dense abode of the nectar of bliss mixed with that [nectar], shining brilliantly with various colors through flowers such as lotuses and water-lilies. //75//
The water, graced by birds such as ruddy geese with their various sweet and melodious calls, is beautiful within and delightful to the mind. //76//

Beautiful on both its banks and fashioned from pure gold, that place is said to possess ten million times the merit of the Gaṅgā; there, even a single cowrie shell [offered] by touch [is of great value]. //77//
In the pericarp [of that lotus], where Hari delights in play, the power is ten millionfold;
there is Kālindī-karṇikā, who is non-different from Kṛṣṇa as a single form. (78)
Pārvatī said:
O Govinda, whose form is fashioned from beauty itself, what is your wonder?
I wish to hear that; tell me, O ocean of compassion. (79)

Īśvara said: In the midst of beautiful Vṛndāvana, which is adorned with the splendor of tinkling anklets, and decorated with the branches and sprouts of excellent trees extending for many yojanas; //80//
In its center is the Yoga-pīṭha in the abode of Mañju, brilliantly radiant; it is fashioned with eight corners and is enchanting with various splendors. (81)
And above that is an auspicious lion-throne made of mani-jewels;
upon it is a lotus with its petals vanished, providing a comfortable resting place within its pericarp. //82//
What can be said of the supreme abode of Govinda? It is praised for its greatness, where the assembly of cowherd girls, established in the mantra of the glorious Govinda, resides in service. //83//

[I worship] Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Vṛndāvana, who possesses divine age and form of the cowherd community, the sovereign of Vraja with perpetual sovereignty, and the sole beloved of the boys of Vraja. //84//
His childhood was emerging from youth; his form was wondrous by virtue of his age;
he is the beginningless origin of all things, the beloved son of Nanda-gopa. //85//
He is sought after by the Vedas, unborn and eternal, the heart-stealer of the cowherd women;
He is the supreme abode, the supreme form, the two-armed Lord of Gokula. //86//
One should meditate upon the son of the cowherd women, the sole cause of the attributeless [Brahman], who is most glorious, ever-new, pure, the dark abode, and enchanting. (87)
Glistening like a row of fresh rain clouds, with beautiful earrings, possessing the lovely luster and pleasant touch of a blooming blue lotus, it brings happiness. //88//
Śyāmamohana, who resembles a mass of people pressed together and is glossy, possesses locks of hair that are exceedingly smooth, dark blue, curly, and entirely fragrant. //89//
Above that, during the southern course [of the sun], it is enchanting with dark crests, radiant with various colors, and adorned with the petals of royal peacocks. //90//
With a crest like a beautiful Mandāra flower or a cow’s tail, adorned with lovely ornaments, and in some places embellished by a crown consisting of rows of large petals; //91//
In some places, he was adorned with crowns and ornaments of many jewels and rubies; his face, resembling ten million moons, was sometimes surrounded by trembling locks of hair. //92//
He has a forehead mark of musk, adorned with beautiful, shining yellow orpiment, and eyes with long lashes as lovely and dark as the petals of a blue lotus. //93//
Her smile was embraced by dancing creeper-like eyebrows, her glance was cast askance, and the tip of her nose was exceedingly captivating with its exquisite, elevated beauty. (94)
The three worlds were enchanted by the rays of the pearl at the tip of her nose;
she was exceedingly beautiful with lower lips that were very glossy and reddened with vermilion. //95//
He wears earrings in the shape of golden makaras, shimmering with various colors;
their radiance shines brilliantly, resembling fine mirrors upon his cheeks amidst the mass of their rays. //96//

Adorned with ear-lotuses, jasmine, and *mandāra* flowers as well as makara-shaped crest-jewels, his chest bears the *śrīvatsa* mark and the *kaustubha* gem, while his neck glitters with a pearl necklace. 97.
Upon his hand shone a divine ruby bracelet mixed with beautiful gold, while he was adorned with armlets and a girdle of tinkling bells. //98//
It is resplendent with feet beautified by the exquisite loveliness of very soft anklets, and it is adorned with camphor, agallochum, musk, shimmering sandalwood, and other such substances. //99//
Adorned with divine body-unguents mixed with gorocanā and other substances, she moves about, her forefeet shining with a smooth yellow cloth, causing people to tremble. //100//
With a deep lotus-like navel, a line of body hair like a curved garland, a pair of well-rounded knees, and enchanting lotus feet. //101//
Adorned with a banner, a vajra, a goad, and a lotus upon his hands and the soles of his feet, he is the sole cause of Brahman, filled by the rows of rays from his moon-like nails. //102//
Some say that a portion of Him is Brahman, non-dual and of the nature of consciousness;
the wise declare Mahāviṣṇu to be a tenth part of that. //103//
That very form, with its three-fold bend (*tribhaṅga*), fashioned from the essence of all graceful emanations, is meditated upon in the hearts of the lords of yogis, such as Sanaka and others. (104)
Beautiful as infinite millions of Kandarpas with their necks turned sideways, he wore shimmering golden earrings upon his noble cheeks, resting on his left shoulder. (105)
Smiling with sidelong glances, as beautiful as ten million gods of love, he [charms] with the sweet, melodious sounds of the flute placed upon his curved lips. //106//
To Him who deludes the three worlds and is immersed in the nectar-ocean of divine love, Śrī Pārvatī said:
"The supreme cause is Kṛṣṇa, known as Govinda, the Great Abode. (107)
What is the wonderful and beautiful secret majesty of the Lord of Vṛndāvana, who is eternally the sole cause of that which is beyond all qualities? //108//
"Tell me that, O Lord of the gods; I wish to hear it, O Master.
Ishvara said:
"The limit of the greatness of the moonbeams from the nails of whose feet cannot be reached. (109)
O Goddess, listen with joy as I describe how great that majesty is:
within infinite millions of cosmic eggs, rising through infinite triple qualities. (110)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are but a ten-millionth part of a ten-millionth part of His power;
endowed with the functions of creation, maintenance, and so forth, they remain as His manifestations of glory. (111)
Portions of even a ten-millionth part of that form—those digits possessing the body of Kandarpa—residing within that cosmic egg, bring about the delusion of the world. (112)
The omnipresent Lord is but a ten-millionth part of a ten-millionth fraction of the splendor shining from his body;
the rays of light from that radiance, which possess the form of the sun, are but a ten-millionth fraction of those [splendors]. //113//

By means of the rays from his own body— consisting of the nectar of the essence of supreme bliss, having the nature of consciousness and supreme fragrance, and being the sole cause of the attributeless [Brahman]— //114//
The rays of light consisting of the moon-gems on the nails of his pair of lotus-feet sustain [the world] as a portion of a ten-millionth part of that [light]. (115)
They say that even the Perfect Brahman has as its cause that which is difficult for the Vedas to fathom;
an infinite croreth part of a fraction of its fragrance is what deludes the universe. //116//
The source of various fragrances, such as the scent of flowers touched by Him, is His beloved primordial nature, Rādhikā, the consort of Kṛṣṇa. 117.
Durgā and the other goddesses, who consist of the three qualities (guṇas), possess not even a ten-millionth part of a ten-millionth fraction of her power;
by the touch of the dust of her feet, ten million Viṣṇus are produced. //118//
By the touch of his lotus feet, you are blessed, O fair-faced one.
Thus ends the Śrī-Vṛndāvana-māhātmya in the Padma Purāṇa;
as it is stated in the Bṛhad-Gautamīya:
"The goddess Rādhikā, who consists of Kṛṣṇa, is declared to be the supreme deity."
"She consists of all prosperity, she is all-beauty, the supreme enchantress.
Likewise, from the *Mātsya* and *Skānda* Purāṇas:
"In Vārāṇasī she is Viśālākṣī; in Puruṣottama she is Vimalā."
Rukmiṇī was in Dvāravatī, while Rādhā was in the forest of Vṛndāvana.
[Now begins the *Puruṣabodhinī* Śruti.
Victorious are the illustrious Śrī Rādhā and Govinda!
First Prapāṭhaka.
Oṃ. Then, as if having attained perfect awakening during deep sleep, Rāma said: "O Goddess, what is this to me? Where is that Kṛṣṇa who is my brother?
Tell me of his radiance and his shadow."
That Vaiṣṇavī said: "O Rāma, listen!
Bhūr, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ, mahaḥ, janaḥ, tapaḥ, satyam, and atalam."
Vitala, Sutala, Rasātala, Talātala, Mahātala, and Pātāla— this golden egg, the Brahmāṇḍa, is fifty crores of yojanas in extent.
Above the infinite crores of such Brahmāṇḍas is the Cause (Kāraṇa).
"Vaikuṇṭha is the eternal abode of Mahā-Viṣṇu above the waters.
He asked, "How can there be a supportless place in a void expanse?
She replied, "There is Lord Śeṣa, seated upon a lotus throne, entirely devoted to meditation on Kṛṣṇa."
Within his infinite pores of the skin are infinite millions of Brahmāṇḍas and infinite millions of causal waters;
above his head are thousands of hoods.
Above the hood is the world of Rudra, known as Śivavaikuṇṭha; this world of Rudra extends for one hundred million yojanas. Above that is the world of Viṣṇu.
The realm of Viṣṇu is seventy million yojanas in extent;
above that is the Sudarśana wheel, thirty million yojanas in extent, which—
Above [this], the district of Mathurā known as Gokula is surrounded by an ocean of nectar.

Within that, in the center of the filaments of an eight-petaled lotus, what is the form of the abode? What is the lotus? What is the yantra? Who are the attendants? And what are the enclosures? When this was asked, she replied: "In the place called Gokula..."
In the district of Mathurā, in the midst of Vṛndāvana, at the foot of a wish-fulfilling tree in the center of a thousand-petaled lotus,
upon the filaments of an eight-petaled lotus, Govinda shines resplendent— dark-complexioned, clad in yellow garments, two-armed, with a peacock feather on His head, flute and staff in hand;
He who is without attributes yet possesses attributes, formless yet possessing form, desireless yet active.
On her two sides are Candrāvalī and Rādhā; from a portion of her arise powers such as Lakṣmī and Durgā. Thus, Lalitā is in the west facing her, and Śyāmalā is in the northwest.
In the north is Śrīmatī, in the northeast Haripriyā, in the east Viśākhā, and in the southeast Śraddhā.
Padmā is in the south, Bhadrā in the southwest;
at the tips of the sixteen petals is Candrāvalī.
To her left is Citrarekhā;
at her side is Śrīśaśirekhā;
and at her side is Kṛṣṇapriyā.
Beside her was Kṛṣṇavallabhā; beside her was Candrāvatī; beside her was Manoharā; beside her...
Yogānandā; by her side, Parānandā;
by her side, the painter Premānandā; by her side, Nandā Madanasundarī.
Beside her is Satyānandā; beside her is Candrā; beside her is Kiśorīvallabhā.
"Compassion and the various virtuous goddesses perform service to Kṛṣṇa"— such is the Vedic statement; such is the Vedic statement.
One attains the eternal abode through mental worship, recitation, meditation, chanting, and all forms of praiseful devotion, and not by any other means—indeed, not by any other means!

The second chapter has also been stated: outside of that, upon the seats of yoga (yoga-pīṭhas) on the petals of a hundred-leaved lotus, the gopīs remain, devoted to Rāma’s pastimes. This [palace] has four gates and is as brilliantly radiant as a hundred thousand suns.
There they are gathered together.
There, in the western front hall of the first enclosure, is Gopikanyā in a golden pavilion; in the second [enclosure] are Śrīdāmā and the others.
In the third [circle] are the small bells and so forth;
in the fourth, cloves and so forth;
in the fifth, at the root of the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpataru).
Aniruddha accompanied by Uṣā is also [there];
in the sixth [direction] are the gods;
