in the seventh is the red-colored Viṣṇu as the door-keeper.
This is Rādhā-kuṇḍa on the outside;
having bathed there, one becomes the body of Rādhā through the vision of the Lord.
It becomes suitable;
having bathed there, Nārada becomes fit for the vicinity of the eternal abode of the Lord.
[He attains] a single intellect, a single mind, a single knowledge, a single self, and a single [consciousness] regarding Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa on their shared seat.

Having the singular form of a lotus, he sits alone upon a seat of Brahman; playing his golden flute, he gazes at her who is golden in nature and imbued with passion. At the foot of the wish-fulfilling tree, she is the supreme, perfected, sattvic, and pure knowledge of fragrance—purely sattvic, devoid of the emotional state of worldly attachment, and thus transcending the quality of *sattva*. Therefore:
There is no difference between the two; it would transcend time, māyā, and the guṇas.
He clarifies that very point with the word "atha" (now): either meaning "immediately after" or "in the auspicious sense."
Here, in the midst of Śrī Vṛndāvana, the letter *ma* is the personified form of the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman Vedas;
the letter *u* is the essence of the Yajurveda; [and] Śrī Rāma—
The letter *a* is also of the nature of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*);
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, though consisting of half a mora, is like Yaśodā, for He is the knower who, as it were,
tastes the aesthetic flavor of the mutual longing for happiness between Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa— the Supreme Brahman, who are existence, consciousness, and bliss.
The nectar of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda) is thus described.

Its defining characteristic is that which is the Praṇava, whose essence is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, which is established in the power of knowledge called Svecchā, and which constitutes the state of body, speech, and mind.

The nature of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* is celebrated as the *Satya*, *Tretā*, and *Dvāpara* ages; that which is the fourth (*turīya*) among Gokula, Mathurā, and Dvārakā is indeed that divine Vṛndāvana— thus was the triad, consistent with all traditions, previously described.
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Atharvaṇīya-Puruṣabodhinī*.
The third chapter:
Now, immediately following—
Bhadra, Śrī, Loha, Bhāṇḍīra, Mahātāla, and Khadiraka.
Bahulā, Kumudā, Kāmyā, Madhu, and Vṛndāvana.
There are twelve forests:
seven forests to the west of the Kālindī and five forests to the east; however, there is a secret [forest] to the north.
The great forest named Gokula, Mathurā, Madhuvana,
Khadiravana, Bhāṇḍīravana, Nandīśvaravana, and the forest like the grove of Nandanānanda, Palāśa, Aśoka—
In these forests— the Ketadruma, Bhadravana, Śeṣaśāyin, Krīḍāvana, and Utsavavana— Kṛṣṇa sports eternally with various pastimes in twenty-four forests.
Among them, [the forest] frequented during the spring season is endowed with the groves of Nanda and others.
Therein there is no suffering, no pleasure, no aging, and no death.
There is no anger;
therein is the glorious Kṛṣṇa in His eternal youth, composed of pure bliss, wearing a jeweled crown from which three pairs of guñjā berries hang like peacock feathers.
On his head was a tilaka of gorocanā; in his ears were crocodile-shaped earrings; he wore a garland of forest flowers, his body adorned with a wreath of mālatī blossoms;

on his hand was a bracelet, on his waist an armlet, and at his hip a girdle of tinkling bells; he wore yellow garments, possessed a deep lotus-like navel, a pair of well-rounded nostrils, and lotus-feet marked with symbols such as the banner and the thunderbolt.
"By a fraction of a fraction [of that], he is the Great Viṣṇu of ten million [parts].
Thus, the wise person should constantly meditate upon Kṛṣṇacandra in such a form.
His primordial nature is Rādhikā, who is eternal, beyond the material qualities (nirguṇā), adorned with every ornament, gracious, and beautiful with manifold loveliness;
by the power of her perfection, such a one has become an ocean of bliss born of love.

"By means of mental worship, recitation, meditation, chanting, and all forms of devotional praise, one attains the eternal abode, and not by any other means—by no other means, by no other means," such is the Vedic declaration; such is the Vedic declaration; such is the Vedic declaration.
Thus ends the third chapter in the Atharvaṇīya-Puruṣabodhinī. //3//
The Fourth Chapter:
Now, the fourth state of Puruṣottama is directly Brahman itself,
wherein supreme renunciation [is established].

The Lord of the World, whose very nature is the Supreme Brahman, resides there as a black banyan tree that is a wish-fulfilling tree; there, Lakṣmī, Jāmbavatī, Rādhikā, Vimalā, Candrāvalī, Sarasvatī, Lalitā, and others [dwell].
I am Subhadra, the complete portion, the form of light, Sudarśana, and the devotee.
Thus, Brahman is fivefold in manifestation:
Mathurā, Gokula, Dvārakā, Vaikuṇṭha-purī, and Śvetadvīpa-purī, the city of Rāma.
These deities abide where there are various cities, such as Surasā, Pātālagangā, Śvetagangā, Rohiṇī, Kuṇḍa, Amṛtakuṇḍa, and so forth.
Where the food is prepared food, rendered free from defects through the touch of Brahman, and independent of the purificatory rites of Śūdras and others;
the meaning is that it is fit for the venerable Jagannātha.
A mantra recited with a different vocalization and practiced in various ways fails.
The mantra is: "O food, from your food [may we prosper]... "For the sake of food, arrange yourselves; King Soma has come to me; may he measure out happiness for me and with splendor."
And by this [phrase] "with strength," the mantra is:
"To Viśvakarman, svāhā! This mantra-king should be joined with the essence, the nectar, Brahman, and the vyāhṛtis: bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ om.
"The earth is your vessel, the sky is your lid; I offer immeasurable nectar into the mouth of the Brāhmaṇa, svāhā!"—
by means of this mantra, there is the alternative view that "food is Brahman," according to the Śruti.
Liberation is described as follows:
"Wherein food is Brahman, the supreme purifier; the essence is peace; liberation is absolute isolation (kaivalya); the earth is perfected; for intellect is indeed the reality," and so forth.
Wherein flows the Yamunā, daughter of Bhṛgu, whose waters are composed of nectar;
where dwell the Vṛndāvanas and the Nīla mountain, Govardhana; and where stands the lion-throne, the Yoga-pīṭha, the palace, and the jewel.
The pavilion [is presided over by] the sixteen Caṇḍikās beginning with Vimalā, and the Gopī;
where, on the shore of the ocean, this eighth day of the month of Māgha is without parts (niraṃśaka).

Homage to Śrī Rādhikā.
I eternally worship the wish-fulfilling gem of Śrīmatī Rādhā’s feet, which is brilliantly radiant, having emerged from the mine that is the womb of Śrī Kīrtidā. 1.

When Kṛṣṇa had assumed the gesture of silence and departed manifestly from this Vraja,

In this regard, a certain auspicious ancient story is heard:

Even today, that Lord Hari, who is affectionate toward His devotees, shines forth in the land of Oḍra; the Sovereign Lord is capable of doing, not doing, or doing that very thing.

"She consists of all prosperity, she is all-beauty, the supreme enchantress. Thus it is said. And as stated in the *Mātsya* and *Skanda* Purāṇas: "Viśālākṣī is in Vārāṇasī, and Vimalā is in Puruṣottama."
"Rukmiṇī is in Dvāravatī, and Rādhā is in the forest of Vṛndāvana. Thus,

And in the *Śrī-Prīti-sandarbha*, it is stated that this very excellence of love (*prema-vaiśiṣṭya*) is the primary [aim]: "The excellence of love is as follows" (in the *Śrīmad-Ujjvala-nīlamaṇi* 5.98):

Even when given cause for distress by me, Rādhā does not harbor resentment in the lap of her heart;

Thus, by virtue of her excellent qualities, Rādhā reigns supreme among all beautiful women.
And in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (10.30.28): "Surely the Lord Hari, the Supreme Controller,
has been propitiated by her," referring to that gopī whom Kṛṣṇa led away into the forest, leaving behind all other women.
And she then considered herself the most excellent of all women;
and among those [daughters], the Gāndharvas were the best, surpassing even the Tāpanīs.
"Only he who worships Mādhava as a devotee without Rādhikā— Mādhava will not be pleased at all, and that practice will be in vain.

The intention is: "Therefore, let him be consecrated to the sovereignty over the entire Brahmāṇḍa. (Thus in Sanskrit.)

Then, O Maheśvarī, one should offer oblations ten times the amount [of the main mantra] using red *campaka* flowers or *padma* lotuses, smeared with the three sweets, into the sacrificial pit prepared according to the prescribed rules. 14.
With bilva leaves or kiṃśuka flowers, or with sugar, sesame, and ghee—one should offer those respective substances according to the prescribed rule, according to one's specific desire. //15//
One who desires sovereignty should offer oblations with lotus seeds and milk-rice;

One desiring prosperity should offer oblations, especially with sesame seeds and clarified butter; and one seeking to paralyze [an enemy] should likewise sacrifice with *kiṃśuka* and *campaka* flowers. //17//

for eradication, with ketaki leaves; and in all cases, with sesame seeds and clarified butter. //18//
One desiring prosperity should offer oblations with honey and clarified butter;
thus, the practitioner who has mastered the mantra shall accomplish all desired objects. //19//
Indeed, by this [mantra] alone one shall surely attain submissiveness to Kṛṣṇa;

[The Hymn of One Hundred and Eight Names of Rādhikā] Now I shall proclaim the one hundred and eight names,

Rādhikā, the beautiful Gopī who brings about union with Kṛṣṇa;
she of restless eyes, the deer-eyed one, the daughter of Gandharva, the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu. //2//

Holding a lute in her hand, with a smiling face, dwelling within a red Aśoka creeper bower, she wanders upon Govardhana; appearing in the guise of a cowherd girl, she is enchanting to the cowherd women. //3//
And Candrāvalī’s co-wife was Darpaṇāsyā Kalāvatī—merciful, of beautiful form, youthful, and captivating to the heart. //4//
She is the beloved of Kṛṣṇa, the friend of Kṛṣṇa, fond of inverted sexual union, highly skilled, delighted by amorous play, moon-faced, and possessed of a beautiful form. //5//
The beloved of Hari, Mahālakṣmī, who has squinting eyes, is a skilled conversationalist;

Rādhā, the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu, is a youthful girl, graceful as a vine;

She is joyful and bestowing rain, heroic and steadfast, both firm and unsteady, the supporter of the earth and the embodiment of fortitude;

She is called *svādhīnapatikā* (one whose husband is under her control), *khaṇḍitā* (the neglected wife), and *abhisārikā* (the woman who goes to meet her lover);

Pālikā, Lālikā, Lajjā, Lālasā, the jewel among women (lalanā-maṇi), Bahurūpā, Surūpā, Suprasannā, and Mahāmatī. //14//

The *kīlaka* is for the purpose of subduing Śrī Kṛṣṇa; the application (*viniyoga*) is in the recitation (*japa*). Salutation to Agastya, the seer (*ṛṣi*), on the head; salutation to the Jagatī meter (*chandas*), on the mouth.

then, upon the full lunar disc, he should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the seat (*pīṭha*),

One should place Adharma and the others in the mouth, on the left side, and at the navel; likewise, one should contemplate the forms of the divine gopīs on the right side. (10)
The bulbous root consists of bliss, the stalk is of the nature of consciousness,
the lotus is the self of all, and the petals are of the form of primordial nature.
One should arrange, one above the other, the filaments called "discernment," the pericarp consisting of the Mātṛkās, and the orbs of fire, sun, and moon.

One should also assign sattva, rajas, and tamas, as well as the state beyond qualities (nirguṇya), and likewise the Self (ātman), the inner Self (antarātman), and the supreme Self (paramātman). //13//
One should place Lakṣmī, Rati, Sarasvatī, Prīti, Kīrti, Śāntikā, Tuṣṭi, and Puṣṭi in the center of the pedestal (pīṭha). //14//
And in the center, one should place the glorious city-dwelling of Vṛṣabhānu;
therein, within the Saṅketakuñja, is the divine forest of Aśoka creepers. 15.
One should meditate upon her, clad in blue garments, beautiful in all her limbs, enriched by the splendor of every ornament, and accompanied by the son of Nanda. //16//

Then, having prepared half of the general portion with pure water from a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), one should provide water for the feet (pādya), the respectful offering (arghya), water for sipping (ācamanīya), the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and the consecration (atiṣecana). //17//
Having established [the deity] with the root mantra, one should offer the *vikṣepārghya* (dispersive oblation) using either water from cool stones or boiled milk. //18//
Into its center, one should place nutmeg, cloves, saffron, and so forth, along with cardamom seeds and camphor; one should consecrate these with the root mantra itself. //19//
Having worshipped the circles of fire, sun, and moon upon the base, the food, and the milk with sandalwood and other offerings, one should then invoke the beloved. 20.
He offered a handful of flowers joined with tulasī blossoms, while carrying within his nostrils the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu, who was the very embodiment of splendor. 21.

Having brought [the deity] within the seat of worship, one should worship with the ritual services; then, beginning with the water for the feet (pādya) and so forth, one should cause [the deity] to enter even more fully by means of the respective mudrās. //22//
With the nectar contained in the special *arghya* vessel, one should consecrate the perfume, flowers, incense, lamp, and the vessel of food offerings seven times with the root mantra. //23//
One should perform the various services individually with supreme devotion for the son of Śrī Nanda by means of the eighteen-syllable mantra. (24)
One should worship Kīrti, Vṛṣabhānu, Yaśodā, and Nanda, as well as the other mother-gopīs, behind the two of them. //25//
One should worship Saṅketa with devotion, as well as Vṛṣabhānupura;
then, having worshipped Varasānu, one should worship Nandīśaila. //26//
Having worshipped Nandagrāma and the creeper of the Aśoka grove, and having worshipped the Pīyūṣa pond, one should worship Mānasarovara. //27//
Then, having worshipped Bhānusarā, one should worship the flower garden;
thereafter, one should worship those eight friends surrounding Rādhā. //28//
One should worship these in sequence: Rādhā, Kṛṣṇā, Lalitā, Viśākhā, Cañcalā, Citrā, Mitrā, and Muditā. //29//
Outside of that, one should worship Gopī, Viśālā, Subhagā, as well as Raṅgavidyā, Raṅgadevī, Gāndharvī, and Gāyikā. (30)
Sundarī, Subhagā, Śobhā, Paurṇamāsī, Candrikā, Vīrā, Vṛndā, Viditā, Vanditā, and likewise Nanditā. //31//
Outside of that, one should diligently worship the Gopīs who bestow all happiness:
Candrā, Candraprabhā, Kāmyā, Mādhurī, Madhurā, and Priyā. //32//
Preyasī, Preṣitā, Preṣyā, Modinī, Śyāmalā, Amalā, Śyāmā, Kāmā, Ramā, Rāmā, Ramaṇī, and Ratnamañjarī. //33//
Śṛṅgāramañjarī, Śīlā, Ratnaśālā, Rasā, Ruṣā, Raṅgiṇī, Māninī, Manyā, Dhīrā, Dhanyā, Dharā, and Dhṛti. //34//
One should worship Bhāmā and Suvarṇavallī in sequence; outside of that, one should worship Campakalatā, Mālatī, Mallikā, and Āruṇā. (35)
Aśokā, Lalitā, Lolā, Mīnākṣī, Madanā, Amati, Sumati, Supratīkā, Sukhadā, Kalikā, and Kalā. //36//
Kādambinī, Kiśorī, Yugmikā, Yugalā, Yugā, Vallabhā, Vallikā, Velā, Vellinī, and Ratnavallarī. //37//
Kamalā, Komalā, Kulyā, Kalyāṇī, Valayāvalā, Dharmā, Sudharmā, Sānandā, Sunandā, Sumukhā, and Mukhā. //38//
Suśrī, Surūpā, Kumudā, Kaumudī, Susmitā, Amitā, Kokilā, Kokilālāpā, Bhāvanī, Suprabhā, and Prabhā. //39//
Madaneśī, Mālinikā, Kanakā, Kanakāvatī, Nīlā, Lalāmā, Lalanā, Mādhavī, and Madhuvibhramā. //40//
Vāsantikā, Sunasā, Premā, another Premavatī, Śṛṅgāriṇī, Śṛṅganī, Sukacā, and Maṇḍanāvalī. //41//
The sixty-four Ramās should be worshipped individually with special arghya and nectar, along with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings. //42//
Outside of that, one should worship the vast and glorious Vṛndāvana, as well as Govardhana, the jewel-mountain, the golden mountain, and the nectar-mountain. 43.
Afterwards, the wise practitioner should worship Indra and the other deities from left to right;
having thus performed the ritual of worship, he should perform the great *ārātrika* ceremony. //44//
Then, having performed the offering of oneself, one should repeatedly release Rādhikā and the Son of Nanda into one's own heart by means of the *saṃhāra-mudrā*. //45//
The ritual procedure [is performed] until midnight by means of the recitation and worship of one's own chosen mantra.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for Śrīmad-Gopeśvarī in the *Śrī-Urdhvāmnāya-Mahātantra*.
Now follows the ritual procedure for Pañcabāṇeśvarī in the *Sammohana-Tantra*.
She herself, the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu, is the sovereign of the five arrows;
O beloved, she performs agitation, melting, and likewise attraction.
Even subjugation and the unsurpassed intoxication—these five great arrows touch the heart of the Son of Nanda. (2)
When the glances of Rādhikā are fixed upon Manmatha, the agitation [of the heart] by means of the arrows of Atri, fire, and the noose is described. //3//
That very [syllable], enriched with the left eye (the letter *i*), is celebrated as "Drāvaṇa" (the Melter);
the seed-syllable of Kāma is called "Ākarṣaṇa" (Attraction) and "Vaśīkaraṇa" (Subjugation). //4//

The third letter of the *pa*-group, adorned with the Earth (the vowel *u*) on the left ear (*u*), followed by Bhṛgu (the letter *sa*) with its own creation (*ḥ*), is declared to be Unmādana, O Maheśānī. //5//
Oṃ, salutations to Rādhikā, the sovereign of the cowherds and beloved of the Pure One;
this eighteen-syllable mantra bestows all spiritual accomplishments. //6//
The sage of this [mantra] is Durvāsas, and its meter is proclaimed to be Anuṣṭubh;
the Praṇava is its seed-syllable, and Svāhā is declared to be its power.
Its meditation, worship, and so forth are proclaimed to be as before. //7//
A young maiden, dressed in exceedingly white garments, with large eyes, devoted to various amorous graces, together with her beloved, seated upon a vast jeweled throne.
One should constantly remember the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu within one's heart. //8//
By repeating the mantra twice with its three sections, the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍ-aṅga*) is performed;
having attained this knowledge, Vyāsa and other preeminent sages [attained their goals]. (9)
The deities beginning with Brahmā, as well as Indra and the other lords of the directions;
likewise Nārāyaṇa, I myself, Lakṣmī, Śeṣa, and Smara. //10//
And all other gods have attained complete sovereignty;
that which was previously concealed in the tantras has now been revealed by me to you. //11//
It should not be given to just anyone; one should guard it carefully from one's sons.
It should be given to a brahmin who is devoted, virtuous, and pure of heart. 12.
For one who is free from greed, meritorious, and devoted to faith and devotion;
otherwise, there would be a loss of accomplishment. Therefore, one should guard [this] with great effort. //13//
O Goddess of gods, they undoubtedly attain scholarship, skill in poetry, victory in battle and debate, the power of subjugation, prosperity, heaven, and even liberation without any effort. (15)
For instance:
the trees Ambra, Jambu, Bakula, Campaka, and Aśoka possess the forms of agitation, liquefaction, attraction, subjugation, and intoxication. (16)
In the spring season, during the Puṣpa constellation, having performed one hundred thousand recitations of the root mantra preceded by the seed-syllable *ra*,
success shall be attained.
Thus ends the exposition of the mantra of Śrī Rādhikā, the Mistress of the Five Arrows, in the Sammohana Tantra.
[The Sadhana of the Five-Syllabled Mantra in the Ūrdhvāmnāya Tantra] Now I shall fully explain Rādhā, whose essence consists of five syllables;
by the mere knowledge of which a man may bring Śrī Kṛṣṇa under his control. (1)
Having uttered the seed-syllable of Ramā, one should then utter "Rādhike" at the end;
this is the Rādhikā-vidyā, ending with the letter *rasa* (ṣ), which grants the desired objects to its devotees. //2//

Sanaka is declared to be its seer (ṛṣi), Jagatī is said to be the meter (chandas), Śrī Rādhā is declared to be the deity (devatā), and the application (viniyoga) is for the attainment of everything. //3//
By repeating the mantra twice, one should perform the ritual placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍ-aṅga-nyāsa*);
one should meditate upon Gaurī, who holds a lotus in her hand and dwells on the shore of the Ocean of Milk. //4//
One should place [the goddess]—whose hand is placed upon Kṛṣṇa’s neck and whose lotus-face is smiling—upon the head, the two eyes, the mouth, and the heart. //5//
One should place the syllables one by one in sequence, arising from the five syllables: one should place "ramā" in the *mūlādhāra* and "rām" in the *svādhiṣṭhāna*.
One should place the third [syllable] in Maṇipūra and the fourth in Anāhata;
one should place Ramā in Viśuddha and all the mantras in Ājñā. //7//
One should draw a triangle joined with a bindu, and then an eight-cornered figure;
then, having drawn a square enclosure (bhūpura), one should perform the worship of the sacred seats (pīṭha-pūjā). //8//
In the *bindu*, one should worship the supreme daughter of Vṛṣabhānu directly;
in the triangle, one should worship Śyāmā, Viśākhā, and Lalitā as well. //9//
Karpūra-mañjarī, Rūpa-mañjarī, Rasa-mañjarī, Lavaṅga-mañjarī, Prema-mañjarī, and Raṅga-mañjarī. //10//
Having likewise worshipped Ānandamañjarī and Ratimañjarī in the eight corners, one should worship the lords of the directions within the Bhūpura.

Then, having offered a handful of flowers accompanied by the eight Siddhas, the mantra-practitioner, having thus performed the worship, should recite [the mantra] for the measure of ten thousand repetitions. //12//
Having established the lamp-dust mixed with the clarified butter of a bull within the mantra as prescribed above and filled with the five colors, //13//
Having joined together a wick made of ten threads into a single, unbroken form, [one should prepare] a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or likewise of bell-metal. //14//
In the absence [of a lamp made of ghee], one should prepare a divine lamp made of clay;
one should set up a stand with its base and also a wick made of that same material. //15//
One should fashion the sacred thread from thread spun by a maiden;
one should perform this unsurpassed rite in this manner for five days. //16//
One attains all desires that have entered the mind; of this there is no doubt—whether in battle, in one's domain, in a dispute, or in the accomplishment of wealth. //17//
Having performed this application, a person shall immediately attain success;
indeed, one should perform this very rite even in other matters as well. (18)
Laṃ raṃ maṃ kṣaṃ vaṃ yaṃ saṃ haṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ—this is the single-syllable [mantra].
Laṃ: obeisance to Indra, the lord of the gods, who is equipped with weapons, vehicles, powers, and retinues, and who is a personal attendant of Śrī Rādhikā.
"I worship the sandals of Indra; salutations, I satiate them; salutations.
Thus ends the practice of the five-syllable mantra in the Ūrdhvāmnāya. Regarding that, the breath control (prāṇāyāma) is as follows:

First, there should be the placement of the *ṛṣi* and so forth; after that, the purification of the hands; then the pervasive placement on the fingers, and likewise the placement on the heart and other limbs.
Three rhythmic claps (tāla) and the binding of the directions (digbandha), followed by breath control (prāṇāyāma),
meditation (dhyāna), worship (pūjā), and recitation (japa)— this is the procedure in all tantras.
Prāṇāyāma: having blocked the right nostril, one performs inhalation (pūraka) four times through the left nostril,
retention (kumbhaka) sixteen times [through both],
and then, blocking both nostrils, exhales eight times through the right nostril.
One should exhale the breath.

Now follows the procedure for the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*): "O Śrī Viṣṇu, O Viṣṇu, obeisance! Today, in the month of [name], on the lunar day of [name], I, [name] Dāsa of the [name] lineage, desiring the perfection of the mantra of [name], [the deity] Śrī Rādhikā..."
I shall perform the *puraścaraṇa* recitation.

For this five-syllabled mantra of Śrī Rādhikā, Sanaka is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Jagatī is the meter (*chanda*), Śrī Rādhā is the deity (*devatā*), and the application (*viniyoga*) is for the attainment of all goals. Śrīṃ.
Namaḥ to the two thumbs;
rāṃ, namaḥ to the two index fingers; dhīṃ, namaḥ to the two middle fingers.
*Keṃ* to the two ring fingers, *namaḥ*. *Śrīṃ* to the two little fingers, *namaḥ*.
*Śrī-rādhike*, *śrī-kara*...
Salutation with both palms and the backs of the hands.
*Śrīṃ*, salutation to the heart. *Rāṃ*, *svāhā* to the head. *Dhiṃ*.
Vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock;
Hūṃ to the armor;
Vauṣaṭ to the three eyes.
Śrīṃ rādhike śrīṃ atrāya phaṭ.
Thus is the six-limbed ritual placement (ṣaḍ-aṅga-nyāsa).
Śrīṃ at the head; Rāṃ in the right eye; Dhiṃ in the left eye.
*Keṃ* on the face; *Śrīṃ* on the heart. Thus is the ritual placement of the syllables (*varṇanyāsa*).
Śrīṃ at the four-petaled Mūlādhāra;
Vaṃ Śaṃ Ṣaṃ Saṃ; Rāṃ at the six-petaled Svādhiṣṭhāna; Kaṃ Bhaṃ.
Maṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ / Dhiṃ in the ten petals of Maṇipūra;
ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ.
Paṃ phaṃ; keṃ in the twelve-petaled Anāhata [cakra];
kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ.
Śrīṃ, in the pure sixteen-petaled [lotus]:
aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ ḷṃ ḹṃ eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ aṃ aḥ. O Śrī-Rādhikā, O Śrī-Rādhikā, O Śrī [lotus] of two petals!
"Lakṣam" means "in the command"; this refers to the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of that [mantra] consisting of the six wheels (*ṣaṭ-cakra*).
For meditation: One should meditate upon Gaurī, who holds a lotus in her hand, who dwells in the waters of the milk ocean,
whose hand is placed upon the neck of Kṛṣṇa, and whose lotus-face is smiling.
Thus is meditation.
Having first performed this and contemplated the identity (*aikya*) of the Guru, the Mantra, and the Deity, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) of the mantra.
For this recitation of that mantra consisting of a specific number [of repetitions], one should perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) amounting to one-tenth of that, and for that [homa], one-tenth again.
The libation (tarpaṇa) is one-tenth of that;
the sprinkling (mārjana) is one-tenth of that; the consecration (abhiṣeka) is one-tenth of that.

"I shall perform the offering of food to the Brahmins. Having taken scents, unbroken rice, and water with kuśa grass, and having performed the entire network of ritual placements (*nyāsa*), [one places them] upon the left hand of the goddess Śrī Rādhikā.
O protector of the most secret of secrets, accept this recitation performed by us;
O Goddess, may there be accomplishment for me; be gracious, O Śrī Rameśvarī!
With this mantra, one should offer the fruit of recitation and other acts of giving.
Now, he describes the ritual application for the offering of lamps;
Śiva said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the auspicious rite for the offering of lamps; by performing which, success in the five-syllable mantra will certainly be attained. (1)
One should draw the wheel consisting of the source of principles (nāyayoni), adorned with a bindu in its center;
at its front, one should depict a beautiful eight-petaled lotus. //2//
Having uttered "Salutation to Lalitā," one should worship the Mistress of the Maṇḍala, who is endowed with the circle of the earth and adorned with weapons at the intermediate directions.
[One should perform] the invocation, the installation, and the bringing into presence. 3 // (4–7)
One should likewise visualize the complete cessation of the Wheel Goddess. //8//
O Ācārya, one should cast a handful of flowers with the respective mudrās for each;
then, having brought a lamp made of gold or likewise of silver— (9)
Copper, bell-metal, iron, or even an auspicious earthen vessel weighing five *tolakas* is used for subjugation (*vaśya*), while one weighing ten *tolakas* is used for attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*). //10//
For subduing, fifteen *tolakas* are used; for killing, twenty *tolakas*;
but for all undertakings, twenty-five *tolakas* bring auspicious results. (11)
Having observed the gravity of the matter at hand—whether it concerns dharma, artha, kāma, or mokṣa, or victory and defeat in battle—one should employ a measure of thirty *tolas* or more. (12)
Having cleansed it with the Astra-mantra, one should fumigate it with the Mūla-mantra;
one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and consecrate it with the Mūla-mantra alone. //13//
One should fill [the vessel] with streams of fragrant ghee while reciting the root mantra;
O Great Goddess, in a formidable rite, one may also fill it with oil. 14.
One should properly prepare fragrant flowers and other offerings;
there, one should place a key measuring sixteen finger-breadths. //15//
The lamp that was made with a certain substance is also composed of that same substance;
having then prepared another lamp upon a hexagonal mandala, [one should proceed]. (16)
One should worship [the deities] from the Heart-mantra to the Weapon-mantra there in that mandala;
one should worship the eternal self-luminous light within that lamp.
One should offer a *añjali* with the words, "Salutation to the Eternal One, the Self-Luminous.
One should light a lamp upon the ground and worship it with ritual offerings (*upacāra*), such as perfumes and the sixteen [services]; thereafter, one should cause the lamp to blaze brightly. //18//
Following the sequence from left to right, one should prepare that pair of lamp-wicks as an unbroken whole for a period of up to five days. 19.
It should be made from the down of wild cotton, pure and firm in its structure, with a strong, unbroken thread spun by a young girl. (20)
The left [hand] with fifteen threads and the right with sixteen;
indeed, the brush must be made in this way for the sake of accomplishing all undertakings. //21//

In the rite of subjugation (vaśya), the southern wick should consist of eighteen threads, while the northern one consists of nineteen; in the rite of attraction (ākarṣaṇa), they consist of twenty threads.
For the purpose of enchantment (*mohana*), the right [hand] has one finger more than the left, with twenty-one fingers;
for killing (*māraṇa*), the right [hand] has one finger more than the left, with twenty-two fingers. //23//
The left [lines] should be calculated everywhere by adding one more to the right;
however, in the case of a grave matter concerning the Guru, one should use twenty-five wicks.
When the king of lamps has been lit for thirty, forty, fifty, or up to a hundred [instants], every desired purpose is accomplished. //25//
Whatever resides in one's heart, even if unattainable within the three worlds, a person brings that under the control of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa in an instant. //26//
And having first performed a great worship, one should offer a lamp.
One seeking a son obtains a son; one seeking wealth obtains wealth. [27] Thus, and so forth.
Now, he states the ritual procedure for the offering of the twin lamps:
Śrī Sanat-kumāra said:
O Brāhmaṇa, tell me in detail the procedure for the offering of lamps, by the mere performance of which Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa become pleased. (1)
Brahmā said:
Listen, my child, I shall describe in detail the gift of lamps;
it is the sole means for attaining the grace of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, of this there is no doubt. //2//
In the month of Kārttika, or Mārgaśīrṣa, or Pauṣa, or the month of Māgha, or Vaiśākha, it should be performed, preceded by the daily ritual bath. //3//
Having resorted to the pure abode, the enchanting field of the Siddhas, as well as Nandagrāma, Saṅketa, and the mountain Varaśānu. //4//
One should resort to one of these places—Govardhana, the pure Yamunā bank, or the wonderful [forest]—and there perform the ritual. //5//

O Sage, having performed his daily rites and other duties in the forenoon, a man should, after making a formal resolve according to the rules, prepare a spacious mandala suitable for the offering of lamps.

Having first fashioned a dot (bindu) joined with a square, and then having conceived an eight-spoked [wheel], one should then construct a sixteen-spoked [wheel] and then a thirty-two-spoked [wheel]. //7//
Construct a vast mandala with sixty-four sides, having properly laid out the circle of the earth according to the ritual procedure using five colors. //8//
O child, one should place a lamp in the center with the sixteen-syllable mantra;
one should have it fashioned from gold or silver as the embodiment of the Yugas.
If it is to be made of clay, one should joyfully fashion the lamp with earth from the excellent mountain peaks and from Nandagrāma. //10//

One should conceive of the lamp as arising from two elements and produced by those elements; therein, one should cause a stream of clarified butter, originating from the two fragrant substances, to fall. //11//
One should cause the clarified butter of both a black and a white cow to be placed [there], having consecrated it with the root mantra according to the sequence of direct and reverse order. 12.

Having prepared the clarified butter with the Mātṛkā mantra, one should place the wick therein; and at the commencement of any undertaking, one should employ a cotton wick produced from a village. //13//
Having properly placed a wick made of that same substance into ghee, and having thus prepared the lamp, one should worship the King of Yantras. //14//
One should worship the Son of Nanda with the eighteen-syllable mantra, and one should worship Rādhikā according to the rules with the sixteen-syllable mantra. //15//
At the conclusion of all the offerings, one should present a handful of flowers;
or else, one should worship Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa in the form of their physical images. //16//
Then one should light a lamp according to the prescribed method for lighting lamps;
one should worship the pair situated in the middle of the lamps with their respective mantras. //17//
In the quadrangle, one should always worship Lalitā and Viśākhikā,
as well as Rādhā and Anurādhā, according to the rules with perfumes and flowers.
Gopālī, Pālikā, and likewise Dhyānaniṣṭhā;
Somābhā, Tārakā, Śaivyā, Padmā, and Bhadrikā. //19//
On the eight-cornered [mandala], one should worship the eight [deities] according to the rules with perfumes and flowers;
then, having formed the yoni-mudrā, O Sage, one should prostrate with devotion. (20)
On the sixteen-sided [figure], one should worship Śyāmā, Mādhavī, Kamalā, as well as Kalā, Candrakalā, Candrā, and again Capalatā. //21//
One should worship Pramodā, Padminī, Pūrṇā, Paramā, Subhagā, Śubhā, Capalā, Vipulā, and Vāmā in sequence with perfumes and flowers. //22//
On the thirty-two-sided [lotus], one should worship Veṇī, Vaśinī, Suprabhā, Prabhā, Mālinī, Śālinī, Śālā, Viśālā, and Kanakaprabhā. (23)
Maṇḍinī, Maṇḍalāmukhyā, Jyeṣṭhā, Śreṣṭhā, Bhāminī, Tvaritā, Pārijāteśī, Sukalā, Surasā, and Rasā. //24//
Veśinī, Keśinī, Keśā, Sukeśā, Mañjaghoṣiṇī, Śubhāvatī, Kāntimatī, Kāntā, Bhānumatī, and Mudā. //25//
One should worship Vasudhā and Vasudhāmā in sequence with perfumes and flowers;
likewise, one should worship the sixty-four [deities] on the perimeter, as well as Paddhī and Poṣiṇī. //26//

She who has the luster of a lotus, who holds a lotus in her hand, who bestows boons, who grants joy, who removes affliction, who captivates, who acts, who is a stream, who sustains, and who paints with diverse colors. //27//
Lalāmā, Lulitā, Lobhadā, Sulocanā, Rociṇī, Suruci, Śobhā, Śubhrā, Śobhāvatī, and Sabhā. //28//

Upon the orb of the earth, one should worship the eight cowherd boys in sequence:

Then one should worship Citrā, the mistress of the first enclosure;
in the second enclosure, one should fully worship Vṛndā and Vīrā. //35//

And [he should worship] the auspicious Śrīmaj-jyotsnāvatī, the mistress of the seventh enclosure;
and on the right side of the lamp, Nanda and Yaśodikā. //38//
On the left, one should worship Kīrti and the cowherd Vṛṣabhānu;

O Lord of Sages, one should maintain a lamp for five days, or likewise for ten days; or one may protect the lamp for a fortnight, or even for a month. (40)
Then, having performed his daily rites, the wise practitioner should extinguish the lamp;

One should cause the king of lamps to float upon the auspicious waters of the Yamunā or similar rivers;
by performing this rite, one shall immediately attain all desires. //42//
By the power of the king of lamps, one directly realizes the couple;
through the mere worship of the lamp, there is nothing whatsoever that cannot be accomplished. //43//
Thus ends the fifth chapter, the procedure for the offering of the Couple-Lamp, from the Sanat-kumāra-saṃhitā.

Now, the hymn:
[The Royal Hymn of the Glance of Śrī Rādhā’s Grace] O you who are worshipped by the hosts of lords of sages, O remover of the sorrow of the three worlds!
O you whose lotus-face is serene, O you who sport on the grounds of the forest groves,
O daughter of the sun-like King of Vraja, O you united with the son of the King of Vraja— when will you make me here the recipient of your compassionate side-glance? //1//
Seated within a pavilion formed by a canopy of Ashoka tree creepers,
her delicate feet reddened by the luster of young sprouts and tender shoots,
her hands radiating the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, she is the abode of abundant prosperity.
When will you make me here the recipient of your compassionate side-glance? //2//

In that Nandana grove of the senses, where the minds of women— whose brows were curved in the auspicious play of the theater of love— were incessantly brought under subjection by the discharge of the arrows of their sidelong glances, accompanied by graceful charm and agitation.
When will you make me here the recipient of your compassionate side-glance? //3//
Her radiant and fair form is like lightning, gold, and the campaka flower;
the splendor of her face eclipses millions of autumnal moons; and her eyes are like those of young cakora birds moving amidst variegated paintings.
When will you here make me the recipient of your compassionate glance? //4//
O you who are intoxicated with the pride of youth, adorned with joy and self-confidence, colored by love for your beloved, skilled in the graceful display of arts,
desiring the kingdom of the forest groves which is blessed by no other, and expert in the art of amorous play!
When will you here make me the recipient of your compassionate glance? //5//
O you who are adorned with necklaces of steady, firm pearls and all manner of graceful gestures and expressions; O you with beautiful breasts like large jars of refined gold;
O ocean of bliss, filled with the powder of your most excellent and gentle smiles!
When will you make me here the recipient of your compassionate side-long glance? //6//
With vine-like arms dancing like waves upon lotus stalks and fibers, her gaze fixed on the blue eyes that flicker with the grace of a creeper’s tip,
she rests in a charming and enchanting union, swaying and shimmering.
When will you make me here the recipient of your compassionate glance? //7//
Upon her neck, which possesses three lines like a conch shell adorned with a golden garland,
there shines the radiance of the three jewels from the auspicious triple-thread necklace; her dark locks of hair, shimmering and entwined with clusters of flowers, fall gracefully.
When will you make me here the recipient of your compassionate glance? //8//
Upon her hips,
which possess the beauty of the trunk of a lordly elephant, there hangs a flower-girdle made charming by a cluster of excellent jewel-bells at its center.
When will you here make me the recipient of your compassionate glance? //9//
In which the lineage of royal swans of the assembly utters a sound more majestic than the tinkling of the beautiful anklets of Mañjughoṣā with her many mantra-chants,

When will you make me here the recipient of your compassionate side-glance? //10//
O Goddess worshipped by the lotus-born Brahmā who bows before the infinite realms of Viṣṇu;

When will you make me here the recipient of your compassionate side-glance? //11//
O Mistress of the sacrifice,

Having heard this wonderful hymn of praise, may the daughter of the Sun (Savitri) constantly make people the recipients of her compassionate glances;

Then there would be entry into the circle of the sons of the Lord of Vraja. //13//
On the full moon day, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight, on the tenth, on the eleventh, and on the thirteenth, he of purified intellect who recites this is himself Śiva. (14)
Whatever desire the practitioner longs for, that very thing he attains;

Standing in the waters of the Rādhā-kuṇḍa— reaching up to the thighs, the navel, the heart, or the neck— the practitioner who recites [the mantra] one hundred times, //16//

The Lord of Śrī Vraja grants entry into His eternal pastimes;

Thus ends the hymn to the compassionate sidelong glance of Śrī Rādhikā in the glorious Ūrdhvāmnāya. Now, the *Trailokyavikrama-kavaca* as declared in the *Saṃmohana-tantra* is written:
Śrī Pārvatī said:
That which was previously concealed by you in the Tantras and other works such as the Yāmalas—the wondrous Rādhā-kavaca named Trailokyavikrama—[is now revealed]. //1//
Therefore, O Lord of Gods, tell me this if I am dear to you:
[the rite] which directly bestows all accomplishments and grants the desired objects of the practitioner. //2//
Śrī Mahādeva said:
Listen, O beloved, I shall proclaim this armor (kavaca), which is difficult even for the gods to obtain; it has been concealed throughout the three worlds so that it might not be told to anyone. 3.
O Goddess, by whose grace I am the lord of all accomplishments, as are Vāgīśa, Hayagrīva, and the divine sage Nārada. (4)
By whose grace Viṣṇu is the sustainer of the three worlds, and by whose grace Brahmā creates the three worlds in an instant. //5//
I have attained the power of reabsorption; of this there is no doubt.
This is the armor named Trailokyavikrama, which is the embodiment of mantras. (6)
Listen to that, O Maheśānī, endowed with devotion and faith: Hari is the seer (ṛṣi) of this armor (kavaca) known as the "Prowess of the Three Worlds. //7//
The meter is Anuṣṭubh and the deity is Rādhikā, the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu;
the application (viniyoga) is proclaimed for the purpose of attaining the love of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. //8//
May Rādhikā protect my head; may the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu protect my crest-lock; may the Gopī always protect my forehead; may she who is the beloved of Govinda protect my eyes. (9)
May Ghoṣeśī protect their noses; may Vrajeśī protect their ears;
may Rati-kriḍā protect their cheeks; and may Gopikā protect their lips. //10//
May Gāndhārī protect the teeth; may Bhāminī protect the tongue; may Kīrtisutā protect the neck; and may Haripriyā protect the facial expression. //11//
May Gopeśī protect my arms; may Gopasundarī protect my feet;
may Kuñjeśī, the Queen of Rādhikā, always protect my right side. //12//
May she who delights in the Rāsa dance always protect my left side; may she who stays at the place of assignation protect my back, and she who wanders in the forest protect my navel. //13//

May the belly of the ninefold youthful [Gopīs] protect me; may the chest of the beautiful women of Vraja protect me; and may she who bestows the rasa of others' wives always protect my two shoulders. 14.
May Gopālī protect the crown of the head; may Gokuleśvarī protect all the limbs.
May Candrānanā protect the private parts; may Rādhā, beautiful in every limb, protect [the whole body]. //15//
May Śrīṃ Klīṃ Saubhāgyavardhinī always protect the Mūlādhāra;
Aiṃ Klīṃ Śrī-Rādhikā Svāhā, may She always protect the Svādhiṣṭhāna. //16//
Klāṃ klīṃ, salutations to Rādhikā; may she always protect Maṇipūra.
Lakṣmī, Māyā, Smara, and Rādhā—may they protect the heart at Anāhata. (17)
Klāṃ Klīṃ, may Rādhā, the embodiment of desire, protect me always;
may Rādhā protect my command; Haṃsa Klīṃ, may she who is dear to Agni protect me. //18//
Oṃ, salutation to Rādhikā, svāhā! May she protect the thousand-spoked [lotus] forever.
May Rādhā, consisting of eighteen syllables, protect me in every place. //19//
May the nine-syllabled [mantra] protect me above; may the ten-syllabled protect me in assembly;
may the eleven-syllabled protect me in gambling, in debate, and in dispute. //20//
May the twelve-syllable mantra protect [me] always at all times and in all places; may the five-syllable mantra of the Mistress of Rādhikā protect me constantly during the day. //21//
May Rādhā of the eight syllables protect me always at night;
may Pūrṇā Pañcadaśī Rādhā protect me within the circle of Vraja. //22//
Thus, O Pārvatī, this secret of Rādhikā has been narrated by me to you; it must be guarded with great effort, like one's own private parts. 23.
This bestower of great siddhis must not be given to just anyone;

There exists no divine armor on earth superior to this;
after reciting the armor, a person should thereafter worship the couple. //25//

Then, having offered a handful of flowers, one shall attain union with Rādhā; the preliminary practice (puraścaryā) for this mantra is proclaimed to consist of one hundred and eight recitations. //26//
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, one becomes the Lord himself manifest;

Svarūpa Haridāsa, Rūpāya, Raghunāthaka, Rūpa,
and the illustrious Sanātana— may they be my refuge in birth after birth.

Among all the abodes of the Lord, there is the Śrīmad-Vraja-maṇḍala, the sole dwelling place of the glorious Rādhā-Govinda—their feet are sought after by the Vedas and others, and they are unattainable even to Lakṣmī and the rest who are worshiped by Brahmā and the other principal deities.
The teacher of that Śrīmad-Vraja-maṇḍala is Śrī Rūpa himself; among the circle of Śrī Rādhikā’s dear joking companions, [he is known as] Śrī Rūpa...

Among Rati-mañjarī and the others, Śrī Rūpa-mañjarī is the foremost. By following her alone, one’s service of love—service which is inaccessible even to Keśava, Śeṣa, and others—becomes directed toward the lotus feet of Śrī Rādhā, the life-bond of [Kṛṣṇa]. In this regard:
The authoritative evidence for this is found in the *Manaḥśikṣā* of the venerable Śrī Raghunātha Dāsa Gosvāmī:
"He who loudly sings with a sweet voice this excellent *Manaḥśikṣā-daikādaśaka*, which accomplishes every goal— "
Being here in the forest of Gokula as a follower of Śrī Rūpa within the community,
such a person obtains the incomparable jewel of worshiping Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa.
In the *Śrī-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī* (10.1):
May all this that is being written by the power of his very command be for the pleasure of the virtuous Śrīmat-Caitanya-Rūpa.
In the *Śrīmad-Bṛhad-Bhāgavatāmṛta* (1.1.11):
"I am a compendium of the essence of the scriptures on devotion to the Lord,
as experienced through the form dear to that Divine Caitanya."
In that very same first section, in the commentary on (1.1.1):
"Obeisances to Caitanyadeva, who serves the nectar of his own name;
by taking refuge in whose form, people have attained the state of being composed of devotion."
In that very commentary, at the conclusion: "By all these labors of writing undertaken by myself,
may the Blessed Lord, who is the glorious Caitanya himself, be forever pleased."
The commentary on this [is as follows]: the illustrious Caitanya, renowned by the name Caitanya, is the son of Śrī Śacī;
he is either the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇadeva Himself, or His very form, or His very embodiment. Alternatively, [it refers to] the illustrious Caitanya’s...
His dear servant is Rūpa, the best of Vaiṣṇavas, who is indeed known by that name;
and from him comes the Blessed One.
[He knows] the future and the destiny of beings, as well as their coming and going.
He knows both knowledge and ignorance; he is the Blessed One of Speech.
This is the intended meaning; such is the general direction.
For example, in the *śrī-kṛṣṇa-līlā* within the context of the relationship between brothers, Kṛṣṇa and Baladeva shine forth, and in the *gaura-līlā*, Caitanya and Nityānanda shine forth.
In their respective roles as attendants, Rūpa and Sanātana are indeed well known to follow each of them accordingly;
yet, although there is no difference whatsoever among them, [they appear distinct].

Nevertheless, in accordance with the power of His divine play (līlā-śakti), this primary opinion of the lotus feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Caitanya should be understood; for instance, the command of Śrī Mahāprabhu in the *Caitanya-caritāmṛta* states:
"Alas, having abandoned my eternal wretchedness which was merely the name of a beggar, my heart has been torn by your wretchedness"—
thus it is said in the *Śrī-sandarbha* and other works.
In order to please the two saintly Śrīla Rūpa and Sanātana,
this is now analyzed by the southerner Bhaṭṭa.

From the *Sva-niyama-daśaka* of Śrī Dāsa Gosvāmī (verse 1): "In the guru, in the mantra, in the name, in the station of the son of the excellent Lord and Śacī, in Svarūpa [Gosvāmī], in Śrī Rūpa [Gosvāmī] accompanied by his associates, and in his first-born," and so forth.

For instance, at the conclusion of the *Śrī-sandarbha*, it says: "The followers of the feet of the venerable Lord Kṛṣṇa-Caitanya-deva, who are recipients of the honor of the assembly of all the kings of Vaiṣṇavas, such as Śrī Rūpa, Sanātana," and so forth.
Therein, [the reference is] to the great souls, the venerable Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja.
"Alas, Rādhā! Where indeed is Kṛṣṇa? Where is Lalitā? Where are you, Viśākhā? Alas, alas, Caitanya Mahāprabhu! Where indeed are you? Alas, Śrī Svarūpa! Where are you?
Alas, Śrī Rūpa and Sanātana!"—thus [they lament] day after day, and so forth.
In that regard,
it is written extensively in the work *Duṅhāra Milana* by the poet Karṇapūra, the son of Śivānanda Sena:
And regarding their meeting in the drama *Caitanya-candrodaya*, as it is said in verse 9.38:
"In the course of time, the news of the pastimes in Vṛndāvana has been lost; therefore, in order to proclaim that [news] specifically—"
The god sprinkled him there with the nectar of compassion,
as well as his own eternal form.
In that very regard, specifically concerning Śrī Rūpa, as it is said (9.29):
"He who was previously bound fast by the multitude of his beloved's qualities, yet was liberated from the attachment to home— being like a supreme rasa, both embodied and yet unembodied."
At Prayāga, the Lord favored Śrī Rūpa equally with incomparable expressions of love and the delights of firm embraces. 9.29.
In that very state, there is the movement of power, as it is said (9.30):
"In the beloved essential nature, in the cherished essential nature, in the essential nature of love, in the innate beauty..."
The Lord spread his own playful forms within his own uniform form that was suited to himself.
For it is said in the Caitanya-caritāmṛta:
"Out of fear of public scandal, the cowherd [Kṛṣṇa] performed ten horse-sacrifices;
through the power of his instruction regarding the cowherd of divine form, he caused the transfer of his own potency."

The entire conclusion regarding the principles of Kṛṣṇa, the principles of devotion, and the principles of rasa has been taught by the Lord as the established doctrine of the Bhāgavatam; furthermore, in that very place, while describing the narration of the middle pastimes:
In the middle of the Tārā [chapter], there is the movement of Śrī Rūpa’s power;
in the twentieth chapter, there is the meeting with Sanātana.
In this regard, there is a verse composed by Śrīla Rūpa Gosvāmī:
"O companion, this beloved Kṛṣṇa is he who met me at Kurukṣetra; likewise, I am that Rādhā, and this is the bliss of the union of the two."
Nevertheless, my mind yearns for the forest on the banks of the Yamunā, where He enjoys the fifth note of His sweet flute as it plays within His mouth.
"How have you, O fool, come to know my heart?"— saying this,
he embraced her with love; then the Lord took that very verse and showed it to her in his own true form.
To examine his form, he asked me about my inner state; how could I know the true nature of form?
Out of your grace, you have spoken of your own essential nature.
Otherwise, there would have been no purpose served by this knowledge; you previously showed me mercy, and by inference,
the Lord says that I shall meet Him at Prayāga.
Recognizing you here as a worthy recipient, my grace has descended;
I have transferred my power and shall speak this instruction to you, which possesses a special flavor.
Regarding the statement of its essential nature (*svarūpa*), it is said: "Upon seeing this verse, you have shown mercy; therefore, I have understood [it]," and so forth.
Thus it was stated by the venerable Śrī Jīva Gosvāmī (in *Śrī Mādhava-mahotsava* 2.106).
May he whose heart is full of compassion lead me— who am utterly base among all people— to the vicinity of his own lotus feet,
and cause me to dwell there repeatedly by means of the paths of his own worship.
I worship that form of Kṛṣṇa here, whose nature is honored.

In the *Śrī-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī* on verse 10.19.16, it is stated in the commentary: "The gopīs experienced supreme bliss upon seeing Govinda"— referring to *rati* (erotic love) which has ascended to the seventh stage, known as *bhāva*, *prema*, *sneha*, *praṇaya*, *māna*, *rāga*, *anurāga*, and *mahābhāva*.

The *Prapāka* composed by my venerable younger brothers [states]: "Having made Himself as many times as there were cowherd women right there, He became the *Ujjvala-nīla* who is not to be seen [by others]"; this has been clearly written by my excellent younger brothers in the *Śrī-lalita-mādhava* and other works within their commentary (*ṭīkā*).
And the commentary says:
He is indeed the younger brother by birth, but in the ultimate sense he is the superior;
for thus says Manu:
The giver of birth and the giver of the Veda—the giver of the Veda is the weightier father.
And in the Rudrayāmala it is said:
"The one who gives birth is called the Guru; the giver of the Veda is the Supreme Guru."
"From him [the Guru] comes the Parātpara-guru, and beyond that, the Parameṣṭhin," and so forth;
thus [it is said] in the *Śrī Hari-bhakti-vilāsa* (1.2), which collects the manifestations (*vilāsa*) of devotion for the sake of awakening.
Nanda’s disciple, the beloved of the Blessed One,
Gopālabhaṭṭa, while pleasing Raghunāthadāsa as well as Rūpa and Sanātana.
Even those who follow authoritative tradition have said: "I worship neither Rādhā nor Kṛṣṇa, nor do I worship Gaurāṅga;
may I become dust upon the lotus feet of Śrīmad-Rūpa in birth after birth."
Those virtuous people who are devoted to the service of the feet of Vṛṣabhānu’s daughter,
who are intensely passionate for the service of the son of Śrī Nanda, and who have taken refuge at the feet of Caitanya—
they remain in Vṛndāvana, always following after Rūpa.
Śrī Gopāla, Sanātana, and others rejoice by his command.
Endowed with the fivefold ritual acts, he should not worship other deities;
for that wise one, though devoid of [external] knowledge and rituals, follows the true form [of the deity].
The Gāyatrī mantra, the mantra of Rādhā, the supreme mantra of Kṛṣṇa,
the excellent mantra of the Great Lord, and likewise the name of Hari,
along with mental service— these are known as the five purificatory rites (saṃskāras).
Gopāla Bhaṭṭa, Raghunātha Dāsa, Śrī Lokanātha, and Raghunātha Bhaṭṭa—
these followers of Rūpa are the sons of Vṛṣabhānu’s daughter.
Śrīla Sanātana and others were devoted to service.
Furthermore:
I repeatedly bow to the pair of lotus feet of Śrī Sanātana,
by even a mere fragment of whose grace the nectar of devotion for Kṛṣṇa may arise.

And in the *Śrī-Ujjvala-nīlamaṇi* (1.1): "Victorious is the Eternal Self, the Lord, who attracts those who know the aesthetic relish by His name, who eternally kindles bliss through His character, and who bestows the festival of His own form."
In that ocean of the nectar of the rasa of devotion (1.1.3):
"May this ocean of the nectar of the rasa of devotion toward my Lord, whose body is eternal and who is the temple of rest, always bring joy."
Elsewhere, I bow to Gopāla Bhaṭṭa, whose everything is the feet of Govinda,
by whom the service [of the Lord] was revealed separately at the command of the illustrious Rūpa.
The divine Lord Śrī Rādhāramaṇa is considered the object of service;
He is this very one who was fashioned by the skillful Śrīla Rūpa.
The reason for this command was heard from the mouth of an authoritative person;
that indeed is well known:
[he appointed] the son of his brother, Kṛpālaya, to the illustrious Prabodhānanda.
I bow to that illustrious Gopāla Bhaṭṭa, the resident of Śrī Vraja.
I perpetually worship Śrī Jīva, who dwells in Vraja, who is devoted to the pair of feet of Śrī Rūpa, and who bestows bliss upon the dull-witted.
The Lord Rādhā-Dāmodara, fashioned by the hand of Śrī Rūpa,
was bestowed upon Jīva Gosvāmī by Śrī Rūpa, that ocean of mercy.
Victorious indeed are the venerable feet of Śrīmad Bhūgarbha Gosvāmī here in the district of Vraja,
by his nephew Lokanātha.
To the venerable Bhaṭṭa named Raghunātha, who was dear to Śrīmat Rūpa and by whom the flute and earring were offered to Śrī Govinda.
This is described in the *Śrī-Caitanya-caritāmṛta*: "I bow to the excellent Dāsa Gosvāmī, whose body is Rūpa and Advaita,
for whom the two feet of Śrī Govinda are the entirety of his millions of lives and his all-in-all."
Likewise:
"I pay homage to the venerable Paramānanda Bhaṭṭācārya, the abode of aesthetic flavor (rasa),
as well as to Rāmabhadra and Vāṇīvilāsa, my instructors."
I bow to those who are dear to Vṛndāvana and have taken shelter at the feet of Śrī Govinda;
I bow to the illustrious Lord of Kāśī, the protector of the world, the servant of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Thus, in the *Śrī-Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*:
"The worship of Śrī Govinda, who is the very form of the retinue of Śrī Rādhā-Gadādhara— the most beloved of Śrī Caitanya."
Of these two, Śrī Rūpa is the ocean of mercy and the true vessel for pure love;
may I always have devotion at his pair of lotus feet in Vraja.
The learned scholar named Śrīmad Gaurīdāsa was a devoted attendant of Lord Caitanya and was affectionately attached to the scholar Śrī Gadādhara.
Therefore, manifesting his friendship, he personally requested Śrī Hṛdayānanda Caitanya— the servant of that Lord— and brought him along.
The ocean of compassion bestowed upon him the authority of service;
he whom they indeed call the illustrious Gaurīdāsa, or Subala.
In the *Āryā-śataka* (verse 1), Śrī Karṇapūra Gosvāmī [describes:
"A blue water-lily for the ears, collyrium for the eyes, and a necklace of great Indra-stones for the chest."
Victory to Hari, the all-enchanting ornament of the beautiful women of Vṛndāvana!
In the *Śrīmuktācarita* (4):
By the power of association with him, this wonderful and excellent narrative of Muktā has been propagated by me.
May there be union for me with that King Kṛṣṇakavi in Vraja, birth after birth.
"Here shines the one entitled to the Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa Kuṇḍa, Śrī Karṇapūra Gosvāmī," and so forth.
To my infinite and supreme guru named Śrī Premikṛṣṇadāsa,
by whose mere fraction of grace the mind may become fixed on Śrī Govinda.
By the power of the Lord’s command, Śrī Rūpa, the ocean of mercy,
has offered his service to my guru, named Haridāsa, with great reverence.
The glorious Govinda, the son of Nanda and an ocean of compassion, is subject to the power of one's service; he begs for food accompanied by milk.

Furthermore, it is well known that once, during a spring day at night while he was wandering in the circle of the rāsa dance, he beheld the wondrous form of the daughter of Śrī Vṛṣabhānu as she moved about, and thereupon fainted at the foot of a tamāla tree.
He was indeed the attendant of that very beloved,
and it is said he was a certain servant of those two by name;
[he remained] in the service of his own people.
He exerts effort for the sake of entering into wisdom.
The illustrious and powerful King Mānasiṃha was solely devoted to the service of the feet of Govinda; he was a devotee at the lotus feet of Caitanya.
But King Pratāparudra, whose mind was intent on the service of sovereignty,
is this king whose mind is overcome by greed for the service of sweetness.
By him, a great temple was caused to be constructed with great effort;
even today, O King, his descendants remain devoted to the service of their Lord.
From the *Prārthanāmṛta* of Śrī Raghunātha Gosvāmī:
May I dwell eternally in Vraja for countless births, solely desiring the service of the feet of Śrī Rūpa and Ratimañjarī.
Following the *Gaura-gaṇoddeśadīpikā* composed by Śrī Karṇapūra Gosvāmī, the former names of some [of the associates] are recorded here (180–184):
She who was formerly known as Śrī Rūpa-mañjarī in Vṛndāvana...
Having become the Gosvāmī named Sādya-rūpa, he attained manifestation.

She who was formerly Rati-mañjarī, most beloved of Rūpa-mañjarī, has today become one whose body is non-different from Gaura; he is the eternal one, worshiped by all. A certain scholar called him Śrī-lavaṅga-mañjarī.
She who was Anaṅga-mañjarī has now become Gopāla-bhaṭṭa;
some say that Śrī Guṇa-mañjarī became Bhaṭṭa Gosvāmī.
Formerly, there was a Bhaṭṭa named Raghunātha, who composed [this work] concerning the Lord who dwells in the cottage by the Śrī-Rādhikā-kuṇḍa, [and] Rāga-mañjarī.
The elder sister of Dāsa Raghunātha was named Rasamañjarī;
the elder sister of Bhūgarbha Ṭhakkura was named Premamañjarī;
and formerly, there was the Gosvāmī named Lokanātha, whose elder sister was Śrī Līlāmañjarī.
In former times, Śivānanda Cakravartin [married] Lavaṅgamañjarī.
In the *Śrī-Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa-Gaṇoddeśa*, it is stated: "Kalāvatī, Rasollāsā, and Guṇatuṅgā reside in Vraja;
they are considered to be absorbed in their practice, singing the song composed by Śrī Viśākhā."
Govinda, Mādhava, Ānanda, and Vāsudeva were, in their respective order,
formerly the two maidservants of Rādhā during her playful dalliance with Rāga-lekhā.
Indeed, these companions, who have been inseparable from Śrī Vṛṣabhānujā throughout her previous and subsequent bodies, are Her dear jesting friends; yet, like maidservants,
they perform tasks such as massaging Her feet, providing water, and accompanying Her on secret trysts, as described in the *Vrajavilāsa-stava* within the *Stavāvalī*.
In order to obtain the special favor of serving him as she desires, Raṅgaṇavallī, Raṅgaṇamālā, and the others—
though they are her most affectionate friends— conduct themselves like maidservants.
Taking her bodice from the edge of the bed, Rūpamañjarī went out secretly and gave it to her dear joking friend.
As for that which is stated as "being a maidservant" (*dāsī*) in the *Śrī-Gaṇoddeśadīpikā* and other works—that is merely an expression of humility because the author himself composed those texts;
it was cited in the *Smaraṇamaṅgaladaśaślokī-vaiṣṇavaraṅgabhāṣya*. Śrī...
As described in the *Govinda-līlāmṛta* (23.89–91):
Śrī Rūpa and Ratimañjarī performed the massaging of their feet,
while other fortunate women fanned them with fans.
After they had thus attended upon him for a moment, they departed from the pleasure-pavilion;
those friends then fell asleep, each in her own bower of *kalpa*-tree creepers.
Led by Śrī Rūpamañjarī, the other maidservants devoted to her service lay down comfortably upon the paved courtyard outside the temple of her pastimes.
Furthermore:
Mañjarī, whose form is preceded by beauty, is a dear companion equal to Śrī Rādhā’s very life;
and Anaṅgamañjarī, whose name is preceded by Cupid, is renowned for being even dearer than her life.
She who is indeed renowned as the beloved of Hari, Mañjarī, intensely yearns for those lotus feet, desiring to follow them in the service of his lotus feet, beginning with the Rāsa dance.
May Śrī Rūpamañjarī, her follower Anaṅgamañjarī,
and those beloved of Hari, the Rāsamañjarīs, reside within my heart.
Now, the *Śrī-rūpa-mañjarī-aṣṭaka*:
She who is difficult for the multitude of people whose souls are perfumed by worldly intellects to attain;
she who is beloved by those experts in bestowing the jewel of the path of manifest passion.
May she, whose form is an eternal cluster of blossoms, who possesses a cage of parrots engaged in play with their beloved friends and companions, accept me. //1//

With a mind constantly elevated by compassionate thoughts for those humans devoid of devotion, her innate compassion flashes forth like a waterfall flowing with the nectar of the activities of the Moon of the Cowherd settlement.
May Mañjarī, whose form is her eternal body, accept me. //2//
May she who sprinkles her circle of friends, the daughters of Vṛṣabhanu, with the nectar of moral conduct;
whose mind leaps with joy at performing various services favorable to them at all times; and who brings auspiciousness in every way even to ignorant-minded people like me—[may she protect us].
May Mañjarī, whose form is her eternal body, accept me. //3//
Having arrived at the forest of Vṛndāvana by the command of Gauracandra— the sole life of the circle of saintly souls who travel the path of divine love,
and a wish-fulfilling creeper that satisfies the desires of devotees throughout the universe— [he remained there].
May Mañjarī, whose form is an eternal body, accept me. //4//
She is the singular, true mine of excellent virtues such as fortitude and profundity;
she is the gem upon the heart of the son of the King of Vraja, colored by her own love;
and she is the servant who eternally bears the mountain-like Rādhikā upon her head.
May Mañjarī, whose form is an eternal body, accept me. //5//
Those virtuous ones who dwell here with the desire for her lotus-feet,
their minds are constantly distressed by the longing to grant their own cherished desires; she, for her part,
regards all the cowherd beauties as equal to her own blood.
May Mañjarī, whose form is her eternal body, accept me. //6//

Her inner agitation stirred by mature passion, she is always trembling like a female bee; yet, conforming to worldly custom, she remains bashful— a drum proclaiming Kṛṣṇa’s fame which puts clusters of jasmine flowers to shame.
May Mañjarī, whose form is her eternal body, accept me. //7//

The dance-performance on the stage of union with the beloved Kṛṣṇa was attended by friends, enemies, and gopīs who were satisfied by the perfection of all secret, delightful pastimes, forms, and so forth, and who had attained full prosperity through them.
May Mañjarī, whose form is the eternal body, accept me. //8//
May he who, knowing the essence of his own purpose, recites these eight verses— which indicate but a mere fraction of the qualities of Rūpamañjarī—
be satisfied by the beloved of Rādhikā, her dear consort.
Herein is granted his fitness for the service of his own lotus-feet. //9//
Furthermore:
Those who have been excluded from the school of Śrī Rūpa, that ocean of mercy,
should certainly not be associated with by those traveling on the path of passion.
Their food— whether fruit, roots, or other gifts such as alms—
must not be consumed nor drunk, even if one’s life-breaths have reached the throat.
Because there is no finality in their own respective offices, nor in others who are merely [devoted] to them, those who are intent upon the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam have no other destination whatsoever.
O tongue, always speak what is called "form";
O mind, ever remember form as being the very nature of compassion;
O head, pay homage to form with a compassionate gaze.
His peerless and slender-bodied son, Raghunāthadāsa.
If there were indeed many births with the desire for the feet of Śrī Rūpa,
that has been accepted by us, and nothing else, both here and quickly.
May the beloved of Hari, who is full of compassion for Śrī Rūpa and Anaṅga-mañjarī, always manifest within the heart of me, whose refuge is none other than her, through her grace.

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled *Sādhana-dīpikā*, as uttered by Rādhākṛṣṇadāsa, a follower of the feet of Śrī Haridāsa Gosvāmī, the sovereign lord of the service of Śrī Govinda-deva. 8. ****************************************************************** (9)
Now, in the ninth chapter, the primary reality is being defined;
as stated in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (1.2.11):
Those who know reality declare that non-dual knowledge is the ultimate truth;
it is designated by such terms as Brahman, the Supreme Self (Paramātman), and the Blessed Lord (Bhagavān).
Among these three principles, the Blessed Lord alone is the primary one;
the Blessed Lord is the Blessed Lord himself,
and he is indeed Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the son of the King of Vraja, Govinda.
In this regard, the authoritative proof is as follows:
Lord Kṛṣṇa is supreme; his form is existence, consciousness, and bliss.
Govinda is without beginning, the beginning of all, and the cause of all causes. (1)
That which is Brahman is indeed the very form of its radiance,
just as the radiance belongs to the one from whom it proceeds throughout millions of cosmic eggs.

I worship that Govinda, the primordial Person, who is Brahman— partless, infinite, and the essence of all beings— who, though appearing divided through the manifold manifestations of the entire earth and other riches across millions of worlds, remains undivided. //40//
In that regard, the Bhagavad-gītā begins with "I am indeed the foundation of Brahman" (15.15) and so forth.
And that which is the Supreme Self is, moreover, a part of a part of this Blessed Lord, as stated in the second [chapter] (2.2.8): [He who knows Me as the unborn and the beginningless...]
Some [meditate on] the Person, four cubits in height, dwelling within the space of their own heart,
possessing four arms and holding a lotus, a discus, and a conch.
They remember the wielder of the mace through meditative concentration.

Regarding the identity of Kṛṣṇa and Brahmā, as stated in [BRS 2.3.218]: "Of those who partake in the likeness of the sun and its rays," and so forth; therefore, among the three principles (*tattva*), the supremacy of the Self-existent Lord, who is the form of the supreme principle (*parama-tattva*), is observed. Consequently...
Among the three types of yoga, bhakti-yoga alone is primary; as stated in the verse beginning "free from desire for anything else," it is accepted as being supreme.
As stated in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (11.11.48):
"O Uddhava, generally there is no means other than the yoga of devotion and the association of the saintly; for I am indeed the ultimate goal of the virtuous. And so forth.
In the *Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu* (1.2.1, 5):
That devotion is declared to be threefold—namely, the means (*sādhana*), the emotion (*bhāva*), and pure love (*prema*).
The one termed "the means" is further divided into two types: that which is based on scriptural injunction (*vaidhī*) and that which follows from spontaneous attachment (*rāgānugā*).
Among these, the predominance of those following through passion (*rāgānugā*) is as follows (BRS 1.2.281):
"Bound by some form of passion, these people, who are the beloveds of Him, go toward Him while worshipping Him; they are the nectar of His lotus feet, whose very nature is divine love (*prema*)."
