Surely, may the happiness of marriage envisioned by us be accomplished by you,
and through that, may the bliss of the rāsa-dance and other pastimes be attained.
Regarding this, he says "that which":
that for the sake of which you have performed the worship and observed the vow of the Noble One, the Power of Consciousness, Kātyāyanī.
The meaning of this which I have stated is that, by way of logical reasoning (*aupapattyena*), it is precisely the bliss of the *rāsa*-dance and other such pastimes;
through marriage and becoming a husband, the specific excellence of the bliss of the *rāsa*-dance and other such pastimes is not attained.

This is the intended meaning. "O virtuous ones" (*satīḥ*), meaning "O truthful ones" (*he satyaḥ*); even in the context of illicit union, you are in every way truly chaste (*sādhvyaḥ*), because your devotion is fixed on me alone—this is the sense.
In reality, they are not [merely] illicit lovers, for they are dearer even than those who are legally wedded.

Alternatively, "satīḥ" is an adjective qualifying the nights; the meaning is that they are the autumnal nights which bring about the manifestation of supreme rasa-bliss, and are devoid of cold, heat, and other such extremes, being filled with moonlight.

Or rather, he states that very greatness of the divine play (krīḍā): because even Satyabhāmā, Lakṣmī, Dharaṇī, and others performed the vow of worshipping the Noble One with this very goal of attaining the bliss of the rāsa-dance and other pastimes,
yet they did not actually attain that bliss.
This is the meaning: that which is delight is this vow;
the rest is the same.
By the venerable Śrī Jīva Gosvāmī’s feet: "Now, regarding the illicit love (*aupapatya*) of Śrī Kṛṣṇa manifested in Vraja..."
It is eternal. Furthermore, the status of Śrī Rādhikā and the others as *parakīyā* (belonging to another) is eternal.
There is no duality in their essential nature (*svarūpa*); however, when the non-material *dvāpara* age meets the material *dvāpara* age, [it appears] in its own form within Śrī Nanda’s...
When the manifestations, such as Vasudeva’s son and others, have assembled in Nandana, the manifestation of the *līlā* occurs.
As it is stated in the source (*Ākara*, LBhāg 1.5.438):
"That *līlā* is traditionally held to be manifest by virtue of being within the scope of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)."
But other such things, being beyond its range, appear unmanifest.
Furthermore, in the absence of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s status as a paramour, there would be an absence of excellence in aesthetic rasa; as it is said in the *Ujjvalanīlamaṇi* (1.19, 21):
"In this very [status] alone is the supreme excellence of the erotic sentiment established."
The lightness mentioned here applies to an ordinary hero;
it does not apply to Kṛṣṇa, who has descended for the sake of the sweet taste of the essence of rasa.
Therefore, in the Eleventh Canto (11.12.13):

"Desiring Me, though they did not know My true nature, these women attained Me, the Supreme Brahman, by virtue of their association with Me—hundreds and thousands of them. They regarded Me, their lover, as a mere paramour.
The commentary on this has already been composed in the *Svadaśaślokībhāṣya*.
In that regard, this is the underlying principle:
where, in accordance with the logic of the world—
It is both contradictory and contrary to the Dharma;
therein lies its lightness.
But where both of those are absent, [therein lies its heaviness].
In that regard, the supreme excellence of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) arises from causes such as numerous obstacles;
therein, because it contradicts the scriptures— such as the worldly injunction that one should never, even in thought, approach another's wife— it is sinful.

Because it is possible [for such a thing to occur], and for that very reason because it is contrary to dharma, there is the possibility of censure; furthermore, by its nature of causing shame, it is contrary to worldly norms.
Therefore, even by Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself [it was said in BhP 10.29.26]:...
For a woman of noble family, sexual union with another man is everywhere despised; it leads away from heaven, brings ill repute, involves hardship, and is fraught with fear.
By this, his own lack of attainment of heaven and so forth has been stated;
for even the noble queens of Vraja said: "Prostitutes abandon a man who has no wealth after having enjoyed and taken pleasure with him" (10.47.7).
Thus, that very [objection] has been raised;
however, in the case of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, since there is no contradiction with the scriptures, sin is impossible, and therefore there is no conflict with dharma.
Therefore, because it is irreproachable, shame and the like are impossible; nor is it contrary to worldly norms.

On the contrary, it is precisely what is most highly esteemed in the world. Thus, by reasons such as its frequent occurrence despite prohibitions, the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) possesses supreme excellence.

For it is understood that their engagement [in such acts] proceeded out of a singular devotion to Him, disregarding the world’s extreme and unbearable shame; and because that devotion is the very essence of the fruit of all sacred scriptures. In this regard, (10.33.29) "A transgression of dharma is seen among the powerful, as well as their audacity."
It is no fault for those who are more powerful, just as it is not a fault for fire to consume everything.

And so forth. Because of the authority of the word [of the scripture], even that which is contrary to worldly dharma is not [contrary to the truth], such as when [the Lord] was wandering in the forest with his attendants for the sake of tending the cows,
marked by the saffron from the breasts of the cowherd girls.

In this regard, the mention made by Akrūra of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s illicit relationship with his wife is indeed untenable, whether considered from the perspective of being his paternal uncle or from the perspective of being his servant.
However, it is only as something to be adopted; nor should it be said that a specific mention of joy was made [therein],
because no word expressive of that [joy] was employed.

Indeed, that Rāsa-līlā, which is sung in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavata and other Purāṇas within various assemblies of sages and kings as being consistent with reason, is certainly to be accepted as most excellent.
Not otherwise;
for their engagement in that single purpose of happiness is shown by the statement in the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam beginning with "O well-born one," and because of their delight in Him, all—

"The state of being the fruit of the treatise is as [stated] in that very same place: 'For the skillful indeed produce delight in you,'" and the commentary explains, "the skillful means those who are proficient in the treatises.
Furthermore, he provides an example of something belonging to another in the *Cākara* (UN 3.18):
Though they have found rest upon the noble path transcended by the outburst of passion,
their desired goals are worshipped by a multitude of virtuous women led by Arundhatī, who are colored by intense faith;
though they belong to the forest, the splendors of Lakṣmī are captivated by the fragrance of their sweetness.
"May those friends of Kṛṣṇa, who are distinct from the three worlds, grant you happiness. To the question "Who are they?", he says:
"They are considered to be of two kinds: maidens and married women belonging to others."
He speaks of the supreme excellence (UN 3.19):
"For here, the state of bliss of the Lord of Cows consists in the concealment of desire."
In this context, regarding the qualification "belonging to another" (*parakīyatva*):

therefore, although Śrī Kṛṣṇa, His abode, His time, His associates, His pastimes, and so forth transcend all worldly categories, nevertheless, in accordance with the world, within the pastime, [He manifests] as consisting of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānandamaya*). Śrī...

Just as the voiding of urine, feces, and so forth is accepted during sexual union, what fault is there in Manu and others— who are of the nature of the retinue for His pastimes— performing the taking of hands (marriage) with Her?
However, in actual physical union, there is indeed a fault.
And that does not exist, just as there has never been a union with the husbands of the cowherd women.
Therefore,
the inhabitants of Vraja considered each their own wives to be standing by their own sides.
Thus, he did not allow them to remain by his side, but rather had them occupy beds appropriate for a wedding;
nevertheless, through the power of yogamāyā, he caused the worldly and Vedic rites suitable for a marriage to be performed, and thus the taking of hands was brought about.
Furthermore, if one accepts a twofold manifestation of Gokula by way of both manifest and unmanifest forms, there would necessarily be a twofold nature of the divine pastimes (*līlā*);
yet, in their essential nature (*svarūpa*), those two do not possess such duality.

Therefore, even during His manifest pastimes with Śrī Rādhikā and the others, because Śrī Kṛṣṇa is *adhokṣaja* (transcendental), and because His retinue, time, pastimes, and so forth are expansions of His own essential potency (*svarūpa-śakti*) and thus possess attributes identical to His own, there is no difference between Him and them.
The state of not being an object of the sense faculties of discursive proliferation (*prapañca*) is its non-manifestness (*aprākaṭya*).

Therefore, through the power of self-luminosity and manifesting by its own will, it becomes manifested; yet, because of the determination that "it is not an object of the eyes, even though [the eyes] are [its] eyes," such is the case for it.
And their state of being objects for the senses of the manifest world is their "manifestness" (*prākaṭya*).
For this very reason, it is said in the *Śrī-laghu-bhāgavatāmṛta* (1.5.391–2):
"That [the Lord], whom even today His own dear ones, afflicted by longing, desire to behold..."
Then Kṛṣṇa, the ocean of mercy, would display various divine pastimes to them.
Even today, Kṛṣṇa is seen sporting within the heart of Vṛndāvana by certain supreme devotees who have become overwhelmed by love.

Thus, in this very Vṛndāvana, there is the direct perception of the pastimes that are beyond the scope of the phenomenal world. However, according to the view that the existence of Vṛndāvana is unmanifest (aprakaṭa), its direct perception here would be untenable, just as in the case of those who were led away to the Brahma-lake.

Furthermore, regarding the existence of the unmanifest Vṛndāvana— (Utkalikā-vallarī 66)— even the great ones, having attained your state and possessing acquired pure love, long for that indescribable grass-hut birth therein.
Since I, though born of base lineage, have been granted residence here in the forest of Vraja by you, I praise that very grace of yours which extends even to the wretched.
Likewise, in the *Śrī-gāndharva-samprārthanāṣṭaka* (verse 1),
there is an inconsistency [if this were not the case] regarding the statement: "While the two of them are sporting here in the pleasure grove of Vṛndāvana," and so forth.

This being the case, as for the perception of forms such as the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*) as having the form of a neem tree (*nimba*) and so forth, that is like the saying: "Even sugar becomes bitter to one whose sense of taste is impaired by bile. [The same applies to] the eye—
Just as one sees a conch shell as yellow due to a defect,

and just as the light of the sun— which is of the nature of pure illumination— acts as a manifestor of darkness for owls, so too, in those who are unworthy and at fault, there is a non-manifestation of its true nature.
And because it is the general rule.

Regarding this, some say that since Śrī Kṛṣṇa is a paramour (aupapatti), Śrī Rādhikā and the others must be "belonging to another" (parakīyā); furthermore, they argue: "Indeed, that excellence of being a paramour and so forth which has been described by the illustrious authors of the scriptures..."
However, that [work] was composed by the authors solely through the desire of another, and not according to their own preference;
for it would otherwise contradict their own aspirations.
As it is said in the *Utkalikāvallī* (45):
O Prince, Lord of the Assembly, when you have approached the female musician together with your companions and are joyfully stealing her garland of flowers,
I shall suddenly enter before you and forcibly behold your face with its hidden smile.
When will [someone] snatch away from your breast the upper garment of you, Bhānumatī?
For in this case, it is not possible for her to steal his flower as if it were her own, nor for him to pull at her upper garment as if it were his own friend's.
Likewise, in the *Kārpaṇya-pañjikā* (35), it is said:
"Searching for one another, when shall I meet you two within the heart of Vṛndāvana and receive a charming reward?"
Likewise: "When,
due to our dependence on our elders, we shall find it difficult anywhere even to look at one another,
I will gladden you both with the wine of mutual messages."
In this context as well, mutual searching and the gazing at one another occur only in relation to the *parakīyā* (the wife of another);
thus [it was said] regarding the illustrious Mahāprabhu’s most intimate devotee, Śrī Raghunātha...
As stated by Dāsa Gosvāmī in the *Vilāpa-kusumāñjali* (88):

"O sweet-faced one, here your brother Śrīdāman, having out of affection given you a vehicle drawn by two bulls and having satisfied the wretched Jaṭilā at the moment of the full moon known as Rakṣā— "

When I have been led away, my parents will run after me out of supreme affection, overwhelmed by the weight of happiness and sorrowful weeping; what further pampering could they possibly provide for me here before them?
Thus it is said many times.

Furthermore, in Vraja, the opulent *śṛṅgāra* (erotic sentiment) of Śrī Kṛṣṇa in His fresh youth should be understood as being characterized by *mahābhāva*. And that [sentiment] manifests through its very nature even during a near separation, without a long-term absence.

By the maxim that "a moment becomes like an eon for those who do not see you," and by the maxim that "in separation, even a night of Brahmā passes like a single night," and by the maxim of a "twinkling of an eye" during the autumnal moonlight rāsa, [the time] occurred as if it were a night of Brahmā, and so forth.
And for this very reason, in the illustrious *Ujjvala-nīlamaṇi* (15.203),
a verse from the *Śrī-haṃsadūta* is provided as an example of one who has attained perfection.
Therefore, in the *Vidagdhamādhava* (1.36),
his appearance as being in the stage of *paugaṇḍa* is shown.
As in the passage beginning, "Now, for a calf whose mother has recently calved, what indeed could be the occasion for distress?",
[the object] is to be meditated upon precisely because fresh youth is ever-present.
As in the *Stava-mālā* (*Utkalikā-vallarī* 17), in passages such as "of the two dark ones, by virtue of the exquisite beauty of their fresh youth," and so forth;
therefore, [the milk] of Śrī Kṛṣṇa—

Because his nature as a "face" (mukhatva) is ever-shining, Śrī Vrajeśvarī and the others never made any effort to marry him; how much less so when his nature is characterized by the state of Mādana, which has ascended to the specific distinctions of Mahābhāva?
Furthermore, it must be stated that such [Mahābhāva] cannot exist without him.
As it is said in the words of the venerable Ṛṣis:
"I bow to the supreme pinnacle of the ecstatic emotion of Śrī Rādhikā and her companions—
that which, even without physical separation, produced a fourth state of union."
Here, [one attains] the pinnacle of existence in the form of *mādana*.
The definition of *mādana* is:
"This *mādana*, which causes the emergence and radiant manifestation of all states of being, is higher than the highest."
He who is the essence of the nectarean rasa always shines within Rādhā alone.
It cannot be described even by that Sage; therefore, it is sufficient [to know this].
Furthermore, those supreme distinctions of ecstatic emotion (bhāva) that manifest among the queens of Vraja have not been fully described here, as they lie beyond the scope of logical reasoning.
Thus, when there is a long-term or recent separation, the *sam̐bhoga* (enjoyment) becomes enriched by the manifestation of the longing for that long-term separation;
what wonder is there in this?
But then, how is it that the venerable Gosvāmīpāda [described] the enriched *sam̐bhoga* as being in the ever-new Vṛndāvana?
Why was it so stated? Because in the *Spaṣṭa-līlā*, there is the identification of Nanda’s son and Vasudeva’s son as one.
As it says (11.12.13): "Desiring Me, [the gopīs] regarded their lover, the paramour, as not being his true form..."
Thus, [the gopīs] said,
"O gentle Uddhava, go to Vraja and bring joy to our parents," and so forth. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Śrīmad-Ujjvala-nīlamaṇi* (15.185–6):
In accordance with the manifestation of a particular pastime of Hari,
this state of separation has been described for the beautiful-browed women of Gokula.
For Hari, who always sports in the forest of Vṛndāvana with the playful amorous pastimes such as the rāsa dance,
there is never any separation from the goddesses of Vraja.
Therefore, in the *Śrī-Rasāmṛta-sindhu* (2.5.128),
the hidden meaning of the *Śrī-Bhāgavata* and other scriptures has been revealed by the venerable Gosvāmīs, as follows:
This state of separation has been described in accordance with the manifest pastimes;
however, there shall never be a separation from Kṛṣṇa for the residents of Vraja.
For as it is stated in the *Yāmala*:
"Kṛṣṇa is one, and he who is born of the Yadus is another; he who is Pūrṇa is beyond even that.
Having abandoned Vṛndāvana, he never goes anywhere else. Thus it is said.

Manifest pastimes (*spaṣṭa-līlā*) reveal the single identity of Śrī Nanda and Yaśodā’s son with Vasudeva’s son; unmanifest pastimes (*aspaṣṭa-līlā*) or secret pastimes (*gūḍha-līlā*) reveal their distinction.
Therefore, by means of the associates (*parikara*) such as Śrī Nanda, Yaśodā, and others—

The journey to Dvāravatī and other places together with the Lord of Vraja and his associates should be understood as being like the passage beginning with "those who are portions [of him], such as Droṇa and others.
In the *Śrī-lalita-mādhava* (10.36),
there is a prayer by Śrī Rādhā:

There, upon that blessed land of Mathurā— which is surrounded by forests exhaling the fragrance of the nectar of your divine play and which shines with its own sweetness— may we dwell, our hearts charmed by the state of being playful cowherd girls.
Clad in [this], perceive the playful movement of the flute shining upon your face. 38.
Kṛṣṇa: My dear, let it be so. Rādhikā: How so?
(Kṛṣṇa looks toward the right, as if hesitating.)
(Entering with Gārgī, Ekānaṃśā suddenly throws aside the curtain.
Ekānaṃśā: Friend Rādhā, do not entertain any doubt.
Since you all reside right here in the glorious Gokula,
this was merely described by me in another way for the sake of passing the time;
let this be kept in mind.
"Let it be understood that Kṛṣṇa has indeed gone there.
Gārgī (to herself): "The words of my father have borne fruit through his kindness."

Just as in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam there is a clear manifestation of the oneness between Śrī Nandanandana and Vasudevanandana, so too in the Śrī Lalita-Mādhava there is a clear manifestation of the oneness between the one born from Vindhyādāra and the one born from Kīrtidā through their shared pastimes.
Just as Śrī Kṛṣṇa went in the form of Vasudeva’s son during the hidden pastimes (gūḍha-līlā), so too did Śrī Rādhā go in the form of Satyabhāmā;
and just as [Kṛṣṇa appeared] in the manifest pastimes (spaṣṭa-līlā) as Vasudeva—
In Nandana, there is the absorption (āveśa) of the two Nanda-nandanās; likewise, in Śrī Satyabhāmā, there is the absorption of Śrī Rādhā.

Now, since there is no "preliminary passion" (pūrva-rāga) in the unmanifest pastimes (aprakaṭa-līlā), a specific feature of the manifest pastimes (prakaṭa-līlā) must be required [there]. Since there is no "abundant sexual union" (samṛddhimān sambhoga) in the manifest pastimes, a specific feature of the unmanifest pastimes must be required [there]. Therefore—
There may be a twofold nature of Gokula by way of its manifest and unmanifest manifestations;
is it the same for the pastimes (*līlā*)? To that, he says: if the opulent enjoyment (*sambhoga*) has not occurred there in the manifest pastimes, then for that purpose—
A specific, unmanifest pastime is to be expected;
it had already occurred there, as it is said: "After the slaying of Dantavakra, He dwelt here for two months in the bliss of delightful pastimes."
Furthermore, there is appropriate delight in one's own [wives],
and that [delight] culminates in passion;
therein, according to the distinction of caste—
Prosperous enjoyment (*sambhoga*) is not described as being like the essence extracted from juice; rather,
it is the pleasure (*rati*) capable [of occurring] with women belonging to others,
and that [pleasure] ends in the state of *bhāva*.
"Excellence [of rasa] arises from the excellence of the recipient; this is *rati*.
Thus, the *sambhoga* (enjoyment) stage, characterized by *rati* as its stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) and possessing full prosperity, is described as the very essence of rasa.
For this very reason, in the manifest pastimes (*prakaṭa-līlā*), the two [the Lord and His consort] have become possessed of the fullness of *pūrvarāga* (preliminary love).
What is the purpose of accepting a specific manifest pastime?
Furthermore, what are the pastimes pertaining to previous passion and so forth for one who has already become manifest?
They are currently unmanifest; what further purpose, such as the stage of "first love" (pūrvarāga) and so forth, would there be upon their manifestation?
When the divine play (līlā) is manifest, there is indeed the tasting of its abundant splendor.
Therefore, the claim that there is an inconsistency because of the specific nature of the manifest pastimes is incorrect;
however, in the science of aesthetics (rasa-śāstra), sexual union (sambhoga) is primarily associated with the night.
And he, possessing great prosperity, was born in the night, as previously described regarding "near" and "far" and so forth.
However, some [maintain that it was] after the slaying of Dantavakra, when [he was] in the full bloom of youth.
Youth is being considered;
the sequential play is eternal,
and that is expressed in the words, "My birth and action are divine."
Regarding the beginning: the calculation of the age of Śrī Nandanandana during that period has already been determined in the *Śrī-Vaiṣṇava-Toṣaṇī*.
That [calculation] extends up to one hundred and twenty-five years. The arrangement of that [period] is as follows in Vraja:
Eleven years [of age].
In that case, because there is no birth from the *sāvitrī* mantra, marriage does not exist due to its contradiction with the *dharma-śāstras*.
The meaning is that in the enjoyment of the pleasure of the *rāsa*-dance play, she is indeed "belonging to another" (*parakīyā*).
In Mathurā,
he spent twenty-four years;
even there, there was no marriage.
Then, immediately after the enjoyment with Satyabhāmā and the others,
[there was enjoyment] with the sixteen thousand maidens.
Thereafter, many sons, grandsons, and others were born.
Then, following the slaying of Dantavakra and the conclusion of his pastimes, he returned to Vraja; and there too—
In the opinion of some, marriage with Śrī Rādhā and others is accepted; that is incorrect,
according to the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam.
Because it has not been described anywhere [in the scriptures],
because there is an absence of the excellence of rasa due to the lack of prohibition by the circle of kinsmen,

and for that very reason, because there is an absence of the separation caused by activities such as grazing cattle, and because of the absence of pastimes such as the distribution of *rāsa* and bestowing honors.
There would be an absence of sending messengers and so forth;
for this very reason, since the feet of Śrī Rūpa have described fresh youth as being ever-present, there is no mention of marriage anywhere among the circles of Śrī Mahāprabhu’s personal associates.
Furthermore, because it has not been described [in those sources],
the description of the wedding in the *Lalita-mādhava* according to the view of the *Śrī-padma-purāṇa* is to be reconciled by means of a difference in *kalpas*.

Therefore, in the opinion of all, the manifest and unmanifest pastimes are indeed *parakīyā* (belonging to another) because they are eternal. Having accepted marriage, one considers the pastimes to be *aparakaṭa* (not hidden) by that very act, and thus maintains the eternality of the *svakīyā* (one's own wife). That is inconsistent. Because of the aforementioned reason, [there is] the constant milking of Śrī Kṛṣṇa by Śrī Vrajeśvarī and the others.
Because marriage is absent due to the manifestation of her being a maiden and the resulting lack of offspring born of the sun;
and because the state of being the most perfect, endowed with fresh youth, is always to be meditated upon by Śrī Rūpa Gosvāmī and others. That, however, [is] Śrī...
Because Kṛṣṇa did not go to Mathurā and other places;
and that Kṛṣṇa was another born of the Yadu lineage, and so forth.
For if he had gone to Mathurā and elsewhere, there would have been a fall from his state of being more complete and so on.
The constant nature of fresh youth as an object of meditation is as stated in the *Stavamālā* (Utkaṭikā-vallarī 17):
"Of the two dark-complexioned ones, by virtue of the beauty of their fresh age..."
"May the sweetness of you two, who are fair with stainless luster and fame and who are the crest-jewels of all that is beautiful, forever flash within my heart. And so forth.
In our view, however, having gone to Mathurā, Dvārakā, and other places in the form of the son of Śrī Vasudeva,
and after the slaying of Dantavakra, He returned again to Vraja; there, in His self-manifested form as the son of Śrī Vrajendra, He performed the manifestation of His divine pastimes.
However, it was understood that after three months, they would have direct union with Kṛṣṇa;
as for him, his state of being both manifest and unmanifest had already occurred previously.
It was written: "Therefore, [this applies] to the son of the illustrious Lord of Vraja, who is the manifestation of Pūrṇatara and the rest;
but not in Mathurā, Dvārakā, and so forth."
Therefore, because the manifest and unmanifest states of the woman belonging to another (parakīyā) are eternal by virtue of her true nature,
there are many instances of present-tense usage, such as in the verse beginning "That abode of people triumphs" (tat tu jayati jananivāsa).
Thus, [regarding] Śrī Kṛṣṇa—

Among the circles of Caitanya Mahāprabhu, it is observed that Śrī Nityānanda, Advaita Ācārya, and others, following the *Śrīmad Bhāgavatam*, accepted the eternal nature of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s conjugal pastimes in Vraja— both manifest and unmanifest— and propagated this within their respective circles.
And among them, Śrī Gadādhara, Svarūpa, Rūpa, Sanātana, Bhaṭṭa, Raghunāthadāsa, Karṇapūra, and others,
having described the state of being "belonging to another" (parakīyatva) in various places within their respective collections of works according to their individual philosophical views;
It is seen to have been set in motion because its mere play (*līlā*) is eternal,
as expressed in such passages as "But that abode of living beings triumphs."

Likewise, Śrī Rāmānujācārya, Madhvācārya, and others establish that even the *līlā* (divine play) is eternal. Therefore, since the *līlā* as a whole is eternal, there is no fault in the eternity of its sequential manifestations; thus, the *parakīyā* [mādhurī] is eternal both in its manifest and unmanifest states.
That, moreover, is considered in its proper sequence:
the Lord Himself, the joy of the illustrious King of Vraja, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Caitanya.
He appeared in the year 1407 of the Śaka era; because he was the teacher of the world, he accepted the title of Ācārya.
Regarding his descent, he stated the primary cause in *Caitanya-caritāmṛta* (1.1.6):
Out of longing, [I wonder]: "What is the greatness of Śrī Rādhā’s love that it can be tasted by me alone? What is the nature of my own wonderful sweetness?
And what kind of bliss does she experience when she perceives me?"
"From that state, the moon-like Hari was born from the ocean of Śacī’s womb," and so forth.

As for the secondary cause, it is the removal of the demonic nature of those great sinners who constitute the burden of the earth, and the inauguration in the Kali age of the primary dharma known as the chanting of the Name.
"His measurement [is given] for the sake of favoring His devotees," and so forth.
Therefore, Śrī Nityānanda-advaita Gadādhara is the very form of the Lord's own nature.

Having manifested His own personal associates, beginning with Sanātana, and having established the religious duties of the age through them, He again engaged for forty-eight years in manifesting the primary cause [of liberation] and the tasting of the primary rasa together with them.

The relish (*āsvādana*), however, is in accordance with the essence of all Vedānta as found in the Śrī Bhāgavatam; for that [pastime] is eternal, whether manifest or unmanifest. And therein [it is said]:
"Having expanded Himself into as many forms as there were cowherd women... (10.33.19).
That Blessed One, though delighting in the Self, sported with them for the sake of divine play.
Thus it has been stated many times.

Therefore, the fact that the son of the Lord of Vraja was an illicit lover among the cowherd women, and that they were indeed "belonging to others" (parakīyā) in relation to him, is eternally manifest at the conclusion of the *krama-līlā*.
For the glorious Mahāprabhu Śrī Kṛṣṇacaitanya, having caused all the devotees to taste that very same relish,
tasted it himself.
In that regard, personal relish is as described in the *Śrī-caitanya-caritāmṛta* (2.1.11):
"The dramatic songs of Caṇḍīdāsa, Vidyāpati, and Rāya."
The *Karṇāmṛta*, the *Śrī Gītagovinda*—
day and night, Mahāprabhu danced and sang with Svarūpa and Rāmānanda in supreme bliss.

Because of the statement, "In the absence of this, by whose inspiration was I set in motion, even though I am of a wretched form," the purpose of the manifestation of the venerable Mahāprabhu was accomplished through the *Śrīmad-ujjvala-nīlamaṇi* and other works composed by the venerable Rūpa Gosvāmī.
Since the primary purpose of manifestation has been lost, the manifestation of Śrī Mahāprabhu would be purposeless;
therefore, [regarding] Śrī Mahāprabhu...
The state of being worthy of service by the most wise ones for one who has tasted [the nectar] is as follows,
in the *Stavāvalī* composed by Śrī Dāsa Gosvāmī (*Śrī Caitanyāṣṭaka*, verse 4):

The compassionate Lord, manifesting through His supreme mercies in Gauḍa that creeper of devotion— which was unknown even to the hosts of sages of old skilled in devotion, which is hidden from the Vedas, and which bears the fruit of the radiant nectar of love— [has appeared].
Will the son of Śacī set foot upon the path of my vision?
Therefore, by the venerable Śrī Rūpa Gosvāmī, who is an embodiment of the power of Śrī Mahāprabhu, it was promised in the *Śrī Smaraṇamaṅgala*—

which serves as a sūtra for the treatises such as the *Śrīmad Ujjvalanīlamaṇi*, *Śrī Vidagdhamādhava*, and *Dānakelikaumudī*, all of which consist of the playful amorous pastimes (*samarthā-rati-vilāsa*)— that [the work would describe] the life-breath of Śrī Rādhā...
Regarding the word "bandhoḥ" (of the friend):
thus it is said in the *Laghu-bhāgavatāmṛta* (1.5.448, 451)—"That pastime is considered manifest by virtue of being beyond the scope of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). Thus it is said.
Then, when the festival arranged by the Lord of Vraja had become manifest,
He revealed there His pastimes beginning with childhood in their proper sequence— those very same pastimes which He performs by the millions both in manifest and unmanifest realms.
Thus, the pastimes of others— whether manifest or unmanifest— are to be prayed for in works such as the *Stava-mālā*, the *Stavāvalī*, the *Gaṇoddeśa-dīpikā*, and so forth;
likewise by the assembly of the associates of Śrī Mahāprabhu.
Among the vast collections of works composed in both Sanskrit and Prakrit, there exist many types of authoritative evidence.
In this regard, the venerable Mahāprabhu, the supreme guru Śrī Mādhavendrapurī Gosvāmī Pāda, prayed at the time of attaining the state of the Blessed Lord:
O Lord, compassionate toward the wretched, O Lord of Mathurā, when will you be seen? My heart is distressed by the longing for your sight.
"My beloved is wandering about; what shall I do? and so forth.

His personal associates tasted these [verses] themselves in both public and private assemblies of Śrī Kṛṣṇacaitanya, and his disciples, grand-disciples, and others have continued to do so even now by means of those very texts.

They relish [the Lord], using present-tense expressions such as "Victorious is the Abode of Beings" (*jayati jananivāsa*) and so forth, because His pastimes alone are eternal. The authorities for this are, for example, the drama titled *Jagannāthavallabha* by the venerable Śrī Rāmānandarāya Gosvāmī Pāda.
The handiwork of Śrī Svarūpa Gosvāmī Pāda,
such as the *Premāmṛta-stotra* and other works by Śrī Gadādhara Paṇḍita Gosvāmī Pāda.
The *Śrī-kṛṣṇa-bhajanāmṛta* and other works of Śrī Narahari Ṭhakkura;
the *Padāvalī* and other works of Śrī Vāsudeva Ghoṣa; Śrī...
The *Śrī Bhaktiratnaprakāśa* and other works by the venerable Raghavapaṇḍita Gosvāmī; the *Bhaktiratnāvalī* and other works by the venerable Viṣṇupurī Gosvāmī; and so forth.
The *Śatanāmastotra* and other works of Śrī Sārvabhauma Bhaṭṭācārya-pāda,
and [the works] of Śrī Prabodhānanda Sarasvatī-pāda.

The works of the venerable Śrī Vṛndāvana-śataka and others by the feet of [Śrīla Sanātana Gosvāmī]; the *Śrī Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī* and others by the feet of the venerable Sanātana Gosvāmī; and the *Śrī Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu* by the feet of the venerable Rūpa Gosvāmī.
The Śrī-Ujjvala-nīlamaṇi, the Śrī-Vidagdha-mādhava, and so forth;
[the works] of the venerable feet of Śrī-Gopāla-bhaṭṭa Gosvāmī.
The *Bhāgavata-sandarbha*, the commentary on the *Śrī-kṛṣṇa-karṇāmṛta*, and so forth;
and the study of the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam* and other scriptures of devotion under the guidance of the disciples of the venerable Śrī Raghunātha Bhaṭṭa Gosvāmī Pāda.
The teaching of [these works], such as the *Muktā-carita* and *Stava-mālā* by the venerable feet of Śrī Raghunātha-dāsa Gosvāmī,
and the *Śrī-ānanda-vṛndāvana-campū* and *Śrī-kṛṣṇāhnika* by the venerable feet of Śrī Karṇapūra Gosvāmī.
The *Kaumudī*, the *Śrī-gauragaṇoddeśadīpikā*, the drama *Śrī-caitanyacandrodaya*, and others; as well as the *Śrī-kṛṣṇapremataraṅgiṇī* by the venerable Śrī-bhāgavatācārya,
wherein [the works of] the venerable Anantācārya...

The *Padāvalī* and other works by Pāda-śrī, Nayanānanda-pāda, and others; likewise, the *Caitanya-bhāgavata* and other texts composed by Śrī Vṛndāvana-Ṭhakkura—the son of the servant of Śrī Nityānanda-prabhu (who was born from the chewing of betel by Śrī Mahāprabhu)—and so forth. That, however, is as follows:
This was written by Śrī Nityānanda Prabhu under direct inspiration;
for it is said thus in the *Śrī Caitanya-caritāmṛta* (1.8.):
"Caitanya-līlāra," "Vyāsa," "Vṛndāvana-dāsa," and so forth—
thus, with the exception of Śrīmad Acyutānanda and others, those who opposed the views of Śrī Mahāprabhu were abandoned by the venerable feet of Śrī Advaitācārya, the son of Śrī Advaita Prabhu.
That, however, is well known from the *Śrī-Caitanya-caritāmṛta* and other sources.
Thus, while summarizing, [the author] refers to the *Śrī-* composed by Śrī Locanadāsa Ṭhakkura.

The *Caitanya-maṅgala*, the *Durlabha-sāra* and others; the *Śrī-govinda-līlāmṛta*, the *Śrī-caitanya-caritāmṛta*, the *Śrī-kṛṣṇa-karṇāmṛta-ṭīkā* and others, composed by the great soul Śrī Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja.
The *Catuḥślokī-ṭīkā* and other works composed by Śrīnivāsācārya, as well as the *Padāvalī* and other compositions by Śrī Narottamadāsa Ṭhakkura and Śrī Govindakavirāja, are renowned everywhere.

Thus, the collection of verses by Śrī Śyāmānanda and others residing in Utkala is well known. Furthermore, there was a certain direct servant of the mantra of the illustrious Mahāprabhu, who [was like] Śrī Rūpa, Sanātana, and the others.

And: regarding the evidence for his being a servant by virtue of the movement of his potency (*śakti-sañcāra*), it is found in the *Manaḥśikṣā* (7.12): "If you desire a residence in the land of Vraja at every birth, [then] here indeed [is he], followed by Śrī Rūpa and his associates."
"Residing in the forest of Gokula," and so forth—
from the first section of the *Śrī-Bṛhad-Bhāgavatāmṛta* (1.1.1): "Obeisances to Lord Caitanya, who relishes the nectar of His own name."
"By taking recourse to whose form," and so forth.
Then Śrī Jīva Gosvāmī Pāda, the nephew of Śrīmad Rūpa Pāda, made him a practitioner of the mantra from that [point].
However, that glorious Mahāprabhu did not have a vision of him;
for in his own book, he wrote that while Śrī Rūpa and others were unmanifest, they were considered both *parakīyā* (belonging to others) and *svakīyā* (belonging to oneself).
Among these, those who are *svakīyā* are the associates (*pārṣada*) of Śrī Caitanya, beginning with Śrī Raghunāthadāsa.
Those who are attached to Śrī Rūpa and others did not accept that;
however, that [work] of Śrī Jīva Pāda was not written according to his own will, but rather was written according to the will of another.
By virtue of his scholarship and by observing the sequence of his writing,
learned men accept it;
and those who have obtained the grace of the glorious Mahāprabhu, having attained [his favor]—

They, however, do not accept form and the other [sensory objects] as compassion in any way whatsoever; the propagation of this view is merely a matter of time. "I consider all of that to be a matter of time," and so forth.
And there is the saying, "Great blessings have many obstacles," and so forth.
Therefore, some say this: Śrī Jīva-pāda was indeed the son of his brother and also his disciple; thus, his own view is that he belongs to his own spiritual lineage (*svakīyā*).

Therefore, according to the principle stated in [Bhagavad-gītā 18.67], "Therefore, the gurus may speak even the secret to a devoted disciple," the opinion of the venerable Rūpa-pāda is indeed his own.
If this is so, then the venerable...
Hostility arose among the associates of Mahāprabhu;
however, Śrīman Mahāprabhu instructed Śrī Rūpa and Sanātana that they were His own.
However, since it is taught that in other cases they belong to others, this would be a more serious contradiction regarding the power of the venerable Śrī Rūpa Gosvāmī-pāda.
For all the disciples of the venerable Śrījīvapāda and others who were instructed by Sañcāra, [the lineage] is entirely that of another;
only within the circle of the venerable Śrījīva Gosvāmipāda’s followers is some wonderful thing seen here and there that contradicts the Guru.
Since even today, within those very lineages and among such disciples, one observes in their respective texts— both manifest and unmanifest— the influence of others; therefore,
[this applies] to the venerable Mahāprabhu and his associates as well.
It is considered that she is indeed the wife of another;
as for the fact that Śrīmad Jīva Pāda wrote that she is his own wife, that was solely by the will of another.
For this very reason, in the *Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-sandarbha*, after stating his own conclusions, he himself has asked for forgiveness for any faults therein through prayer. As it is said:
"Whatever has been wavered by me, who am most insignificant..."
May the glorious one, the beloved of Gokula, whose nature is forgiveness, forgive that.
Regarding that, he describes the tradition of the lineage of disciples: "There was a certain Vaiśya named Gopāladāsa, a dear disciple of the venerable Śrī Jīva Gosvāmī.
Overcome by his request, [the author] composed this from his own [experience]."
This has been established as the final conclusion;
for this very reason, in various places within the works of the venerable Rūpa, Sanātana, and others,
acts such as cutting [the hair] have been performed.
Having done so, I have also offered my apologies for my own faults here and there;
as was done in the *Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-sandarbha* and in the *Śrī-Laghu-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī* (at its very end), where it says: "Whatever has been wavered by me, who am most insignificant..."
This *Līlā-stava-ṭippaṇī*, which is a commentary on the *Līlā-stava*, is indeed the *Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*; it was composed by me, though I am most insignificant, at his command in a concise manner.
Whatever I have written here either through lack of understanding or with understanding, or whatever I have hastily cut away— may both of these be forgiven by the Supreme;
oh, what else indeed has been manifested in my mind?
If their strength consists merely of water, then what need is there for those whose families are filled with apprehension?
In the *Harināmāmṛta*, that name is clearly inscribed. As it is said:
"May he who revealed this work known as the *Harināmāmṛta* for such a purpose—may that friend of mine, named Gopāladāsa, be auspicious in both worlds."
And in the auspicious invocation of the *Śrī-Gopāla-Campū* (GCP 1.5): "May this work, known by the name *Gopāla-Campū*, bring joy on all sides to the cowherds who are the attendants of Śrī-Gopāla."

And in the commentary on the *Śrīmad-Ujjvala-Nīlamaṇi*: "Whatever has been written here by my own will and whatever by the will of others, that which possesses a connection between what precedes and what follows— let that which precedes be first and that which follows be subsequent."
And in the Śrī-Bhāgavata-Sandarbha, this is further analyzed by the southern scholar Bhaṭṭa, while pleasing the two saintly ones, Śrīla Rūpa and Sanātana. ||o||
Having thoroughly examined the first manuscript of that work—which was disordered, missing, and fragmentary—and having rearranged it, Jīvaka writes it down. //o//
And so forth.
A Brāhmaṇa from Gauḍa named Śrī Kṛṣṇadāsa was a disciple for the study of the sacred knowledge (vidyā) of Śrī Jīva, but not a disciple for the mantras.
Because he did not accept them as disciples.
If it is argued that his activity was directed toward making them disciples, then why did Śrījīva renounce the discipleship of Śrīnivāsa, Narottama, and others?
Therefore, while they remained unmanifest,
the servant of Kṛṣṇa himself, out of a desire for his own spiritual authority, manifested his discipleship under their mantras. Wherein was the cutting and so forth performed upon their books?
In some places it has been elaborated;

for this very reason, in works such as the *Śrī-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*, it is not accepted by all because it is a subject of doubt in various instances. Therefore, according to the maxim that "the invalidity of one implies the invalidity of the other," [this applies to] one's own...

In the Siddhānta, because it is not accepted by all the associates (pārṣadas) of Śrī Caitanya, whereas the view of the venerable Śrī Jīva Pāda—that it belongs to others (parakīya) due to its dependence on another—is accepted by everyone; thus, [the former] is considered consistent.
Thus [ends the work of] the servant of the feet of the venerable Haridāsa Gosvāmī, the master of service to the divine couple Śrī Rādhā-Govinda.

The Ninth Chapter of the *Bhakti-sādhana-dīpikā* uttered by the servant of Śrī Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa. **Chapter Ten:** At the outset, in order to clearly describe its specific excellence (*vaiśiṣṭya*), [the author says]:
The definition of supreme devotion is set forth according to the opinion of the virtuous.
That is to say:

supreme devotion is the practice of Kṛṣṇa in a manner that is free from desire for anything else and unobstructed by [the pursuit of] knowledge, ritual action, and so forth, performed in a way that is entirely favorable [to Him].
As stated in the Śrī Nārada Pañcarātra:
"Devotion is said to be the service of Hṛṣīkeśa by means of the senses, which is free from all adjuncts and rendered pure through being directed toward Him alone."
And in the third skandha of the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (3.29.11–13),
the characteristic of bhakti-yoga that is beyond the modes is indeed illustrated:
"That devotion which is causeless and uninterrupted toward Puruṣottama."
Even when offered the states of residing in the same world, possessing equal power, proximity, identical form, or even oneness with Me,
people do not accept them without My service.
That very same [discipline] is declared to be the ultimate yoga known as bhakti-yoga,
by which one transcends the three modes of nature and attains my own state of being.
The description of the excellence of the devotee found in the verse beginning with "sālokya" culminates in the definition [of devotion] through the manifestation of its purity.

It destroys the afflictions, bestows auspiciousness, and brings about lightness in liberation; it is extremely difficult to attain, its essence is a particular intense bliss, and it attracts the glorious Kṛṣṇa.
The greatness of the threefold devotion that will be described hereafter is proclaimed in succession by these six verses, taken two at a time.
Furthermore:
even a very slight inclination would indeed lead to the realization of the reality of devotion;
mere reasoning alone certainly cannot do so, because it lacks a firm foundation.
Regarding this, it has also been stated by the ancients:
"Even an object that has been established with effort by skilled inferents may be demonstrated in an entirely different way by others who are more proficient."
That devotion is said to be threefold: as practice (sādhana), as feeling (bhāva), and as love (prema).
In that regard, devotional service as a means (*sādhana-bhakti*) is that which is to be accomplished through effort; it is designated as a "means" because its state is something yet to be achieved.
However, the manifestation within the heart of that state which is eternally established is what constitutes the goal to be achieved.
That method of practice is said to be twofold: the prescriptive (vaidhī) and that which follows from attachment (rāgānugā).
Among these, the *vaidhī* [type of devotion] is that wherein engagement arises because of not yet having attained [the goal] through passion;
it is called *vaidhī* devotion because it occurs solely by means of the instruction of the scripture.
As it is said in the second [chapter] (2.1.6):
"Therefore, O Bhārata, the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Self, the Sovereign Hari,
should be heard, glorified, and remembered by one who desires fearlessness."

In this regard, the qualified person (adhikārī) is one who, by some extraordinary fortune, has developed faith in its service; he is neither excessively attached nor possessed of dispassion— such a person is qualified for this.
As it is said in the Eleventh Canto (11.20.28):
"If a person develops faith in My stories and the like by chance,
being neither despondent nor overly attached, for him the yoga of devotion bestows perfection."
Now, regarding *rāgānugā* (the path of following through passion):
that which follows after [the Lord] who is radiant and manifest among the inhabitants of Vraja and others,
being itself of the nature of passion (*rāga*), is called *rāgānugā*.

Commentary: The construction is as follows: "That devotion which is followed by a devotion consisting of passion (rāga), which shines among the inhabitants of Vraja and others, in such a way that it becomes clearly manifest and well-expressed;
this is what is called 'the path of passionate attachment' (rāgānugā). [End of] Vraja...
In the phrase "among the inhabitants of Vāsi and so forth," the word *jana* indicates human beings in general,
while the word *ādi* (and so forth) includes animals, birds, and the like.
Therefore it has been said: "Beholding this form, which is the good fortune of the three worlds, even cows, birds, trees, and deer bore horripilation."
"Shining forth" (*virājamānām*) means shining intensely;
it does not mean being overwhelmed by sovereignty, knowledge, and so forth, as is the case with other abodes or their attendants.
Regarding the word *anusṛta* (followed), "following" here consists of emulating the nature and activities of the eternally perfected residents of Vraja;
and that [emulation] culminates in being devoted to those who are themselves followed by Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s dearest ones.
"Following after in this way" is the resultant meaning; and that consists in being a performer of such service pertaining to body, speech, and mind, while remaining in accordance with him.
Dependence upon those most dear to Śrī Kṛṣṇa is described in the Eleventh Canto (11.3.21):

"Therefore, one who desires to know the supreme good should take refuge in a guru who is deeply learned in the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, who is firmly established in Brahman, and who is the abode of tranquility."

And the commentary states: "Desiring to know the highest good, [he approaches one] who is proficient in the Word-Brahman known as the Veda; for otherwise, due to the reason that he would be unfit to dispel doubts."
He is proficient in the supreme Brahman and in direct realization;
otherwise, because there would be an absence of the movement of awakening [regarding it].
Regarding his proficiency in the supreme Brahman:
He states that which indicates [the means] as "having tranquility as its support.
In that very context, the Blessed Lord said to the illustrious Uddhava (Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam 11.10.12):
"The teacher should be the lower fire-drill, and the student the upper fire-drill."
The teaching that brings about their union is the junction of knowledge, which bestows happiness.
Commentary: The first is the lower [fire-drill];
the joining of those two is the middle, which is the churning-stick—the teaching, that is, the instruction.
Knowledge (*vidyā*) is the understanding arising from the scriptures;
therein, [the teacher] is like fire existing at the junction (*sandhi*). Thus says the Śruti: "The teacher is the prior form, the pupil is the subsequent form," and so forth. Therefore, that—
"For the sake of knowledge, one should approach a teacher alone";
"A person who has a teacher knows"; "This is not to be attained by logic."
And there are such statements as, "The mind is to be withdrawn," and so forth.
Likewise, the arising of that state [of devotion] occurs only through association with a guru who is most dear to Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
and not otherwise.
This is the essential nature [of the spiritual master]. Therefore, it is said in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (11.17.27):
"One should know the spiritual master to be Me; one should never despise him.
One should not envy him with the notion that he is a mere mortal, for the guru embodies all the gods."
Regarding the statement, "The manifestation in the heart of an eternally established reality is the goal" (BRS 1.2.2),
this means that the manifestation of the eternally established reality within the hearts of the devotees who are its practitioners constitutes the goal (*sādhyatā*).

When the sweetness of such-and-such states of being and so forth is heard, the intellect requires that which is to be relied upon— the Guru— as stated in BRS 1.2.292. Regarding that [Guru] who is to be resorted to:
The sweetness of his being is seen most clearly;
when such a spiritual master, whose form is Śrī Kṛṣṇa, is beheld, greed arises spontaneously. As it is said in BRS 1.2.241: [text follows]
Washed by the waters of my gaze, his body adorned with a multitude of horripilations, stumbling yet blooming within, and even bearing a most intense trembling—
that certain man reached the very threshold of my eyes.
Since you have been born, why does your mind not find delight here in this home?
Now, it is generally the case that the guru of hearing and the guru of the instruction of worship are one and the same;
as it has been stated accordingly in the *Śrī Bhakti-sandarbha* (206):
"In that regard, one who regards the guru as oneself and as the deity should learn the *bhāgavata* duties through sincere devotion,
by which Hari— the Self and the giver of the self— is pleased" (BhP 11.2.21).
In this context, the Lord is the deity.
The necessity of a teacher for the instructions is also stated in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (10.87.33):

"Those who, though having conquered their senses and breath, strive here to restrain the extremely restless horse of the mind— which remains unsubdued— become exhausted by their lack of skillful means."
Afflicted by hundreds of calamities, they abandon the feet of their teacher and perish like merchants in the ocean who have not secured a helmsman.

Commentary: Those who, having taken refuge in the feet of the Guru, strive to restrain with their senses and vital breaths— which have been conquered due to their similarity to difficult terrain— the very horse of the mind that is exceedingly restless, intoxicated, and unbridled, in order to turn [the mind] inward toward the Blessed One.
They are exhausted by their methods; they weary themselves in those various methods. Consequently, they become possessed of hundreds of calamities.
For this very reason, they remain here, dwelling in suffering within the ocean of saṃsāra.
The meaning is that they reach [this state] in this very way; just as merchants who have not taken on a *karṇadhāra*— that is, those who have not engaged a navigator— [perish] in the ocean,
so it is in this case.

The sense is that when one understands the dharma of the Lord through the method of practicing devotion to the Lord as demonstrated by the glorious guru, and when, by His grace, one is no longer overcome by calamities, the mind very quickly becomes steady.
Now, in the Brahmavaivarta [Purāṇa]:
Through devotion to the Guru, He is met; through remembrance, He is served by the wise.
Even when met, He is not attained by living beings who are intent on egoism.

Therefore, the necessity of worshipping him is stated in the *Nārada-pañcarātra* as follows: "He who knows the teacher who proclaims Vaiṣṇava knowledge to be like Viṣṇu himself, and worships him with speech, mind, and body—he is a knower of the scriptures; he is truly a Vaiṣṇava."
"Indeed, even one who merely recites a single quarter-verse [of scripture] is always worthy of worship;
